docs.title: AddressSanitizer Memory Checking
docs.text:
C and C++ are very unsafe and error-prone programming languages. Address Sanitizer is a tool developed by Google for detecting memory access errors such as use-after-free and memory leaks. It has been integrated into GCC versions >= 4.8 and can be used for both C and C++ code. Address Sanitizer uses runtime instrumentation to track memory allocations, which means you must build your code with AddressSanitizer to take full advantage of its features.

  • Use after free (dangling pointer dereference)
  • Heap buffer overflow
  • Stack buffer overflow
  • Global buffer overflow
  • Use after return
  • Use after scope
  • Initialization order bugs
  • Memory leaks

This article will introduce the memory detection tool AddressSanitizer using the 8 scenarios above.

docs.title: 1.Use after free
docs.text:
Take the following code as an example. First, memory for one integer is allocated with the new keyword and its address is assigned to the pointer ptr. Then the memory is released with the delete keyword. However, after the release, the program still tries to access the freed memory through the pointer ptr and assign the value 10 to that memory location — this is a use-after-free error.

#include <iostream>

int main() {
  int* ptr = new int;
  delete ptr;
  *ptr = 10;  // Use after free
  return 0;
}

Add the following option at compile time.

-fsanitize=address

Run the generated binary and you get the following result.

docs.title: 2.heap buffer overflow
docs.text:
First, an array of two integers is allocated on the heap with the new keyword, and the array's starting address is assigned to the pointer arr. Then the program tries to store the value 10 in the third position of the array (index 2), which is outside the valid bounds of the array, causing a heap buffer overflow error.

#include <iostream>

int main() {
  int* arr = new int[2];
  arr[2] = 10;  // Heap buffer overflow
  delete[] arr;
  return 0;
}

Same usage as above:

g++-13 heap_buffer_overflow.cc  -Wall -g -fsanitize=address

Then:

./a.out

You get the following detection result.

docs.title: 3.stack buffer overflow
docs.text:
In the vulnerableFunction function, a character array buffer of 8 characters is defined. Then std::cin is used to read data from standard input into buffer, without limiting the input size. If the number of characters entered exceeds the size of buffer, a stack buffer overflow error occurs.

void vulnerableFunction() {
  char buffer[8];
  std::cin >> buffer;  // Stack buffer overflow
  std::cout << "You entered: " << buffer << std::endl;
}

Same usage as above.

docs.title: 4.global buffer overflow
docs.text:
The global buffer (the buffer array) is defined in the program's global scope without sufficient input-size restrictions. If the number of characters entered exceeds the size of the buffer, a global buffer overflow error occurs. Similar to a stack buffer overflow, a global buffer overflow can lead to program instability and security problems.

#include <iostream>

char buffer[8];

int main() {
    std::cin >> buffer; // ​全局​缓冲区​溢出​错误​
    std::cout << "You entered: " << buffer << std::endl;
    return 0;
}

Same usage as above, and you get:

docs.title: 5.use after return
docs.text:
In the function f, the address of the local variable i is returned, but in the main function, an attempt is made to access the already-destroyed local variable through the returned pointer. When this scenario occurs, the binary can be checked by setting ASAN_OPTIONS=detect_stack_use_after_return=1.

g++-13 stack_use_after_return.cc -Wall -g -fsanitize=address
ASAN_OPTIONS=detect_stack_use_after_return=1 ./a.out

The code:

#include <iostream>

int *f() {
  int i = 42;
  int *p = &i;
  return p;
}

int main() { return *f(); }

We then get:

docs.title: 6.use after scope
docs.text:
The address of the local variable x is assigned to the pointer p; however, after leaving that inner scope, an attempt is made to access the out-of-scope local variable x through the pointer p, causing a use-after-scope error. This is also undefined behavior.

#include <iostream>
int main() {
  int* p = 0;
  {
    int x = 0;
    p = &x;
  }
  *p = 5;
  return 0;
}

Compile and run:

g++-13 stack_use_after_scope.cc -Wall -g -fsanitize=address
ASAN_OPTIONS=detect_stack_use_after_scope=0  ./a.out

From my own testing, clang++ can detect it, while g++ cannot.

docs.title: 7.Initialization order bugs
docs.text:
In two different source files there is initialization involving the global variable a, but the order of initialization is unspecified. In the init_order_b.cc file, the value of a is used, but because the initialization order is inconsistent, undefined behavior can result.

The code is as follows:

// init_order_a.cc
int duplicate(int n) { return n * 2; }
auto a = duplicate(2);

// init_order_b.cc
#include <iostream>

extern int a;
auto b = a;  

int main() {
  std::cout << b << std::endl;
  return 0;
}

When we write code like this, the result is undetermined: it may be 4 or it may be 0, depending on the order of initialization.

For example:

clang++ init_order_a.cc init_order_b.cc  -Wall -g -fsanitize=address

This way the output is 4, while compiling b first and a second yields 0.

clang++ init_order_b.cc init_order_a.cc  -Wall -g -fsanitize=address

When this kind of problem occurs, we can use AddressSanitizer to check the initialization order.

ASAN_OPTIONS=check_initialization_order=true ./a.out

docs.title: 8.memory leak
docs.text:
Memory for one integer is allocated dynamically with the new keyword, but it is not released with delete before the program ends, causing a memory leak.

#include <iostream>

int main() {
  int* ptr = new int;
  // Missing delete ptr; // Memory leak
  return 0;
}

Set ASAN_OPTIONS=detect_leaks=1.

ASAN_OPTIONS=detect_leaks=1 ./a.out

docs.title: How to check memory, from C++​那些​事
docs.text:
When we write C/C++ code, memory problems are everywhere; both at work and in interviews, the topic of memory is inescapable.

Today, using one example, we will get hands-on with valgrind for checking C++ memory, step by step.

Three problems are simulated:

  • Detecting an invalid memory release
  • Detecting a write overflow
  • Detecting a read overflow

You will learn:

  • How to detect these three problems
  • How to debug with gdb + valgrind together

Feel free to join the discussion.

docs.title: 1. A sample to start with
docs.text:
Take a look at the code below; we will find quite a few problems:

  • strcpy is unsafe — no matter how large the memory is, it may overflow
  • msg is accessed out of bounds when printing
  • The destructor does not release memory

Doesn't it look just like code you once wrote yourself? Ha.

This section will detect these problems.

class Message {
private:
    char *msg;

public:
    Message(const char *text) {
        msg = new char[3];
        std::strcpy(msg, text);
    }

    void printOutOfRange() {
        std::cout << msg[5] << std::endl;
    }

    ~Message() {

    }
};

int main() {
    Message message("hello");
    message.printOutOfRange();

    return 0;
}

docs.title: 2.valgrind
docs.text:
Installing valgrind:

brew install valgrind // mac
sudo apt-get install install // ubuntu

For installation on more systems, see the official site:

https://valgrind.org/downloads/

docs.title: 3. Usage
docs.text:
First, when compiling, it is recommended to use debug, -g, so that you can detect which line of the code has the problem.

g++ val_test.cc -g

Then we execute:

valgrind --leak-check=full ./a.out

We then get the information valgrind gives us:

At this point, we can see several problems above:

  • Invalid write

Occurs at val_test.cc::11

  • Invalid read

Occurs at val_test.cc:10

  • Memory leak

1 allocs, 0 frees, 3 bytes allocated.

This information lets us quickly locate which line of code has the problem.

docs.title: 4. Debugging with gdb
docs.text:
When we add --vgdb-error=0, we can debug the code very conveniently — debugging on one side while seeing where the problems are.

valgrind --leak-check=full --vgdb-error=0 ./a.out

Afterwards, we attach with gdb

gdb -q a.out

Paste the target line above into gdb, then continue, and we can see the code for the corresponding line along with the further information valgrind keeps printing.

This section walked you through memory problems in practice. If it helped you, feel free to share it.

docs.title: 《C++​那些​事​》Hand-Written C++ Versions of Fn, FnOnce, and FnMut
docs.text:
If you write C++, you have surely used std::function, but have you ever thought about this: std::function can be copied and called over and over — so what if I want a callback that "can only be called once"? For one-shot events or a move-only task queue, std::function is a poor fit: it requires copyability, so things like unique_ptr simply cannot be stored in it.

Rust's design here is beautiful: the three traits Fn/FnMut/FnOnce separate closure mutability from call count crystal clear. So the question is: can we hand-write a C++ version? Hence this post.

docs.title: 1. Goal
docs.text:
We want to implement three class templates:

  • FnOnce<Ret(Args...)>: can be called only once; after the call the state is consumed (moved), and move-only captures are supported;
  • FnMut<Ret(Args...)>: can be called multiple times, with mutable captures;
  • Fn<Ret(Args...)>: can be called multiple times, with immutable captures, and is copyable.

The relationship among the three also copies Rust: Fn is a subset of FnMut, and FnMut is a subset of FnOnce. In other words, whatever Fn can do, the interfaces of FnMut and FnOnce can accept.

docs.title: 2. Design
docs.text:
The core is still the same old type erasure: the base class holds a virtual invoke, and the derived class wraps the real callable object. The differences lie in three details:

(1) the parameter of FnOnce::invoke is &&; once the call finishes, the wrapped closure is moved away, and calling again after the first call directly trips an assertion;

(2) FnMut::invoke is not const, which allows modifying the captures;

(3) Fn::invoke is const, and at the same time the derived class must provide clone to support copying the outer Fn.

template <class>
class FnOnce;

template <class Ret, class... Args>
class FnOnce<Ret(Args...)> {
 public:
  FnOnce() = default;

  template <class F>
  FnOnce(F functor) : impl_(std::make_unique<Model<F>>(std::move(functor))) {}

  Ret operator()(Args... args) && {
    return std::move(*impl_).invoke(std::forward<Args>(args)...);
  }

  explicit operator bool() const { return impl_ != nullptr; }

 private:
  struct Concept {
    virtual ~Concept() = default;
    virtual Ret invoke(Args&&... args) && = 0;
  };

  template <class F>
  struct Model final : public Concept {
    Model(F functor) : functor_(std::move(functor)) {}
    Ret invoke(Args&&... args) && override {
      return std::move(functor_)(std::forward<Args>(args)...);
    }
    F functor_;
  };

  std::unique_ptr<Concept> impl_;
};

There is a point interviewers love to catch here: operator() is restricted to being callable only on rvalues (the && qualifier), which together with std::move(*impl_) welds the semantics shut — want to call it? Move yourself out first. This is a "consuming callback".

FnMut and Fn loosen the restrictions on the same skeleton:

template <class Ret, class... Args>
class FnMut<Ret(Args...)> {
 public:
  Ret operator()(Args... args) {
    return impl_->invoke(std::forward<Args>(args)...);  // ​非​ const，​可改​捕获​
  }
  // Concept::invoke ​非​ const，​其余​同​ FnOnce
};

template <class Ret, class... Args>
class Fn<Ret(Args...)> {
 public:
  Fn(const Fn& other) : impl_(other.impl_->clone()) {}  // ​拷贝​走​ clone

  Ret operator()(Args... args) const {
    return impl_->invoke(std::forward<Args>(args)...);  // const
  }
  // Concept::invoke ​为​ const，​并​提供​ virtual clone
};

docs.title: 3. Conversion Relations
docs.text: We copy Rust's rules verbatim: Fn can convert to FnMut, and FnMut can convert to FnOnce; the reverse direction is not allowed. The implementation simply gives FnMut/Fn a way to construct from a stricter type, handing the internal impl over. That way, an interface taking FnOnce (say, one-shot task submission) accepts any closure, while an interface taking Fn (say, a repeatedly fired callback) only accepts immutable ones.

docs.title: 4. Tests
docs.text:
#include <cassert>
#include <memory>

int main() {
  // move-only ​捕获​：std::function ​塞​不​进去​，FnOnce ​没​问题​
  auto ptr = std::make_unique<int>(42);
  FnOnce<int()> take = [p = std::move(ptr)] { return *p; };
  assert(std::move(take)() == 42);

  // ​只能​调用​一次​：​再次​调用​断言​失败​
  // std::move(take)();  // crash: impl_ == nullptr

  // FnMut：​计数器​累加​
  int count = 0;
  FnMut<int()> mut = [&count] { return ++count; };
  mut();
  assert(mut() == 2);

  // Fn：​可​拷贝​、​可​重复​调用​
  Fn<int()> fn = [] { return 1; };
  auto copy = fn;
  assert(fn() == copy());

  return 0;
}

After it runs, you can compare it with std::function: putting a unique_ptr capture into a std::function fails to compile outright (it requires CopyConstructible), and that is exactly the reason this implementation exists.

The complete code has been placed in the Planet community; grab it there if you are interested. Finally, two questions to think about:

(1) Why does FnOnce::operator() need the && qualifier, and what would happen without it?

(2) Why must Fn's copy constructor go through clone instead of directly copying the unique_ptr?

docs.title: A Small gRPC Demo from C++​那些​事
docs.text: Popular RPC frameworks on GitHub include gRPC and brpc, along with Tencent's powerful internal trpc and others; these RPC frameworks support different languages and platforms. Today let's talk about how to use gRPC, starting from a simple demo. The whole project is built with CMake — a very standard way to manage an RPC project. All the code has been updated to the Knowledge Planet community; see the QR code at the end for how to get it.

docs.title: 1. Step-by-Step Environment
docs.text:
If your computer is a Mac, sorry — for now you cannot use the latest version of gRPC. The latest gRPC uses abseil, and compilation has problems that the official team has not resolved yet. If you know how to solve this, please leave a comment; I have not found a solution so far.

So, it is recommended to install a lower version of gRPC on your Mac, or install directly on Linux, where the latest gRPC works — installed in one go without any problems.

Installation:

git clone -b v1.57.0 git@github.com:grpc/grpc.git

Then initialize the submodules:

git submodule update --init

Build and install with CMake:

cd cmake
mkdir build
cd build
cmake -DgRPC_INSTALL=ON -DgRPC_BUILD_TESTS=OFF   -DCMAKE_INSTALL_PREFIX=/usr/local/grpc ../..

make -j8
make -j8 install // root ​权限​

You can change the installation directory above; note that root privileges are required at install time.

After installation, add its bin directory to your PATH, for example:

export PATH=/usr/local/grpc/bin:$PATH

docs.title: 2. String Reversal Demo
docs.text: With the environment ready, we can get our hands dirty.

docs.title: 2.1 The Protocol
docs.text:
The first thing is to define the RPC protocol:

syntax = "proto3";

package stringreverse;

service StringReverse {
    rpc sendRequest (StringRequest) returns (StringReply) {}
}

message StringRequest {
    string original = 1;
}

message StringReply {
    string reversed = 1;
}

A very simple protocol: you request with one string and get one string back.

docs.title: 2.2 The Client
docs.text:
Build the RPC request string, then just call the sendRequest interface to send it out.

std::string str = "hello world grpc!";
std::cout << "Original string: " << str << std::endl;
StringRequest request;
StringReply reply;
ClientContext context;
request.set_original(str);
Status status = stub->sendRequest(&context, request, &reply);
if (status.ok()) {
    std::cout << "Reversed string: " << reply.reversed() << std::endl;
}
// do something

docs.title: 2.3 The Server
docs.text:
Implement the string reversal logic by inheriting from Service.

class ReverseServiceImplementation final : public StringReverse::Service {
    Status sendRequest(ServerContext* context, const StringRequest* request,
                     StringReply* reply) override {
    // ​反转​逻辑​
  }             
}

Finally, just register the service:

builder.RegisterService(&service);
std::unique_ptr<Server> server(builder.BuildAndStart());
std::cout << "Server listening on port: " << server_address << std::endl;

docs.title: 3. Running
docs.text:
Create a build directory:

mkdir build
cmake ..
# ​输出​

docs.text: Last updated：2026-10-13

docs.title: C++ Inter-Process Communication in Practice
docs.text:
Inter-process communication is a very important topic, especially since many large projects bear its traces — for example, PostgreSQL uses pipes for inter-process communication during copy. In this section, based on this theme, we will use C++ to build a demo of two processes communicating through a pipe. This section combines the content of the previous few sections to give a fairly complete practical example:

  • mutex
  • condition_variable
  • thread

Note: the complete code for this section will be put in the Knowledge Planet community.

First, a very simple use of pipes:

  • Create a pipe

It handles creating a pipe, forking, and invoking the shell.

// FILE *popen(const char *command, const char *type);
pipe = popen(command.c_str(), "w");
  • Close a pipe
// int pclose(FILE *stream);
pclose(pipe);

Next, all we need to do is write into it and read from it. The principle is also very simple, for example:

This writes the data into the pipe created above.

// size_t fwrite( const void* buffer, size_t size, size_t count, FILE* stream );
size_t written = fwrite(data.c_str(), sizeof(char), data.size(), pipe);

To read from the pipe, we can use fread or fgets. fgets stops when it reads a newline character or reaches the buffer size, while fread reads as much data as possible until the specified number of bytes is reached or end-of-file is encountered. Similarly, the fwrite above can be replaced with fputs.

Now that the basic usage of pipes has been covered, how do we write a complete demo?

It's simple: we just create two threads, one for reading and one for writing. The writer thread writes data into the pipe, and the reader thread reads from it.

For example:

std::thread writer_thread(write_to_pipe);
std::thread reader_thread(read_from_pipe);

writer_thread.join();
reader_thread.join();

All the writer thread needs to do is call fwrite to throw data in:

ProcessWriter writer("cat > /tmp/pipe");

// ​写入​数据​
std::string message = "Hello pipe!\n";
if (!writer.write(message)) {
  std::cerr << "Failed to write data to pipe" << std::endl;
}

Similarly, the reader thread takes the data:

ProcessReader reader("/tmp/pipe");
// ​读取数据​
std::string message;
while (reader.read(message)) {
  // do something
}

The final result is:

Read from pipe: Hello pipe!

docs.title: C++ Short URL Service Demo
docs.text:
Real short URL services are relatively complex, involving things like hash algorithms and number-dispatching systems.

Today we are simply simulating a short URL implementation from the perspective of a small project.

How can you quickly implement one in just a few dozen lines of code? The key points involved are:

  • How to shorten a long URL
  • How to store the mapping relationship

The mapping relationship goes without saying — just use a map persisted in memory. If a database is involved, you need to write it into the database through interfaces such as the database's JDBC/ODBC.

For shortening the long URL, a random algorithm plus fixed-length approach is adopted here.

docs.title: 1. Randomness
docs.text:
Use uniform_int_distribution to generate a random number in the [a, b] interval. Here we randomly pick one character at a time from the string below, and the final concatenation is the short URL.

string characters{
      "abcdefghijklmnopqrstuvwxyzABCDEFGHIJKLMNOPQRSTUVWXYZ0123456789"};

It contains:

  • digits
  • lowercase letters
  • uppercase letters
uniform_int_distribution<int> distribution(0, characters.size() - 1);
string code;
for (int i = 0; i < length; ++i)
  code += characters[distribution(generator)];

docs.title: 2. Storage
docs.text:
Just store it in a map each time, for example:

if (links.count(originalLink)) {
  return links[originalLink];
}

shortCode = generateRandomCode(len);
string shortenedLink = base_url + shortCode;
links[shortenedLink] = originalLink;

The base URL is kept here, for example:

string baseUrl = "https://www.google.com.hk/search";
LinkShortener shortener(baseUrl);

string originalLink = "https://www.google.com.hk/search?q=asdsad&oq=asdsad&aqs=chrome.0.69i59j69i57j69i59l2.634j0j4&sourceid=chrome&ie=UTF-8";
string shortenedLink = shortener.shortenLink(originalLink, 8);

Finally, this URL can be shortened to:

https://www.google.com.hk/searchtXuOlOSt

Isn't that simple? The tests and complete code for this section have been updated in the Knowledge Planet community. Welcome to join and learn together~

docs.title: C++17 and SQLite Folder Size Statistics
Project Practice: Folder Size Calculation and Storage with C++17 and SQLite
docs.text:
This section unfolds around a project background: suppose your business needs to periodically check the size of certain folders and persist the results. How would you accomplish this project in C++?

This section walks you through a small project that uses C++17 and SQLite to implement a folder size calculation and storage system, helping you manage your file system better.

docs.title: Project Goals
docs.text:
We will implement the following features: 1. Recursively calculate the size of a specified directory and its subdirectories. 2. Save the calculation results to an SQLite database for easy subsequent querying and analysis. 3. Highly extensible: you can easily modify the project to add multi-threading support, optimize performance, or store the results in another database.

Note: lazy version — the complete code has been updated to the Knowledge Planet community.

docs.title: 1. Environment
docs.text:
First, you need to make sure the following tools are installed in your development environment: - A C++17-capable compiler: such as g++; you can check the version with the following command:

g++ --version
Make sure g++ supports the C++17 standard.

  • SQLite3: we will use SQLite for database operations; you can install it via a package manager: 
    sudo apt-get install sqlite3 libsqlite3-dev
    After installation, the SQLite development library libsqlite3-dev ensures we can use SQLite properly in C++.

docs.title: 2. Creating the Project Structure
docs.text:
We will split the code into several modules to keep a clear architecture: - folder_size.h / folder_size.cpp: responsible for recursively calculating the size of directories and their subdirectories. - database.h / database.cpp: encapsulates the SQLite database operation logic. - main.cpp: the main program entry, responsible for controlling the overall flow.

The project directory structure is as follows: 

project/
│── folder_size.h
│── folder_size.cpp
│── database.h
│── database.cpp
└── main.cpp

docs.title: 3. Code Implementation
docs.text: Next, we will implement each module step by step.

docs.title: 3.1 Directory Calculation Module
docs.text:
C++17 provides the std::filesystem library to recursively traverse directories and calculate sizes. So its core implementation is as follows:

uintmax_t total_size = 0;
for (const auto& entry : fs::recursive_directory_iterator(dir_path)) {
  if (fs::is_regular_file(entry.path())) {
    total_size += fs::file_size(entry.path());
  }
}

If you want to calculate the root directory, just calculate it once more.

docs.title: 3.2 SQLite Database Operations
docs.text:
Include:

#include <sqlite3.h>

Usage:

sqlite3_close(db_); // ​关闭​

// ​插入​
for (const auto& [folder, size] : folder_sizes) {
  const std::string insert_sql = 
      "INSERT OR REPLACE INTO FolderSizes (Folder, Size) "
      "VALUES ('" + folder + "', " + std::to_string(size) + ");";
  if (!ExecuteSQL(insert_sql)) {
    return false;
  }
}

// ​执行​
sqlite3_exec

docs.title: 4. Compiling and Running
docs.text:
Compiling the project is very simple:

mkdir build
cmake ../
make -j8

Then run the program to calculate the directory size and store it in the database:

./folder_size_calculator

The program will recursively calculate the size of the specified directory and save the results to the folder_sizes.db database.

docs.title: 5. Querying the Database
docs.text:
Finally, you can query the contents of the database through

the SQLite command-line tool:

sqlite3 folder_sizes.db
sqlite> SELECT * FROM FolderSizes;

This will display all the saved directories and their corresponding sizes.

End of this section

docs.title: Start Your Benchmark Testing with C++​那些​事
0. Introduction
docs.text:
Goal of this section: complete a small Benchmark project!

In everyday development, how do you test the performance of your own interfaces? How do you quickly set up a Benchmark testing framework in C++?

This section will get you started with Benchmark, step by step.

docs.title: 1. Project Structure
docs.text:
We will use vector versus list insertion as the example to explain the Benchmark project.

This project is managed with Bazel. If you don't know how to configure the related environment yet, please refer to the earlier video courses/documentation.

Create a project structure of:

Benchmark uses Google's open source project:

https://github.com/google/benchmark.git

In the past, using a third-party library meant compiling the source yourself, generating an so library, and then linking it — too much hassle! Here, using Bazel management, you only need to add the dependent git project in the WORKSPACE. For example, here we use version v1.7.1 of google benchmark.

git_repository(
    name = "google_benchmark",
    remote = "https://github.com/google/benchmark.git",
    tag = "v1.7.1",
)

After that, we need to implement the main logic. Create a src directory and add a BUILD file inside: the purpose is to compile the cpp files. Note: this depends on the benchmark library, and the usage is @the name configured above//:benchmark

cc_binary(
    name = "vector_list",
    srcs = ["vector_list.cc"],
    deps = [
        "@google_benchmark//:benchmark",
    ]
)

With that, you can use it in the cc file:

#include <benchmark/benchmark.h>

docs.title: 2. Demo Time
docs.text:
Write two insertion functions — very simple. The framework is shown below, with a few things worth explaining:

  • state is the runtime state information of the benchmark
  • for example: sleep control, input parameter control, and so on
  • state.range(0) gets the 0th parameter
  • DoNotOptimize means no compiler optimization
// ​测试​ std::vector ​的​插入​速度​
static void BM_vectorInsert(benchmark::State& state) {
    for (auto _ : state) {
        std::vector<int> v;
        for (size_t i = 0; i < state.range(0); ++i) {
            v.insert(v.begin() + i, i);
        }
        benchmark::DoNotOptimize(v);
    }
}

// ​测试​ std::list ​的​插入​速度​
static void BM_listInsert(benchmark::State& state) {
    for (auto _ : state) {
        std::list<int> l;
        for (size_t i = 0; i < state.range(0); ++i) {
            l.insert(l.begin(), i);
        }
        benchmark::DoNotOptimize(l);
    }
}

The main entry calls:

  • Range(8, 8 << 10) means starting from 8, multiplying by 8 each time, up to 8192. This corresponds to the state.range(0) above — the number is passed in as a parameter
  • BENCHMARK_MAIN means using google benchmark's main function. We know every executable has a main; the reason this file can execute is that this macro expands to the main function. Have you learned it?
// ​定义​基准​测试​
BENCHMARK(BM_vectorInsert)->Range(8, 8<<10);
BENCHMARK(BM_listInsert)->Range(8, 8<<10);

// ​运行​基准​测试​
BENCHMARK_MAIN();

docs.title: 3. Summary
docs.text: This section walked you step by step through google benchmark and applying it to our own project. You can do lots of interesting things with it. The source code for this section has been put into the Knowledge Planet community for everyone to learn from — welcome to join and discuss~

docs.title: A Modern C++ HTTP Server
docs.text:
Recently members of the Knowledge Planet community kept asking me whether I had any network-related projects, so I wrote a complete project based on modern C++ and managed with CMake.

The project has the following features:

  • Extensive use of modern C++ features
  • C++20 related
    • cortouine
    • concept
    • std::format
    • std::span
  • C++17 related
    • if statement initializers
    • structured bindings
    • optional
  • Efficient event-driven mechanism
  • Uses epoll to implement the event loop and manage large numbers of client connections. epoll is an efficient tool for handling high-concurrency I/O on the Linux platform; it can listen for events on multiple file descriptors simultaneously, effectively reducing system call overhead and improving the concurrency of I/O operations.
  • The server listens for connection events via non-blocking epoll_wait in the main event loop, avoiding the performance bottlenecks of traditional blocking I/O.
  • Coroutines and asynchronous programming
  • Adopts C++20 coroutines to simplify the implementation of asynchronous tasks, providing a way of writing that resembles synchronous code and making the logic clearer. The project uses co_await to asynchronously read and write client data, reducing the overhead of thread context switching.
  • Implements the two classes SocketAwaiter and AsyncSocketOperation to encapsulate asynchronous read and write operations on sockets, making it much simpler and more natural to write asynchronous processing code.
  • Asynchronous handling of file I/O operations
  • The server supports asynchronously reading the contents of HTML files. Asynchronous file reading is implemented with std::async to avoid blocking the main thread, so client requests can be responded to faster.
  • When handling requests, the required files are read asynchronously and cached in memory, reducing the impact of I/O operations on performance.
  • Non-blocking socket operations
  • Uses fcntl to set sockets to non-blocking mode, ensuring that accept and read/write operations do not block the server's main thread. This is especially important in high-concurrency scenarios and can significantly improve the server's concurrent processing capability.

docs.title: Protobuf ZeroCopy Serialization | C++​那些​事
docs.text: Last updated：2026-10-13

docs.title: 1. ZeroCopyStream
docs.text:
protobuf has something called ZeroCopyStream at the IO interface layer. For IO interface design, protobuf provides related serialization and deserialization interfaces, such as:

// Read a protocol buffer from the given zero-copy input stream.  If
// successful, the entire input will be consumed.
bool ParseFromZeroCopyStream(io::ZeroCopyInputStream* input);

// Write the message to the given zero-copy output stream.  All required
// fields must be set.
bool SerializeToZeroCopyStream(io::ZeroCopyOutputStream* output) const;

The original design intent of ZeroCopyStream is to minimize the number of buffer copies, that is, to omit copying the data inside the stream into the user's buffer. Therefore, the stream can return a buffer that actually points directly to the final data structure where the bytes are to be stored, and the caller can interact with this buffer directly, eliminating the intermediate copy operation.

For example, the classic IO stream:

char buffer[[]BUFFER_SIZE];
input->Read(buffer, BUFFER_SIZE);
DoSomething(buffer, BUFFER_SIZE);

Then the stream basically just calls memcpy() to copy the data from protobuf into the user's buffer. If we use ZeroCopyInputStream, we only need:

const void* buffer;
int size;
input->Next(&buffer, &size);
DoSomething(buffer, size);

Here no copy is performed; the caller ends up reading directly from the buffer.

ZeroCopyStream provides two base classes: ZeroCopyOutputStream/ZeroCopyInputStream.

Taking InputStream as an example, we can usually customize our own ZeroCopyStream by inheritance, implementing the following four interfaces.

// implements ZeroCopyInputStream ----------------------------------
bool Next(const void** data, int* size);
void BackUp(int count);
bool Skip(int count);
int64 ByteCount() const;

Some rpc frameworks basically all customize their own Stream, for example: sofa-pbrpc

https://github.com/baidu/sofa-pbrpc/blob/master/src/sofa/pbrpc/buffer.h

docs.title: 2. Demo
docs.text:
Define a protobuf protocol, for example: authentication:

syntax = "proto3";

message BasicAuth {
  string username = 1;
  string password = 2;
}

Then write the serialization and deserialization:

  • Serialization
BasicAuth auth_message;
auth_message.set_username("user123");
auth_message.set_password("password");

StringOutputStream output_stream(&buf);

auth_message.SerializeToZeroCopyStream(&output_stream);
  • Deserialization
ArrayInputStream input_stream(buf.data(), buf.size());
BasicAuth auth_message;
if (!auth_message.ParseFromZeroCopyStream(&input_stream)) {
    std::cerr << "Failed to parse data." << std::endl;
}

std::cout << "Username: " << auth_message.username() << std::endl;
std::cout << "Password: " << auth_message.password() << std::endl;

Then we can call it:

int main() {
    std::string buf;
    buf.reserve(512);
    ser(buf);
    deser(buf);
    return 0;
}

Output:

Username: user123
Password: password

docs.title: Accelerating Python with pybind11
docs.text:
Usually, for time-consuming operations we prefer to implement them in C++ and then have Python call the corresponding interface. Or, because of an underlying library, we need to expose a Python API to the outside. In these cases we typically need to support accessing C++ from Python — how do we do that?

There are quite a few ways. This section uses pybind11 as the example to introduce a complete project template. If you have this kind of need later, you can modify it based on the template.

Note: (lazy version) all the code for this section is also available in the Knowledge Planet community.

docs.title: 1. Macro Expansion
docs.text:
Suppose we take a rather time-consuming sort as the example. If we want to write a sort in C++ and then use it in Python, how do we write it?

The C++ program is fairly simple: expose an interface that does the sorting, for example:

std::vector<int> sort_vector(const std::vector<int>& input) {
  std::vector<int> result = input;
  std::sort(result.begin(), result.end());
  return result;
}

So here comes the question: how does pybind11 use this interface?

Just use a pybind11 macro to define a module, for example:

PYBIND11_MODULE(sort_module, m) {
    m.doc() = "pybind11 example plugin"; // Optional module docstring

    m.def("sort_vector", &sort_vector, "A function that sorts a list of integers");
}

After the macro expands, it is PyInit_sort_module.

When we import an xxx library in Python, the Python interpreter automatically calls the entry function for loading an extension module written in C/C++, and that entry function is the PyInit_sort_module below:

static ::pybind11::module_::module_def pybind11_module_def_sort_module [[maybe_unused]];

[[maybe_unused]] static void pybind11_init_sort_module(::pybind11::module_ &);

extern "C" [[maybe_unused]] __attribute__((visibility("default"))) PyObject *PyInit_sort_module();

extern "C" __attribute__((visibility("default"))) PyObject *PyInit_sort_module() {
    {
        const char *compiled_ver = "3" "." "11";
        const char *runtime_ver = Py_GetVersion();
        size_t len = std::strlen(compiled_ver);

        if (std::strncmp(runtime_ver, compiled_ver, len) != 0 || (runtime_ver[len] >= '0' && runtime_ver[len] <= '9')) {
            PyErr_Format(PyExc_ImportError,
                         "Python version mismatch: module was compiled for Python %s, "
                         "but the interpreter version is incompatible: %s.",
                         compiled_ver, runtime_ver);
            return nullptr;
        }
    }

    pybind11::detail::get_internals();
    auto m = ::pybind11::module_::create_extension_module("sort_module", nullptr, &pybind11_module_def_sort_module);

    try {
        pybind11_init_sort_module(m);
        return m.ptr();
    } catch (pybind11::error_already_set & e) {
        pybind11::raise_from(e, PyExc_ImportError, "initialization failed");
        return nullptr;
    } catch (const std::exception &e) {
        ::pybind11::set_error(PyExc_ImportError, e.what());
        return nullptr;
    }
}

void pybind11_init_sort_module(::pybind11::module_ & m) {
    m.doc() = "pybind11 example plugin";

    m.def("sort_vector", &sort_vector, "A function that sorts a list of integers");
}

So if we don't use this macro, importing the library will raise an error:

>>> import sort_module
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "<stdin>", line 1, in <module>
ImportError: dynamic module does not define module export function (PyInit_sort_module)

docs.title: 2. CMake + pybind11
docs.text:
pybind11 is used in C++ as follows:

  • Headers
#include <pybind11/pybind11.h>
#include <pybind11/stl.h>
  • Macro
PYBIND11_MODULE(sort_module, m) {
    // ​你​的​实现​
}

So how do you download and link pybind11 in CMake?

Just use the FetchContent module, for example:

FetchContent_Declare(
    pybind11
    URL https://github.com/pybind/pybind11/archive/v2.12.0.tar.gz
    )

Then add your module in CMakeLists:

pybind11_add_module(sort_module sort_module.cc)

CMake will download pybind11 for you and build it at the same time.

docs.title: 3. Usage
docs.text:
The above generates an so file. Install it into Python's site-packages directory, and it will be recognized on import. Below is a demo of our custom module:

import sort_module

def test_sort():
    input_list = [5, 2, 3, 1, 4]
    sorted_list = sort_module.sort_vector(input_list)
    print(f"Original list: {input_list}")
    print(f"Sorted list: {sorted_list}")

if __name__ == "__main__":
    test_sort()

Run:

(base) ➜  build python ../test.py
Original list: [5, 2, 3, 1, 4]
Sorted list: [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]

docs.title: C++ Stack Calculator Design
docs.text:
Write a stack calculator with the following design:

  • Supports the +, -, *, / operations
  • Supports postfix input

For example: 

2 3 +
Output: 
5
How do we implement it?

The two most crucial questions are:

1.How to tokenize

2.How to implement the stack

docs.title: 1. How to Tokenize
docs.text:
First, define the input as a string separated by spaces; then we can use istringstream to split out each token. The basic framework is:

std::istringstream iss(expression);
std::string token;
while (iss >> token) {
}

docs.title: 2. How to Implement the Stack
docs.text:
For a calculator, the core is pushing onto and popping off the stack.

  • Push when a number is encountered
  • Pop and calculate when an operator is encountered

We can then write the framework:

if (isNumber(token)) {
  pushNumber(token);
} else if (isOperator(token)) {
  popAndCal(token);
} else {
  throw std::runtime_error("Invalid token in expression.");
}

popAndCal is the core of the calculation, for example:

void popAndCal(const std::string& token) {
  if (operandStack.size() < 2) {
    throw std::runtime_error("Invalid expression.");
  } else {
    double operand2 = operandStack.top();
    operandStack.pop();
    double operand1 = operandStack.top();
    operandStack.pop();
    double result = performOperation(operand1, operand2, token);
    operandStack.push(result);
  }
}

Then what we want is stored in the stack, and finally we just return the top.

Isn't that simple? Feel free to discuss it with me.

docs.title: C++ Pure Virtual Functions and Abstract Classes
About the Author
docs.text: WeChat official account:

docs.title: 1. Pure Virtual Functions and Abstract Classes
docs.text:
A pure virtual function (or abstract function) in C++ is a virtual function that we do not implement! We only declare it! A pure virtual function is declared by assigning 0 in its declaration! 

// ​抽象类​
Class A {
public: 
    virtual void show() = 0; // ​纯虚​函数​
    /* Other members */
};

  • Pure virtual function: a virtual function without a function body
  • Abstract class: a class that contains a pure virtual function

An abstract class can only be used as a base class to derive new classes; you cannot create objects of an abstract class. Pointers and references of an abstract class -> objects of classes derived from that abstract class!

Code examples: abstract_base.h, pure_virtual.cpp

docs.title: 2. Implementing an Abstract Class
docs.text:
Inside an abstract class: a pure virtual function may be called from within a member function, but pure virtual functions cannot be used inside constructors/destructors.

If a class is derived from an abstract class, it must implement all the pure virtual functions of the base class before it becomes a non-abstract class. 

// A​为​抽象类​
class A {
public:
    virtual void f() = 0;  // ​纯虚​函数​
    void g(){ this->f(); }
    A(){}  // ​构造函数​
};

class B : public A{
public:
    void f(){ cout<<"B:f()"<<endl;}  // ​实现​了​抽象类​的​纯虚​函数​
};

Code example: abstract.cpp

docs.title: 3. Important Points
docs.text:
• A pure virtual function makes a class abstract 

    // ​抽象类​至少​包含​一个​纯虚​函数​
class Base{
public: 
    virtual void show() = 0; // ​纯虚​函数​
    int getX() { return x; } // ​普通​成员​函数​

private:
     int x; 
};

  • Pointers and references of abstract class type 

    class Derived : public Base { 
public: 
    void show() { cout << "In Derived \n"; } // ​实现​抽象类​的​纯虚​函数​
    Derived(){} // ​构造函数​
}; 

int main(void) 
{ 
    //Base b;  // error! ​不能​创建​抽象类​的​对象​
    //Base *b = new Base(); error!

    Base *bp = new Derived(); // ​抽象类​的​指针​和​引用​ -> ​由​抽象类​派生​出来​的​类​的​对象​
    bp->show();
    return 0; 
}

  • If we do not override the pure virtual function in the derived class, the derived class also becomes abstract 

    // Derived​为​抽象类​
class Derived: public Base 
{ 
public: 
//    void show() {}
};

  • An abstract class can have constructors 

    // ​抽象类​
class Base { 
    protected: 
        int x; 
    public: 
        virtual void fun() = 0; 
        Base(int i) { x = i; }  // ​构造函数​
}; 
// ​派生类​
class Derived: public Base 
{ 
    int y; 
public: 
    Derived(int i, int j) : Base(i) { y = j; } // ​构造函数​
    void fun() { cout << "x = " << x << ", y = " << y; }
};

  • Constructors cannot be virtual, while destructors can be virtual destructors 

    // ​抽象类​
class Base  {
public:
    Base(){ cout << "Constructor: Base" << endl; }
    virtual ~Base(){ cout << "Destructor : Base" << endl; }

    virtual void func() = 0;
};

class Derived: public Base {
public:
    Derived(){ cout << "Constructor: Derived" << endl; }
    ~Derived(){ cout << "Destructor : Derived" << endl;}

    void func(){cout << "In Derived.func()." << endl;}
};

    When a base class pointer points to a derived class object and the object is deleted, we may want the appropriate destructor to be called. If the destructor is not virtual, only the base class destructor gets called.

docs.text:
An abstract class is inherited and implemented by its derived classes!

docs.title: 1. A First assert Example
docs.text:
assert is a macro, not a function.

The assert macro's prototype is defined in (C) and (C++). Its effect is: if its condition returns an error, program execution is terminated.

assert can be disabled by defining NDEBUG, but this must be done at the beginning of the source code, before include . 

void assert(int expression);

Code example: assert.c 

#include <stdio.h> 
#include <assert.h> 

int main() 
{ 
    int x = 7; 

    /*  Some big code in between and let's say x  
    is accidentally changed to 9  */
    x = 9; 

    // Programmer assumes x to be 7 in rest of the code 
    assert(x==7); 

    /* Rest of the code */

    return 0; 
}
Output: 
assert: assert.c:13: main: Assertion 'x==7' failed.
As you can see, the output reveals the source file, the line number, and the location of the error!

docs.title: 2. Assertions vs. Normal Error Handling
docs.text:
• Assertions are mainly used to check for situations that are logically impossible.

For example, they can be used to check the state the code expects before it starts running, or to check the state after running completes. Unlike normal error handling, assertions are usually disabled at run time.

  • To ignore assertions, add the following at the beginning of the code: 
    #define NDEBUG          // ​加上​这​行​，​则​ assert ​不可​用​

Code example: ignore_assert.c

docs.title: About the Author

docs.title: What Is a Bit Field?
docs.text:
A "bit field" (or "bit segment") is a data structure that can store data compactly in bit form and allows the programmer to operate on the bits of the structure. One benefit of this data structure is that it saves storage space for each data unit; when a program needs thousands of data units, this approach becomes especially important. A second benefit is that bit fields make it easy to access part of the content of an integer value, which simplifies the program source code. The drawback of this data structure is that bit field implementations depend on the specific machine and system, and different platforms may produce different results, which makes bit fields inherently non-portable.

  • The in-memory layout of bit fields is machine-dependent
  • The type of a bit field must be an integral or enumeration type; the behavior of bit fields within signed types is implementation-defined
  • The address-of operator (&) cannot be applied to a bit field; no pointer can point to a bit field of a class

docs.title: Using Bit Fields
docs.text:
Bit fields are usually declared with a struct. The struct declaration gives each bit field member a name and determines its width:

struct bit_field_name
{
    type member_name : width;
};
Elements Description bit_field_name Name of the bit field struct type Type of the bit field member; must be int, signed int, or unsigned int member_name Name of the bit field member width The number of bits occupied by the member

For example, declare the following bit field:

struct _PRCODE
{
    unsigned int code1: 2;
    unsigned int cdde2: 2;
    unsigned int code3: 8;
};
struct _PRCODE prcode;

This definition makes prcode contain two 2-bit bit fields and one 8-bit bit field. We can assign to them using the struct member operator:

prcode.code1 = 0;
prcode.code2 = 3;
procde.code3 = 102;

Note that when assigning, the value must not exceed the capacity of the bit field member. For example, prcode.code3 is an 8-bit bit field member whose capacity is 2^8 = 256, that is, the assignable range is [0,255].

docs.title: Size and Alignment of Bit Fields
Size of a Bit Field
docs.text:
For example, the following bit field:

struct box 
{
    unsigned int a: 1;
    unsigned int  : 3;
    unsigned int b: 4;
};

There is an unnamed bit field in the middle of this bit field struct, occupying 3 bits, which serves only as padding and has no actual meaning. The padding makes the structure use 8 bits in total. But the C language uses unsigned int as the basic unit for bit fields, so even if the only member of a structure is a 1-bit bit field, the structure's size is the same as an unsigned int. On some systems unsigned int is 16 bits; on x86 systems it is 32 bits. The rest of this article assumes unsigned int is 32 bits.

docs.title: Alignment of Bit Fields
docs.text:
A bit field member is not allowed to straddle the boundary of two unsigned ints. If the total number of bits declared for the members exceeds the size of one unsigned int, the compiler automatically shifts the bit field members so that they align to unsigned int boundaries. For example:

struct stuff 
{
    unsigned int field1: 30;
    unsigned int field2: 4;
    unsigned int field3: 3;
};

field1 + field2 = 34 bits, which exceeds 32 bits. The compiler moves field2 into the next unsigned int unit for storage, leaving a 2-bit gap between stuff.field1 and stuff.field2; stuff.field3 immediately follows stuff.field2, so the structure is now 2 * 32 = 64 bits in size.

This hole can be filled with the unnamed bit field member mentioned earlier; we can also use an unnamed bit field member of width 0 to force the next bit field member to align with the next integer. For example:

struct stuff 
{
    unsigned int field1: 30;
    unsigned int       : 2;
    unsigned int field2: 4;
    unsigned int       : 0;
    unsigned int field3: 3; 
};

Here there is a 2-bit gap between stuff.field1 and stuff.field2, while stuff.field3 is stored in the next unsigned int, so the structure is now 3 * 32 = 96 bits in size.

For the accompanying code see: bit.cpp

docs.title: Initialization and Re-mapping of Bit Fields
Initialization
docs.text:
Bit fields are initialized the same way as ordinary structs. Two ways are listed here:

struct stuff s1= {20,8,6};

Or assign values to the bit field members directly:

struct stuff s1;
s1.field1 = 20;
s1.field2 = 8;
s1.field3 = 4;

docs.title: Re-mapping of Bit Fields (Re-mapping)
docs.text:
Declare a bit field with a size of 32 bits:

struct box {
    unsigned int ready:     2;
    unsigned int error:     2;
    unsigned int command:   4;
    unsigned int sector_no: 24;
}b1;

docs.title: Zeroing a bit field via re-mapping
docs.text:
int* p = (int *) &b1;  // ​将​ "​位域​结构​体​的​地址​" ​映射​至​ "​整形​（int*) ​的​地址​" 
*p = 0;                // ​清除​ s1，​将​各​成员​归零​

docs.title: Re-mapping a 32-bit bit field to unsigned int via a union (union)
docs.text:
First, a brief introduction to unions:

A "union" is a special kind of class and also a constructed data-structure type. Within a "union" you can define several different data types. A variable declared as being of this "union" type allows any of the data types defined by the "union" to be stored in it; these data share the same stretch of memory in order to save space.

A "union" has some similarities to a "struct", but the two are fundamentally different. In a struct, each member has its own memory space, and the total length of a struct variable is the sum of its members' lengths (empty structs excepted, and ignoring boundary adjustment). In a "union", the members share a stretch of memory, and the length of a union variable equals the length of its longest member. It should be made clear that this "sharing" does not mean loading multiple members into a union variable at the same time; it means the union variable may be assigned the value of any member, but only one value at a time — assigning a new value overwrites the old one.

We can declare the following union:

union u_box {
  struct box st_box;     
  unsigned int ui_box;
};

On x86 systems both unsigned int and box are 32 bits; through this union, st_box and ui_box share the same block of memory. Exactly which bit of the unsigned int corresponds to which bit of the bit field depends on the compiler and the hardware. To zero the bit field using the union, the code is as follows:

union u_box u;
u.ui_box = 0;

Learning reference: http://www.yuan-ji.me/C-C-%E4%BD%8D%E5%9F%9F-Bit-fields-%E5%AD%A6%E4%B9%A0%E5%BF%83%E5%BE%97/

docs.title: Implementing C++ Polymorphism in C | C++​那些​事
docs.text: Last updated：2026-10-13

docs.title: About the Author
docs.text: WeChat official account:

docs.title: 1. A C++ Implementation Example
docs.text:
Polymorphism in C++: C++ maintains a virtual function table, and by the assignment compatibility rules we know that a base class pointer or reference can point to a derived class object.

If a base class pointer or reference calls a virtual function of the base class, that base class pointer looks up the function address in its own virtual function table. If the base class pointer or reference points to a derived class object, and that derived class has overridden the base class's virtual function, then the pointer calls the derived class's overridden virtual function.

See the example code at: c++_examp.cpp

docs.title: 2. C Implementation
docs.text:
• Encapsulation

The C language has no concept of a class, but it does have structs, so we can consider using a struct to simulate one;

Use function pointers to encapsulate attributes and methods inside a struct.

  • Inheritance

Struct nesting

  • Polymorphism

The function pointers of a class and of its subclass differ

Inside a C-language struct there are no member functions, so how do we implement a function shared by the parent struct and the child struct? We can consider simulating it with function pointers. But that approach has a flaw: the parent's and the child's own function pointers point not to something like the virtual function table maintained in C++ but to a block of physical memory; if too many functions are simulated this way, it becomes hard to maintain.

To simulate polymorphism, the function pointer variables must stay aligned (identical in content and identical in variable alignment). Otherwise, a parent class pointer pointing to a child class object will crash at run time!

See the example code at: c_examp.c

docs.title: C++ const Constants and Qualifiers | C++​那些​事
docs.text: Last updated：2026-10-13

docs.title: About the Author
docs.text: WeChat official account:

docs.title: 1. The Meaning of const
docs.text: A const type is a type declared with the type qualifier const; the value of a const-type variable or object cannot be updated.

docs.title: 2. The Role of const
docs.text:
• It can define constants
const int a=100;

  • Type checking

    • The difference between const constants and #define macro-defined constants:

      A const constant has a type, so the compiler can perform safety checks; a #define macro definition has no data type — it is mere string replacement, so no safety check is possible.Thanks to the two experts who pointed out the problem here; see: issue

    • const constants support all types.

    • In other cases it is just a const-qualified variable; do not confuse it with a constant.

  • Preventing modification, providing protection and making the program more robust

void f(const int i){
    i++; // error!
}

  • Saving space and avoiding unnecessary memory allocation

    • A const initialized with an integral/enum type and a constant expression (i.e. a constant expression) behaves in use much more like a compile-time constant: if you never take its address and only use its value, it is usually optimized into an immediate, just like #define; only taking its address or an odr-use across translation units puts it into memory, and there is only one copy in the whole program.
    • After #define expands into a literal, it is compiled into instructions as an immediate; the instructions themselves occupy memory too, so multiple uses mean multiple occurrences (see the discussion in issue #5).
    • Note: not all const variables are constant expressions — only those of integer/enum type initialized with a constant expression are; other const variables are merely const-qualified variables (e.g. floating point, user-defined types); constexpr is the correct way to express compile-time constants.

docs.title: 3. const Objects Are Local to a File by Default
docs.text:
Note: non-const variables are extern by default. To make a const variable accessible in other files, it must be explicitly specified as extern in the file.

Accessing a variable not modified by const across different files

// file1.cpp
int ext;
// file2.cpp
#include<iostream>

extern int ext;
int main(){
    std::cout<<(ext+10)<<std::endl;
}

Accessing a const constant across different files

// extern_file1.cpp
extern const int ext=12;
// extern_file2.cpp
#include<iostream>
extern const int ext;
int main(){
    std::cout<<ext<<std::endl;
}

Summary:You can see that variables not modified by const need no explicit extern declaration! A const constant, however, requires an explicit extern declaration and must be initialized! Because a constant cannot be modified after its definition, it must be initialized at definition time.

docs.title: 4. Defining Constants
docs.text:
const int b = 10;
b = 0; // error: assignment of read-only variable ‘b’
const string s = "helloworld";
const int i,j=0 // error: uninitialized const ‘i’

The above contains two errors: + b is a constant and cannot be changed! + i is a constant and must be initialized! (Because a constant cannot be modified after its definition, it must be initialized at definition time.)

docs.title: 5. Pointers and const
docs.text:
There are four const forms related to pointers:

const char * a; // ​指向​const​对象​的​指针​或者说​指向​常量​的​指针​。
char const * a; // ​同​上​
char * const a; // ​指向​类型​对象​的​const​指针​。​或者说​常​指针​、const​指针​。
const char * const a; // ​指向​const​对象​的​const​指针​。

Summary: If const is on the left side of *, then const modifies the variable the pointer points to, i.e. what the pointer points to is a constant;if const is on the right side of *, const modifies the pointer itself, i.e. the pointer itself is a constant.

Another way to read it Read the English from right to left, taking "to" as the divider: what comes before "to" describes the pointer's trait, and what comes after "to" describes the target's trait 

const char * p; //p is a pointer to const char
char const * p; //​同​上​
char * const p; //p is a const pointer to char
const char * const p; //p is a const pointer to const char
When the pointer itself is qualified with const, the pointer can no longer change the address it points to When the target's type is char, the content can be modified through the pointer, e.g. *char='y'; When the target's type is const char, the content cannot be modified through the pointer

Concrete usage is as follows:

(1) Pointer to a constant

const int *ptr;
*ptr = 10; // error

ptr is a pointer to a const object of type int; the const qualifies the int type — the type of the object ptr points to — not ptr itself, so ptr need not be given an initial value. But you cannot modify the pointed-to object's value through ptr.

Besides, you also cannot use a void* pointer to hold the address of a const object; you must use a pointer of type const void* to hold the address of a const object.

const int p = 10;
const void * vp = &p;
void *vp = &p; // error

Another key point: it is allowed to assign the address of a non-const object to a pointer to a const object.

Assigning the address of a non-const object to a pointer to a const object:

const int *ptr;
int val = 3;
ptr = &val; // ok

We cannot modify the value of val through the ptr pointer, even though it points to a non-const object!

We cannot use a pointer to a const object to modify the underlying object; however, if the pointer points to a non-const object, the object it points to can be modified in other ways. The value pointed to by a const pointer can be changed — just not through the const object pointer! Modify it as follows:

int *ptr1 = &val;
*ptr1=4;
cout<<*ptr<<endl;

Summary:1. For a pointer to a constant, the object's value cannot be modified through the pointer.2. You cannot use a void* pointer to hold the address of a const object; you must use a pointer of type const void* to hold the address of a const object.3. Assigning the address of a non-const object to a pointer to a const object is allowed; to modify the value of the pointed-to object you must do it through other means, not directly through the current pointer.

(2) Constant pointer

A const pointer must be initialized, and the value pointed to by a const pointer can be modified, but its pointing cannot.

#include<iostream>
using namespace std;
int main(){
    int num=0, num1=1;
    int * const ptr=# // const​指针​必须​初始化​！​且​const​指针​的​指向​不能​修改​
    ptr = &num1; // error! const​指针​不能​修改​指向​！
    cout<<*ptr<<endl;
}

The code produces a compile error: a const pointer cannot change what it points to.

#include<iostream>
using namespace std;
int main(){
    int num=0, num1=1;
    int * const ptr=# // const​指针​必须​初始化​！​且​const​指针​的​指向​不能​修改​
    *ptr = 1;
    cout<<*ptr<<endl;
}

Nothing goes wrong with this code; it normally outputs 1.

Finally, when the address of a const constant is assigned to ptr, since ptr points to a variable rather than a const constant, an error is reported: a const int* -> int * error!

#include<iostream>
using namespace std;
int main(){
    const int num=0;
    int * const ptr=# // error! const int* -> int*
    cout<<*ptr<<endl;
}

If the above is changed to const int *ptr, or to const int *const ptr, both work fine!

(3) Constant pointer to a constant

Having understood the previous two cases, this one is fairly easy to understand:

const int p = 3;
const int * const ptr = &p;

ptr is a const pointer that then points to a const object of type int.

docs.title: 6. Using const in Functions
docs.text:
const qualifying a function's return value

This is basically the same in meaning as const qualifying ordinary variables and pointers:

(1) const int

const int func1();

This by itself is meaningless, because the return value is itself assigned to another variable!

(2) const int*

const int* func2();

The content pointed to by the pointer is immutable.

(3) int *const

int *const func2();

The pointer itself is immutable.

const qualifying function parameters

(1) The passed-in parameter and the pointer itself are immutable inside the function — meaningless!

void func(const int var); // ​传递​过来​的​参数​不可​变​
void func(int *const var); // ​指针​本身​不可​变​

This indicates that the parameter cannot be modified inside the function body, but here it has no significance: var is itself a formal parameter and will not change within the function. The same applies when the passed-in formal parameter is a pointer.

When an input parameter uses "pass by value", the function automatically creates a temporary variable to copy the parameter, and that input parameter never needed protection in the first place, so do not add const.

(2) The content pointed to by the parameter pointer is a constant and immutable

void StringCopy(char *dst, const char *src);

Here src is an input parameter and dst is an output parameter. After adding const to src, if a statement inside the function body tries to change the content of src, the compiler will point out the error. This is one of the effects of adding const.

(3) The parameter is a reference, to improve efficiency while preventing modification.

void func(const A &a)

For parameters of non-inner data types, a function declared like void func(A a) is bound to be rather inefficient, because the function body will create a temporary object of type A to copy the parameter a, and the temporary object's construction, copying and destruction all take time.

To improve efficiency, the function can be declared as void func(A &a), because "pass by reference" merely borrows the parameter's alias and needs to create no temporary object.

But the function void func(A &a) has a drawback:"pass by reference" may modify the parameter a, which we do not expect. Solving this problem is easy — just add const, and the function finally becomes void func(const A &a).

By analogy, should void func(int x) be rewritten as void func(const int &x) to improve efficiency? Not necessary at all: parameters of inner data types involve no construction or destruction, and copying is very fast — "pass by value" and "pass by reference" are nearly equal in efficiency.

Summary:1. For input parameters of non-inner data types, you should change "pass by value" to "pass by const reference" in order to improve efficiency. For example, change void func(A a) to void func(const A &a).2. For input parameters of inner data types, do not change "pass by value" to "pass by const reference". Otherwise you neither achieve the efficiency gain nor keep the function easy to understand. For example, void func(int x) should not be changed to void func(const int &x).

This settles two interview questions:

  • If a function takes a pointer, does that pointer need const, and what is the difference between placing const at different positions of the pointer;
  • If the function's parameter is an instance of a complex type, what is the difference between passing it by value or by reference, and when should const be added to the passed reference parameter.

docs.title: 7. Using const in Classes
docs.text:
In a class, any function that does not modify data members should be declared const. If, while writing a const member function, you accidentally modify a data member, or call another non-const member function, the compiler will point out the error, which undoubtedly improves the robustness of the program.

A member function specified with the const keyword is called a constant member function. Only constant member functions are qualified to operate on constants or constant objects; member functions not specified with the const keyword cannot be used to operate on constant objects.

const member variables of a class must be initialized through the initialization list, as shown below:

class Apple{
private:
    int people[100];
public:
    Apple(int i); 
    const int apple_number;
};

Apple::Apple(int i):apple_number(i)
{

}

const objects can only access const member functions, while non-const objects can access any member function, including const member functions.

For example:

// apple.cpp
class Apple
{
private:
    int people[100];
public:
    Apple(int i); 
    const int apple_number;
    void take(int num) const;
    int add();
    int add(int num) const;
    int getCount() const;

};
// apple.cpp
Apple::Apple(int i) : apple_number(i)
{
}
int Apple::add(int num)
{
    take(num);
    return 0;
}
int Apple::add(int num) const
{
    take(num);
    return 0;
}
void Apple::take(int num) const
{
    std::cout << "take func " << num << std::endl;
}
int Apple::getCount() const
{
    take(1);
    //    add(); // error
    return apple_number;
}
int main()
{
    Apple a(2);
    cout << a.getCount() << endl;
    a.add(10);
    const Apple b(3);
    b.add(100);
    return 0;
}
// main.cpp

Compile: bazel run basic_content/const/class_const/first_example:main

At this point an error is reported: getCount() is a const member function, and overload resolution inside it matches only the const version (int add(int num) const); only after that const version is commented out would the error come from calling the non-const add(). That is: const objects can only access const member functions, while non-const objects can access any member function (see issue #338).

When the call is changed to:

const Apple b(3);
b.add(); // error

This proves that const objects can only access const member functions.

Besides initializing const constants through the initialization list as above, we can also use the following methods:

First: combine the constant definition with static, that is:

static const int apple_number

Second: initialize it outside:

const int Apple::apple_number=10;

Of course, if you compile with C++11, you can initialize directly at the declaration and simply write:

static const int apple_number=10;
// ​或者​
const int apple_number=10;

Both are supported in C++11!

Just add -std=c++11 when compiling!

This brings up static; here is a brief note on it:

In C++, static static member variables cannot be initialized inside the class. Inside the class there is only a declaration; the definition must be outside the class definition body, usually initialized in the class's implementation file.

Declared in the class:

static int ap;

Used in the class implementation file:

int Apple::ap=666

For this item, C++11 does not allow declaration together with initialization — that is, the usage above.

docs.title: The Complete C++ const Family
docs.text:
Outline

  • const
  • constexpr
  • C++20
  • consteval
  • constinit

Note: all code examples in this article have been posted to the Knowledge Planet.

docs.title: 1. const
docs.text:
const is one of the earliest keywords we meet when learning C++/C. It is usually used as a cv-qualifier to indicate that an object is immutable. It does not guarantee compile-time evaluation; when exactly the evaluation happens is up to the compiler. For example:

const int a = 1; // ​编译​时​
const auto x = getdata(); // ​运行​时​

const can sometimes be used in compile-time constant expressions, but there are exceptions, for example:

const double count_1 = 3.3;
std::array<double, static_cast<int>(count_1)> moreDoubles1 {1.1, 2.2, 3.3};

This produces an error: the value of 'count_1' is not usable in a constant expression

But this is fine:

const int count = 3;
std::array<double, count> doubles {1.1, 2.2, 3.3};

The essence is compile-time expression evaluation, and so C++11 introduced constexpr.

docs.title: 2. constexpr
docs.text:
constexpr can be used to specify that a variable's value may appear in a constant expression; here we only need to change const to constexpr in the earlier example for it to work.

constexpr double count_2 = 3.3;
std::array<double, static_cast<int>(count_2)> moreDoubles2 {1.1, 2.2, 3.3};

constexpr does not necessarily execute only at compile time. Its essential meaning is that it can be computed at compile time, but if a constexpr variable or function is used at run time, it can also execute at run time.

For example, result1 and result2 are completely different: result1 is computed at compile time, while result2 is computed at run time. A question to leave you with: do you know why?

So a function specified as constexpr is not necessarily computed at compile time.

constexpr int compileTimeSum(int a, int b) {
    return a + b;
}

int main() {
    constexpr int result1 = compileTimeSum(3, 5); 
    int x = 10;
    int result2 = compileTimeSum(x, 20);  
    return 0;
}

Then who can guarantee that? Along comes C++20.

docs.title: 3.1 consteval
docs.text:
consteval solves the problem above: it can only be used on functions and forces every call to happen at compile time. If we now change constexpr to consteval above, what happens to result2?

It errors out: call to consteval function 'compileTimeSum(x, 20)' is not a constant expression

consteval int compileTimeSum(int a, int b) {
    return a + b;
}

int main() {
    constexpr int result1 = compileTimeSum(3, 5); 
    int x = 10;
    int result2 = compileTimeSum(x, 20);  
    return 0;
}

If consteval is used on a variable, it also errors: error: a variable cannot be declared 'consteval'.

https://en.cppreference.com/w/cpp/language/consteval

docs.title: 3.2 constinit
docs.text:
constinit forces static or thread-local variables to undergo constant initialization.

  • Cannot be used together with constexpr or consteval
  • A non-type specifier whose role is that of an assert
  • Guarantees that the variable is statically initialized
  • Can only be used with static or thread_local

For example, the following fails to compile: error: 'constinit' can only be applied to a variable with static or thread storage duration

constinit int a = 100;  
int main() {  
      ++a; 
      constinit auto b = 100;  // error
      // b has thread storage duration
      constinit thread_local auto b = 100;
}

docs.title: C++ Dereference Operator * | C++​那些​事
docs.text: Last updated：2026-10-13

docs.title: 0. Introduction
docs.text:
When we work with pointers, we usually use *, for example:

int a = 1;
int *ptr = a;
std::cout << *ptr << std::endl;

Beyond that, does it have any other uses?

The answer is yes; for example, in C++ there are also the following three:

  • ::*
  • .*
  • ->*

So do you know what each of these three means?

::* is called the Pointer to member declarator.

Let me give an example:

In the example below, how would you take the address of w_?

If you write double * d = &w_; that is invalid, because it is not known where w_ lives, so you need a pointer to member declarator; that makes the binding possible, and once you have this pointer you can access the member. Let's continue with the other two.

class Rectangle {
 public:
  double w_, h_;

  Rectangle(double w, double h) : w_(w), h_(h) {}
  double area() { return w_ * h_; }
};

int main() {
  Rectangle r{2.1, 3.2};
  double Rectangle::* w = &Rectangle::w_;
  r.*w = 2.2;
  std::cout << r.w_ << std::endl;
};

.* is called pointer to member of object. This one is fairly easy to understand: it is the pointer for accessing a member of an object; a pointer to member lets you refer to non-static members of a class object. You cannot use a pointer to member to point to a static class member, because the address of a static member is not associated with any particular object.

So, in the example above, this line of code changes the value of member w to 2.2.

r.*w = 2.2;

docs.title: 3. ->*
docs.text:
->* is called pointer to member of pointer. This one is even easier to understand: it is similar to ., except that it operates on the address of a member of a **pointer object*,

so the corresponding example becomes:

Rectangle r{2.1, 3.2}, *pr;
pr = &r;
std::cout << pr->*w << std::endl;

For more details, please read cppreference.com.

https://en.cppreference.com/w/cpp/language/pointer#Pointers_to_members

Did you get it? End of this section~

docs.title: C++ iv
docs.text:
int* p = nullptr;
std::shared_ptr<int> s(p); // ​计数器​1
std::shared_ptr<int> s2(s); // ​计数器​2
assert(s.use_count() == 2);

This piece of code raises several questions:

  • Why is the use count of the smart pointer constructed from a nullptr raw pointer not 0?
  • Is delete nullptr safe?

docs.title: 1. The Semantics of an Empty shared_ptr
docs.text:
Looking directly at the shared_ptr source code, what "empty" means is:

  • A shared_ptr constructed by default construction
  • A shared_ptr constructed from nullptr_t

Only these two cases count as empty; a shared_ptr constructed from a raw pointer owns that pointer, regardless of whether it is null.

They correspond to the three constructors below.

private:
    element_type*      __ptr_;
    __shared_weak_count* __cntrl_;

public:
    _LIBCPP_HIDE_FROM_ABI
    _LIBCPP_CONSTEXPR shared_ptr() _NOEXCEPT
        : __ptr_(nullptr),
          __cntrl_(nullptr)
    { }

    _LIBCPP_HIDE_FROM_ABI
    _LIBCPP_CONSTEXPR shared_ptr(nullptr_t) _NOEXCEPT
        : __ptr_(nullptr),
          __cntrl_(nullptr)
    { }
    shared_ptr(_Yp* __p, _Dp __d)
        : __ptr_(__p)
    {}

In the case above, where the raw pointer is nullptr, what happens on delete nullptr? And what happens if you delete twice?

docs.title: 2. delete nullptr
docs.text:
Given the following code, does it crash when run, or run normally?

#include <iostream>

int main() {
    int *p = nullptr;
    delete p;
    std::cout << "delete once" << std::endl;
    delete p;
    std::cout << "delete twice" << std::endl;

}

The answer is: it prints normally.

See cppreference for the specific reason:

If expression evaluates to a null pointer value, no destructors are called, and the deallocation function may or may not be called (it's unspecified), but the default deallocation functions are guaranteed to do nothing when passed a null pointer.

https://en.cppreference.com/w/cpp/language/delete

If the expression evaluates to a null pointer value, no destructors are called, and the deallocation function may or may not be called (unspecified), but the default deallocation functions are guaranteed to do nothing when passed a null pointer.

Reading tips

This article discusses the difference between initialization and assignment in C++; see also the class initializer list.
