docs.title: Ways to Return Multiple Values in C++
docs.text:
Today let me pose another fairly classic interview question: how can a function return multiple results? How many ways can you think of?

In fact, this question tests a great deal of knowledge, covering:

  • pointers
  • references
  • lambda
  • functional
  • tie
  • tuple
  • struct binding
  • template deduction
  • and so on

This article will answer the question using different methods. First, let's transform the problem: use a / b to simulate it (below, the case where the divisor is 0 is not considered) and return the quotient and the remainder. Simply put, the question becomes: in how many ways can a function return the quotient and the remainder?

Now let's get to the point. Note: all the code in this section was first published in the Knowledge Planet; if you are interested, scan the QR code below.

docs.title: 1. Pointers and References
docs.text:
Change the interface by adding two parameters, using pointers and references.

void divideWithReferences(int dividend, int divisor, int& quotient, int& remainder) {
  quotient = dividend / divisor;
  remainder = dividend % divisor;
}

void divideWithPointers(int dividend, int divisor, int* quotient, int* remainder) {
  if (quotient) *quotient = dividend / divisor;
  if (remainder) *remainder = dividend % divisor;
}

The drawback of this approach is plain to see: once there are more than two return values, the interface becomes very long. Moreover, if the interviewer requires you not to change the function interface, this method is unusable.

docs.title: 2. Tuple + Tie
docs.text:
The combination of tuple and tie provides a concise way for a function to return multiple values. By using std::tie, we can unpack the elements of the tuple into different variables, improving the clarity of the code.

This method counts as one of the standard answers; it is fairly simple and clear, and a pair also works if the return values are two.

std::tuple<int, int> divide(int dividend, int divisor) {
    return std::make_tuple(dividend / divisor, dividend % divisor);
}


std::tie(quotient, remainder) = divide(14, 3);
std::cout << quotient << ", " << remainder << std::endl;

docs.title: 3. Struct Binding
docs.text:
Transforming the above, structured bindings introduced in C++17 further simplify code that returns multiple values. Using auto with structured bindings makes the code more intuitive and easier to understand.

If the interviewer asks you to further refine the method above, it can become the code example below, which uses structured bindings to make the code more elegant.

auto divide(int dividend, int divisor) {
  struct result {
    int quotient;
    int remainder;
  };
  return result{dividend / divisor, dividend % divisor};
}
auto [quotient, remainder] = divide(14, 3);

docs.title: 4. Function Callbacks
docs.text:
In everyday projects, especially open-source projects, a callback is a commonly used technique: by passing a callback that handles the return values, users customize the processing, which realizes returning multiple values and yields a more flexible code structure. This is very useful for scenarios such as asynchronous programming and event handling.

void divide(int dividend, int divisor, std::function<void(int, int)> callback) {
  callback(dividend / divisor, dividend % divisor);
}

docs.title: 5. Custom Out
docs.text:
A custom out is a way of wrapping things in a struct, making the output parameters members of the struct. This approach improves the readability of the code and is especially suitable for functions that need to return multiple values.

template <class T>
struct out {
  std::function<void(T)> target;

  out(T* t)
      : target([t](T&& in) {
          if (t) *t = std::move(in);
        }) {}

  template <class... Args>
  void emplace(Args&&... args) {
    target(T(std::forward<Args>(args)...));
  }

  template <class X>
  void operator=(X&& x) {
    emplace(std::forward<X>(x));
  }

  template <class... Args>
  void operator()(Args&&... args) {
    emplace(std::forward<Args>(args)...);
  }
};

void divide(int dividend, int divisor, out<int>& quotient_out, out<int>& remainder_out) {
  quotient_out.emplace(dividend / divisor);
  remainder_out.emplace(dividend % divisor);
}

docs.title: 6. Template Deduction
docs.text:
C++ template deduction provides developers with a more flexible and concise way of writing code. With template deduction, we can handle data of different types without explicitly specifying the types.

template <typename T1, typename T2>
struct many {
  T1 quotient;
  T2 remainder;
};

template <class T1, class T2>
many(T1, T2) -> many<T1, T2>;

many<int, int> divide(int dividend, int divisor) {
  return many{
      dividend / divisor,
      dividend % divisor,
  };
}

auto [quotient, remainder] = divide(14, 3);

All in all, C++ provides many ways to achieve multiple return values, and each has its applicable scenarios. Choosing the right one depends on the specific requirements; developers can use these features flexibly according to code structure and readability.

docs.title: A Deep Dive into the mutable Keyword in C++
docs.text: In C++, the mutable keyword is often regarded as a tool for "piercing through" the const restriction. In some cases, although we want to impose const protection on an object, we still need to modify some of its data members. This article explores in depth the use cases of mutable and the design philosophy behind it, and discusses how it solves specific programming needs in C++.

docs.title: 1. The Basic Use of the mutable Keyword
docs.text:
We know that when a member function is qualified with const, that member function guarantees it will not modify the object's state. In actual programming, however, we sometimes want to modify a data member while still marking the member function const. This is what the mutable keyword is for:

class Foo  
{  
private:  
    mutable bool done_;  
public:  
    void doSomething() const {
        // ​在​ const ​成员​函数​中​修改​ mutable ​成员​
        done_ = true;
    }  
};

In the example above, doSomething() is declared const, indicating that it does not change the object's state. done_, however, is marked mutable, which means we can still modify done_ even inside a const method. This design lets us manage the data that does need modification while keeping the function's interface semantics unchanged.

docs.title: 2. Logical Constness vs. Bitwise Constness
docs.text:
Constness in C++ falls into two categories: logical constness and bitwise constness. Logical constness means that the object's state appears unchanged from the outside, while bitwise constness means that the object's bits in memory remain unchanged. The mutable keyword allows us to define logical constness: even if some of the object's internal data changes, the object's state shows no observable change in a logical sense.

For example, in a thread-safe class we might use boost::mutex to protect data access. To acquire the lock inside a const method, we can declare the mutex as mutable:

class ThreadSafeClass {
private:
    mutable std::mutex mtx_;
    int data_;
public:
    int getData() const {
        std::lock_guard<std::mutex> lock(mtx_);
        return data_;
    }
};

In the example above, although the getData method is declared const, we need the lock to keep data access thread-safe. We therefore declare mtx_ as mutable, to allow modifying it inside a const method. In this case, we say the class's logical state has not changed; the modification exists only to ensure thread safety.

docs.title: 3. mutable in Lambda Expressions
docs.text:
Since C++11, mutable can also be used in lambda expressions to allow the modification of variables captured by value. By default, variables captured by value in a lambda are immutable. If you need to modify a captured variable inside the lambda, you can use mutable:

int x = 0;
auto f1 = [=]() mutable { x = 42; };  // OK: ​可以​修改​捕获​的​ x
auto f2 = [=]() { x = 42; };  // Error: ​按值​捕获​的​变量​不能​被​修改​

In this case, mutable allows us to modify the captured variables inside the function body without affecting the values of the outer variables.

docs.title: 4. Avoiding const_cast
docs.text:
Without the mutable keyword, we might need const_cast to handle these special cases. const_cast can strip away an object's constness, but it has drawbacks: const_cast can remove const protection entirely, letting us make arbitrary modifications to and method calls on the object, which degrades the code's readability and safety.

By comparison, the mutable keyword provides a finer-grained form of control. With mutable, we can set up "exceptions" on specific data members, allowing modification inside const methods without stripping the constness from the whole object. mutable therefore handles these special cases more safely.

docs.title: 5. The Design Philosophy of Using mutable
docs.text:
The design philosophy of the mutable keyword lies in preserving the interface's logical constness. In most cases, we want to write const-correct code, which means the object's state does not change unless explicitly modified. mutable allows us to make concessions in some internal implementation details — such as caching, reference counting, or debug information — without breaking the consistency of this interface design.

When designing an interface, we should be clear about when and why an object's state needs to be modified. The mutable keyword keeps the code unchanged at the logical level while still providing the ability to modify specific data members. This requires the designer to think it through carefully, making sure the use of mutable does not destroy the notion of the object's constness, and to use it only when it is genuinely needed.

docs.title: C++ restrict and Compiler Optimization | C++​那些​事
docs.text: Last updated：2026-10-13

docs.title: C++ restrict and Compiler Optimization
docs.text: While reviewing a ClickHouse PR (ClickHouse#19946) I saw __restrict used in real code and studied it on the spot: how much optimization room can one keyword give the compiler? Conclusion first: in hot loops where "the compiler cannot prove two pointers do not alias", restrict delivers a clearly visible speedup.

docs.title: 1. Background: Why Pointer Aliasing Slows Code Down
docs.text:
When the compiler optimizes loops, its worst fear is two pointers referring to the same memory (aliasing). Look at this classic scenario:

void add(int* a, int* b, int* out, int n) {
  for (int i = 0; i < n; ++i) {
    out[i] = a[i] + b[i];
  }
}

If out and a alias, then writing out[i] may change a[i], so the compiler dares not reorder reads and writes, dares not use vector instructions, and can only proceed honestly one instruction at a time. restrict, in turn, is the programmer's promise to the compiler: memory accessed through this pointer will not alias with any other pointer. With that promise made, the compiler can let loose.

docs.title: 2. Measurement: The Aggregate Computation Hotspot
docs.text:
The benchmark below simulates the hot path of a database aggregation computation (a simplified version of the ClickHouse PR); the only difference between the two versions is __restrict:

#include <vector>
#include <memory>
#include <benchmark/benchmark.h>

#define LEN 1<<20
using AggregateDataPtr = char *;

struct AvgState {
  uint64_t numerator{0};
  uint64_t denominator{0};

  double divide() { return numerator / denominator; }
};

class Column {
public:
  std::vector<uint64_t> & data() {return data_; }

private:
  std::vector<uint64_t> data_;
};

template <class Derived>
class IAggregate {
public:
  void addBatch(size_t batch_size, AggregateDataPtr state, Column *args) __attribute__((noinline)) {
      for (size_t i = 0; i < batch_size; ++i) {
          static_cast<const Derived *>(this)->add(state, args, i);
      }
  }

  void addBatchWithoutOpt(size_t batch_size, AggregateDataPtr state, Column *args) __attribute__((noinline)) {
      for (size_t i = 0; i < batch_size; ++i) {
          static_cast<const Derived *>(this)->addWithoutOpt(state, args, i);
      }
  }
};

class AvgAggregator final : public IAggregate<AvgAggregator> {
public:
  static AvgState& data(AggregateDataPtr __restrict place) { return *reinterpret_cast<AvgState *>(place); }
  static AvgState& data_without_opt(AggregateDataPtr place) { return *reinterpret_cast<AvgState *>(place); }

  void add(AggregateDataPtr __restrict state, Column * args, uint64_t row_num) const {
    data(state).numerator += args[0].data()[row_num];
    ++(data(state).denominator);
  }

  void addWithoutOpt(AggregateDataPtr state, Column * args, uint64_t row_num) const {
    data_without_opt(state).numerator += args[0].data()[row_num];
    ++(data_without_opt(state).denominator);
  }
};

static void BM_loop_with_optimize(benchmark::State& state) {
    AvgAggregator avgAggregator;
    Column column;
    for (size_t i = 0 ; i < LEN; i++) {
        column.data().push_back(i);
    }
    Column arg0[] = {column};
    // Code inside this loop is measured repeatedly
    for(auto _ : state) {
        auto avgState = std::make_unique<AvgState>();
        avgAggregator.addBatch(LEN, reinterpret_cast<AggregateDataPtr>(avgState.get()), arg0);
    }
}

static void BM_loop_without_optimize(benchmark::State& state) {
    AvgAggregator avgAggregator;
    Column column;
    for (size_t i = 0 ; i < LEN; i++) {
        column.data().push_back(i);
    }
    Column arg0[] = {column};
    // Code inside this loop is measured repeatedly
    for(auto _ : state) {
        auto avgState = std::make_unique<AvgState>();
        avgAggregator.addBatchWithoutOpt(LEN, reinterpret_cast<AggregateDataPtr>(avgState.get()), arg0);
    }
}

BENCHMARK(BM_loop_without_optimize);
BENCHMARK(BM_loop_with_optimize);

https://quick-bench.com/q/ccjuWr_JcLozAfy3Gxf3uVu76Yk

https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/19946

docs.title: 3. Results and Summary
docs.text:
(1) The version with __restrict (BM_loop_with_optimize) is clearly faster: once the two state pointers numerator/denominator are annotated, the compiler keeps them in registers and the loop fully vectorizes; the un-annotated version reloads from memory every time;

(2) restrict is currently not a standard C++ keyword; the mainstream approach is compiler extensions: GCC/Clang use __restrict (or __restrict__), MSVC uses __restrict, and C++26 is discussing standardization (the std::indirect/no_alias proposals);

(3) warning: restrict is a promise with no insurance — if aliasing occurs, it is undefined behavior. Only use it on hot paths where you can prove there is no aliasing (for example, independent state blocks returned by an allocator).

One-sentence summary: in a hot loop with multiple pointer reads/writes and genuinely no aliasing, __restrict is an extremely cost-effective optimization. The accompanying code is in the benchmark above; feel free to run it yourself on quick-bench.

docs.title: C++ string ABI Compatibility | C++​那些​事
docs.text: Last updated：2026-10-13

docs.title: A Real-World Project Problem: Avoiding the C++ String ABI Compatibility Pitfall
docs.text:
Why do many people dislike C++ string and reinvent the wheel instead? One of the reasons is the C++ string ABI problem — have you ever run into it?

I previously hit a C++ string ABI compatibility problem while using Conan with cross-platform libraries. This section introduces the background of ABI and compiler-related content, and talks about how to avoid this pitfall. If you have run into it, feel free to leave a comment~

docs.title: 1. Background of the ABI Change
docs.text:
After GCC 5.1, support for C++11 was strengthened and some new features were introduced. In that release, libstdc++ introduced a new library ABI and updated the implementations of std::string and std::list. These changes conform to the C++11 standard, which forbids Copy-On-Write strings and requires lists to be able to track their size.

In real projects using Conan, developers can choose which ABI to use by adjusting compiler.libcxx:

  • libstdc++: uses the old ABI.
  • libstdc++11: uses the new ABI.

Choosing the appropriate ABI ensures compatibility with other dependency libraries, especially when using different versions of compilers or libraries.

docs.title: 2. Compiler Default Settings
docs.text:
When compiling with GCC, if --with-default-libstdcxx-abi=gcc4-compatible is not explicitly specified, GCC uses the new C++11 ABI by default. This means:

  • If your code or dependency libraries were compiled under the old ABI, you may encounter undefined-symbol errors when you try to link.

For example, when compiling the following code:

// lib.cc
#include <string>
void foo(const std::string& s) {}

Using the command:

g++-14 -D_GLIBCXX_USE_CXX11_ABI=0 -c lib.cc

This generates the symbol __Z3fooRKSs, which is the old ABI format.

However, when you compile and link another file that uses the new ABI, an error like the following may appear:

g++-14 main.cc lib.o

Undefined symbols for architecture x86_64:
  "foo(std::__cxx11::basic_string<char, std::char_traits<char>, std::allocator<char> > const&)", referenced from:
      _main in ccbWGoYh.o
ld: symbol(s) not found for architecture x86_64
collect2: error: ld returned 1 exit status

docs.title: 3. Solutions
docs.text:
To make the compilation pass, there are two solutions:

Option 1: Manually specify the ABI

When compiling all source files, make sure to manually add -D_GLIBCXX_USE_CXX11_ABI=0 for compatibility with the old library, for example:

g++-14 -D_GLIBCXX_USE_CXX11_ABI=0 main.cc lib.o

Option 2: Compile all files with the new ABI

If you are willing to use the new C++11 ABI, you can use -D_GLIBCXX_USE_CXX11_ABI=1 when compiling the library file, so that the two symbols match:

g++-14 -D_GLIBCXX_USE_CXX11_ABI=1 -c lib.cc
g++-14 main.cc lib.o

Now the symbols match at link time, and the undefined-symbol error no longer appears.

docs.title: 4. Symbol Comparison
docs.text:
By viewing the symbols under the different ABIs with the nm command, you can see the difference between the two directly:

g++-14 -D_GLIBCXX_USE_CXX11_ABI=0 -c lib.cc
nm lib.o | grep foo  
# ​输出​: 0000000000000000 T __Z3fooRKSs

g++-14 -D_GLIBCXX_USE_CXX11_ABI=1 -c lib.cc
nm lib.o | grep foo  
# ​输出​: 0000000000000000 T __Z3fooRKNSt7__cxx1112basic_stringIcSt11char_traitsIcESaIcEEE

docs.title: 5. Summary
docs.text: ABI is a huge pitfall encountered when upgrading C++ and during compilation; I hope this article makes these things clear.

docs.title: C++ Template Disambiguation | C++​那些​事
docs.text: Last updated：2026-10-13

docs.title: 1. Background
docs.text:
I recently came across this piece of code:

 auto chunk_left = first_sort_key.template GetChunk<ArrayType>(left);

What does the .template here mean?

This section starts from a real example and explores that meaning.

docs.title: 2. template disambiguator
docs.text:
In C++, when using dependent names of templates, a template disambiguator is sometimes needed to help the compiler distinguish these names. "Dependent names" are types or values that depend on template parameters, and the compiler cannot determine their exact meaning before the template is instantiated. This can cause the compiler to produce ambiguity when parsing these names.

The template disambiguator uses the keyword "template" to tell the compiler explicitly that a particular name is a template. The compiler can then parse the name correctly, without ambiguity.

The keyword template can only be used with the operators :: (scope resolution), -> (member access through a pointer), and . (member access). The following are all valid examples:

  • T::template foo();
  • s.template foo();
  • this->template foo();
  • typename T::template iterator::value_type v;

    Official reference:

    https://en.cppreference.com/w/cpp/language/dependent_name

    Given the code below, what do we get if we leave out .template?

    template <typename T>
auto foo_is_not_a_template() {
  // ((T::foo) < 34) > (::val())
  return T::foo<34>::val();
}

    It gets parsed as: ((T::foo) < 34) > (::val())

    The corresponding .template example is:

    template <typename T>
auto foo_is_a_template() {
  return T::template foo<34>::val();
}

    The call is then correctly parsed as a template, foo<34>.

    The complete code for this section will be published in the Knowledge Planet; join if you are interested. Thank you!

docs.title: C++ vs Rust Destructor Comparison | C++​那些​事
docs.text: Last updated：2026-10-13

docs.title: C++ vs Rust Destructor Comparison
docs.text:
In Rust, mem::forget is used to prevent an object's destructor from running, skipping the cleanup work so that the release of resources is left to other mechanisms to manage.

For example:

let file = File::open("foo.txt").unwrap();
mem::forget(file);

So how do you prevent destruction in C++ — that is, skip the destructor?

This section gives three ways to do it; the complete code examples are also in the Knowledge Planet.

docs.title: 1. placement new
docs.text:
placement new lets us manually manage an object's construction and destruction. If we do not manually call the object's destructor, we can skip the object's destruction, achieving an effect similar to mem::forget.

For example:

alignas(Foo) std::byte storage[sizeof(Foo)];  // ​分配​对齐​的​原始​内存​块​
Foo* pfoo = new (storage) Foo();  // ​在​这块​内存​上​构造​Foo​对象​

In the code above, placement new creates the object pfoo, but we do not call the destructor, thereby skipping the object's cleanup logic.

docs.title: 2. Using a Custom Deleter for Smart Pointers
docs.text:
Another way to achieve similar functionality is to customize the deleter of a smart pointer to prevent the object from being destroyed. We can define a deleter that does nothing, thereby avoiding the call to the destructor.

std::unique_ptr<Foo, NoOpDeleter> pfoo(new Foo(), NoOpDeleter{});

Using the custom deleter NoOpDeleter, we can prevent std::unique_ptr from calling the destructor when it leaves scope, achieving an effect similar to mem::forget.

docs.title: 3. union
docs.text:
The union approach is quite magical — do you know how it works? Feel free to discuss it in the comments~

template <class T>
union Wrapper {
  T value;
  ~Wrapper() {}
};

struct Foo {
  ~Foo() { std::cout << "dtor foo\n"; }
};

Wrapper<Foo> f; 
// f.value.~Foo);  ​必须​手动​调用​

docs.title: C++ decltype Type Deduction | C++​那些​事
docs.text: Last updated：2026-10-13

docs.title: About the Author
docs.text: WeChat official account:

docs.title: 1. Basic Usage
docs.text:
The syntax of decltype is:

decltype (expression)

The parentheses here are indispensable. decltype's job is to "query the type of an expression", so the statement above has the effect of returning the type of the expression. Note that decltype merely "queries" the type of the expression; it does not "evaluate" the expression.

docs.title: 1.1 Deduce the Type of an Expression
docs.text:
int i = 4;
decltype(i) a; //​推导​结果​为​int。a​的​类型​为​int。

docs.title: 1.2 Used Together with using/typedef to Define Types
docs.text:
using size_t = decltype(sizeof(0));//sizeof(a)​的​返回值​为​size_t​类型​
using ptrdiff_t = decltype((int*)0 - (int*)0);
using nullptr_t = decltype(nullptr);
vector<int >vec;
typedef decltype(vec.begin()) vectype;
for (vectype i = vec.begin; i != vec.end(); i++)
{
//...
}

Like auto, this also improves the readability of the code.

docs.title: 1.3 Reusing Anonymous Types
docs.text:
In C++, we sometimes come across anonymous types, such as:

struct 
{
    int d ;
    double b;
}anon_s;

And with the help of decltype, we can reuse this anonymous struct:

decltype(anon_s) as ;//​定义​了​一个​上面​匿名​的​结构​体​

docs.title: 1.4 Combined with auto in Generic Programming to Track a Function's Return Type
docs.text:
This is also the biggest use of decltype.

template <typename T>
auto multiply(T x, T y)->decltype(x*y)
{
    return x*y;
}

See the complete code at: decltype.cpp

docs.title: 2. Deduction Rules
docs.text:
For decltype(e), the deduction result is affected by the following conditions:

If e is an unparenthesized id-expression or a class member access expression, then decltype(e) is the type of the entity named by e. In addition, if e is an overloaded function, this causes a compile error. Otherwise, suppose the type of e is T; if e is an xvalue, then decltype(e) is T&&. Otherwise, suppose the type of e is T; if e is an lvalue, then decltype(e) is T&. Otherwise, suppose the type of e is T; then decltype(e) is T.

An identifier refers to a token defined by the programmer, excluding keywords, literals, and other tokens the compiler needs; the expression corresponding to a single identifier is an id-expression. For example: 

int arr[4]
Here arr is an id-expression, while arr[3]+0 is not.

For example:

int i = 4;
int arr[5] = { 0 };
int *ptr = arr;
struct S{ double d; }s ;
void Overloaded(int);
void Overloaded(char);//​重载​的​函数​
int && RvalRef();
const bool Func(int);

//​规则​一​：​推导​为​其​类型​
decltype (arr) var1; //int[] ​标记​符​表达式​

decltype (ptr) var2;//int *  ​标记​符​表达式​

decltype(s.d) var3;//doubel ​成员​访问​表达式​

//decltype(Overloaded) var4;//​重载​函数​。​编译​错误​。

//​规则​二​：​将亡值​。​推导​为​类型​的​右值​引用​。

decltype (RvalRef()) var5 = 1;

//​规则​三​：​左值​，​推导​为​类型​的​引用​。

decltype ((i))var6 = i;     //int&

decltype (true ? i : i) var7 = i; //int&  ​条件​表达式​返回​左值​。

decltype (++i) var8 = i; //int&  ++i​返回​i​的​左值​。

decltype(arr[5]) var9 = i;//int&. []​操作​返回​左值​

decltype(*ptr)var10 = i;//int& *​操作​返回​左值​

decltype("hello")var11 = "hello"; //const char(&)[9]  ​字符串​字面​常量​为​左值​，​且​为​const​左值​。


//​规则​四​：​以上​都​不是​，​则​推导​为本​类型​

decltype(1) var12;//const int

decltype(Func(1)) var13=true;//const bool

decltype(i++) var14 = i;//int i++​返回​右值​

Learning reference: https://www.cnblogs.com/QG-whz/p/4952980.html

docs.title: C++ enum Enumerated Types | C++​那些​事
docs.text: Last updated：2026-10-13

docs.title: About the Author
docs.text: WeChat official account:

docs.title: Traditional Behavior
docs.text:
Enumerations have the following problems:

  • Unrestricted scope, which easily leads to naming conflicts. For example, the following fails to compile:

enum Color
{
    RED,
    BLUE
};
enum Feeling
{
    EXCITED,
    BLUE
};

int main()
{
    Color a = BLUE; // error
    Feeling b = EXCITED;
    std::cout << a << ":" << b << std::endl;
    return 0;
}
- Implicit conversion to int - The actual type used to represent the enumeration variable cannot be explicitly specified, so forward declaration of enumeration types is not supported.

See the concrete implementation at: tradition_color.cpp

docs.title: Classic Practice
docs.text:
A simple way to solve the naming conflicts caused by the unrestricted scope is to add a prefix when naming enumeration values, e.g. changing the example above to COLOR_BLUE and FEELING_BLUE.

Generally speaking, for the sake of consistency we prefix all the constants. But code that defines enumerations this way looks cumbersome. C programs may have to do it this way, though C++ programmers probably dislike this approach. The alternative is a namespace: 

namespace Color 
{
    enum Type
    {
        RED=15,
        YELLOW,
        BLUE
    };
};

After that, you can define a new enumeration variable with Color::Type c = Color::RED;. After using namespace Color, the prefix can even be omitted, which simplifies the code. However, because a namespace can be extended with more content later on, the scope it provides is not very well sealed. In a large project, it is still possible for different people to give the same enumeration type name to different things.

A more "effective" approach is to use a class or a struct to restrict the scope, for example: defining new variables works the same way as with the namespace above, but now you need not worry about the class being modified elsewhere. A struct is used here rather than a class because we want these constants to be publicly accessible in the first place.

struct Color1
{
    enum Type
    {
        RED=102,
        YELLOW,
        BLUE
    };
};

See the concrete implementation at: classic_practice.cpp

docs.title: C++11 Enum Classes
docs.text:
The approach above solves the first problem but is powerless against the other two. Fortunately, the C++11 standard introduced "enum classes", which solve the problems above rather well.

  • The scope of the new enum is no longer global
  • No implicit conversion to other types
/**
 * @brief C++11​的​枚举​类​
 * ​下面​等价​于​enum class Color2:int
 */
enum class Color2
{
    RED=2,
    YELLOW,
    BLUE
};
Color2 c2 = Color2::RED;
cout << static_cast<int>(c2) << endl; //​必须​转​！
  • A specific type can be specified to store the enum
enum class Color3:char;  // ​前向​声明​

// ​定义​
enum class Color3:char 
{
    RED='r',
    BLUE
};
char c3 = static_cast<char>(Color3::RED);

See the concrete implementation at: classic_practice.cpp

docs.title: Enumerated Types in Classes
docs.text:
Sometimes we want certain constants to be valid only inside a class. Since macros defined by #define are global, they cannot achieve this, so we think of using const-qualified data members instead. const data members do exist, but their meaning is not what we expect.

A const data member is constant only within the lifetime of a single object; for the class as a whole it is mutable, because the class can create multiple objects, and the const data members of different objects can have different values.

A const data member cannot be initialized in the class declaration. The following usage is wrong, because when no object of the class has been created, the compiler does not know what the value of SIZE is. (Before the C++11 standard)

class A 
{
  const int SIZE = 100;   // ​错误​，​企图​在​类​声明​中​初始化​ const ​数据​成员​ 
  int array[SIZE];  // ​错误​，​未知​的​ SIZE 
};

The correct place is the initializer list of the class's constructor:

class A 
{
  A(int size);  // ​构造函数​ 
  const int SIZE ;    
}; 
A::A(int size) : SIZE(size)  // ​构造函数​的​定义​
{ 

} 
A  a(100); // ​对象​ a ​的​ SIZE ​值为​ 100 
A  b(200); // ​对象​ b ​的​ SIZE ​值为​ 200

How can we establish a constant that holds throughout the whole class?

Do not count on const data members; use enumeration constants in the class instead. For example:

class Person{
public:
    typedef enum {
        BOY = 0,
        GIRL
    }SexType;
};
//​访问​的​时候​通过​，Person::BOY​或者​Person::GIRL​来​进行​访问​。

Enumeration constants occupy no storage space in the object; they are all evaluated at compile time.

The drawback of enumeration constants is that their implicit data type is integer, their maximum value is limited, and they cannot represent floating point.

docs.title: 1. Compilation Differences Between C++ and C
docs.text:
In C++ you often see functions decorated with extern "C" in header files; what does that do? It is used so that C++ can link against functions defined in C modules.

Although C++ is compatible with C, the symbols generated after compiling a function in a C++ file differ from those generated by the C language. Because C++ supports function overloading, the symbols generated by the C++ compiler carry information about the function's parameter types, while C's do not.

For example, after the function int add(int a, int b) is compiled by a C++ compiler into a .o file, add becomes something like add_int_int, whereas in C it would be something like _add. That is to say: the same function produces different symbols when compiled in C and in C++.

This leads to a problem: if C++ uses a function implemented in C, the compile/link step errors out, saying the corresponding symbol cannot be found. This is where extern "C" comes into play: it tells the linker to look for C-style symbols like _add instead of C++-mangled symbols.

docs.title: 2. C++ Calling a C Function
docs.text:
An example of C++ calling a C function: when including the C header file, you need to add extern "C"

//add.h
#ifndef ADD_H
#define ADD_H
int add(int x,int y);
#endif

//add.c
#include "add.h"

int add(int x,int y) {
    return x+y;
}

//add.cpp
#include <iostream>
#include "add.h"
using namespace std;
int main() {
    add(2,3);
    return 0;
}

Compile:

//Generate add.o file
gcc -c add.c

Link:

g++ add.cpp add.o -o main

Without adding extern "C" you get errors:

> g++ add.cpp add.o -o main                                   
add.o：​在​函数​‘main’​中​：
add.cpp:(.text+0x0): `main'​被​多次​定义​
/tmp/ccH65yQF.o:add.cpp:(.text+0x0)：​第一次​在​此​定义​
/tmp/ccH65yQF.o：​在​函数​‘main’​中​：
add.cpp:(.text+0xf)：​对​‘add(int, int)’​未定义​的​引用​
add.o：​在​函数​‘main’​中​：
add.cpp:(.text+0xf)：​对​‘add(int, int)’​未定义​的​引用​
collect2: error: ld returned 1 exit status

After adding extern "C":

add.cpp

#include <iostream>
using namespace std;
extern "C" {
    #include "add.h"
}
int main() {
    std::cout << add(2, 3) << std::endl;
    return 0;
}

When compiling, be sure to first generate the intermediate file add.o with gcc.

gcc -c add.c

Then compile:

g++ add.cpp add.o -o main

If you build with bazel, run: bazel run basic_content/extern/extern_c++:main

Usually, to make C code universally usable — callable both from C and from C++ — the header file is often written like this:

#ifdef __cplusplus
extern "C"{
#endif
int add(int x,int y);
#ifdef __cplusplus
}
#endif

That is, when C++ calls this interface, it calls it the C-interface way. This approach means C++ users need no extra extern C, and the standard library headers essentially do the same thing — otherwise, why would you be able to use the C functions in stdio.h directly without extern C?

The source code for the examples above:

  • add.h

  • add.c

  • add.cpp

docs.title: 2. C Calling a C++ Function
docs.text:
extern "C" is a syntax error in C, so it must go in a C++ header file.

// add.h
#ifndef ADD_H
#define ADD_H
extern "C" {
    int add(int x,int y);
}
#endif

// add.cpp
#include "add.h"

int add(int x,int y) {
    return x+y;
}

// add.c
extern int add(int x,int y);
int main() {
    add(2,3);
    return 0;
}

Compile:

g++ -c add.cpp

Link:

gcc add.c add.o -o main

The source code for the examples above:

  • add.h

  • add.c

  • add.cpp

To sum up, we can derive the usage rules: in a C header file, its external functions can only be declared extern; the C language does not support the extern "C" declaration, and including extern "C" in a .c file causes a compile syntax error. So all uses of extern "C" go in the files related to the cpp program or in its header files.

This gives the following forms:

(1)C++ calling a C function:

//xx.h
extern int add(...)

//xx.c
int add(){

}

//xx.cpp
extern "C" {
    #include "xx.h"
}

(2)C calling a C++ function

//xx.h
extern "C"{
    int add();
}
//xx.cpp
int add(){

}
//xx.c
extern int add();

Unlike C++ calling a C interface — where C++ really can call the compiled C functions — here, C calling C++ merely compiles the C++ code as if it were C code and then calls it. In other words, C cannot directly call C++ library functions.

docs.title: C++ friend | C++​那些​事
docs.text: Last updated：2026-10-13

docs.title: About the Author
docs.text: WeChat official account:

docs.title: 0. Overview
docs.text:
friend provides a mechanism for an ordinary function or a class member function to access the private or protected members of another class. That is to say, there are two forms of friend:

(1)Friend function: an ordinary function accesses the private or protected members of some class.

(2)Friend class: member functions of class A access the private or protected members of class B

Advantage: improves the running efficiency of the program.

Disadvantage: breaks the encapsulation of the class and the transparency of the data.

Summary: - Can access private members - Breaks encapsulation - Friendship is not transitive - Friendship is one-way - The form and number of friend declarations are not restricted

docs.title: 1. Friend Functions
docs.text:
Declared in any region of the class declaration, while the definition is outside the class.

friend <​类型​><​友元​函数​名​>(<​参数表​>);

Note that a friend function is just an ordinary function, not a member function of the class; it can be called from anywhere, and inside the friend function the private or protected members of the class are accessed via the object name.

See the concrete code at: friend_func.cpp

#include <iostream>

using namespace std;

class A
{
public:
    A(int _a):a(_a){};
    friend int geta(A &ca);  ///< ​友元​函数​
private:
    int a;
};

int geta(A &ca) 
{
    return ca.a;
}

int main()
{
    A a(3);    
    cout<<geta(a)<<endl;

    return 0;
}

docs.title: 2. Friend Classes
docs.text:
The friend class is declared inside the class's declaration and implemented outside the class.

friend class <​友元类​名​>;

If class B is a friend of class A, then class B can directly access A's private members.

See the concrete code at: friend_class.cpp 

#include <iostream>

using namespace std;

class A
{
public:
    A(int _a):a(_a){};
    friend class B;
private:
    int a;
};

class B
{
public:
    int getb(A ca) {
        return  ca.a; 
    };
};

int main() 
{
    A a(3);
    B b;
    cout<<b.getb(a)<<endl;
    return 0;
}

docs.title: 3. Notes
docs.text:
• Friendship is not inherited If class B is a friend of class A, and class C derives from class A, then friend class B has no way to directly access the private or protected members of class C.

  • Friendship is not transitive If class B is a friend of class A, and class C is a friend of class B, then friend class C has no way to directly access the private or protected members of class A; that is, no such thing as a "friend of a friend" relationship exists.

docs.title: C++ inline Functions | C++​那些​事
docs.text: Last updated：2026-10-13

docs.title: About the Author
docs.text: WeChat official account:

docs.title: 1. Inline Inside a Class
docs.text:
Declare the methods in the header file

class A
{
public:
    void f1(int x); 

    /**
     * @brief ​类中​定义​了​的​函数​是​隐式​内联​函数​,​声明​要​想​成为​内联​函数​，​必须​在​实现​处​(​定义​处​)​加​inline​关键字​。
     *
     * @param x
     * @param y
     */
    void Foo(int x,int y) ///< ​定义​即​隐式​内联​函数​！
    {

    };
    void f2(int x); ///< ​声明​后​，​要​想​成为​内联​函数​，​必须​在​定义​处加​inline​关键字​。  
};

Define inline functions in the implementation file:

#include <iostream>
#include "inline.h"

using namespace std;

/**
 * @brief inline​要​起​作用​,inline​要​与​函数​定义​放在​一起​,inline​是​一种​“​用于​实现​的​关键字​,​而​不是​用于​声明​的​关键字​”
 *
 * @param x
 * @param y
 *
 * @return 
 */
int Foo(int x,int y);  // ​函数​声明​
inline int Foo(int x,int y) // ​函数​定义​
{
    return x+y;
}

// ​定义​处加​inline​关键字​，​推荐​这种​写法​！
inline void A::f1(int x){

}

int main()
{


    cout<<Foo(1,2)<<endl;

}
/**
 * ​编译器​对​ inline ​函数​的​处理​步骤​
 * ​将​ inline ​函数​体​复制到​ inline ​函数调用​点处​；
 * ​为​所用​ inline ​函数​中​的​局部变量​分配内存​空间​；
 * ​将​ inline ​函数​的​的​输入​参数​和​返回值​映射​到​调用​方法​的​局部变量​空间​中​；
 * ​如果​ inline ​函数​有​多个​返回​点​，​将​其​转变​为​ inline ​函数​代码​块​末尾​的​分支​（​使用​ GOTO）。
 */

Inlining can improve a function's efficiency, but not every function should be defined as inline! Inlining comes at the cost of code bloat (duplication); it merely saves the overhead of the function call, thereby improving the function's execution efficiency.

  • If the time spent executing the code in the function body is large compared with the overhead of the function call, the efficiency gain will be smaller!

  • On the other hand, every call to an inline function duplicates code, which increases the program's total code size and consumes more memory space.

Inlining should not be used in the following cases:

(1)If the code in the function body is fairly long, inlining leads to a comparatively high memory-consumption cost.

(2)If a loop appears in the function body, the time spent executing the code in the function body exceeds the overhead of the function call.

docs.title: 2. Can a Virtual Function (virtual) Be an Inline Function (inline)?
docs.text:
• A virtual function can be an inline function; inline may qualify a virtual function, but it cannot be inlined when the virtual function exhibits polymorphism.
  • Inlining is a compile-time suggestion to the compiler, while the polymorphism of virtual functions happens at run time; the compiler cannot know which code gets called at run time, so a virtual function cannot be inlined when it behaves polymorphically (at run time).
  • inline virtual can be inlined only when the compiler knows which class the called object belongs to (e.g. Base::who()); this happens only when the compiler has an actual object rather than a pointer or reference to the object.
#include <iostream>  
using namespace std;
class Base
{
public:
    inline virtual void who()
    {
        cout << "I am Base\n";
    }
    virtual ~Base() {}
};
class Derived : public Base
{
public:
    inline void who()  // ​不写​inline​时隐式​内联​
    {
        cout << "I am Derived\n";
    }
};

int main()
{
    // ​此处​的​虚​函数​ who()，​是​通过​类​（Base）​的​具体​对象​（b）​来​调用​的​，​编译​期间​就​能​确定​了​，​所以​它​可以​是​内联​的​，​但​最终​是否​内联​取决于​编译器​。 
    Base b;
    b.who();

    // ​此处​的​虚​函数​是​通过​指针​调用​的​，​呈现​多态性​，​需要​在​运行​时​期间​才能​确定​，​所以​不能​为​内联​。  
    Base *ptr = new Derived();
    ptr->who();

    // ​因为​Base​有​虚析构​函数​（virtual ~Base() {}），​所以​ delete ​时​，​会先​调用​派生类​（Derived）​析构​函数​，​再​调用​基类​（Base）​析构​函数​，​防止​内存​泄漏​。
    delete ptr;
    ptr = nullptr;


    return 0;
}

docs.text: Last updated：2026-10-13

docs.title: About the Author:
docs.text: Personal WeChat official account:

docs.title: 1. Special Symbols in Macros
docs.text: They come in several kinds: #, ##, \

docs.title: 1.1 The Stringize Operator (#)
docs.text:
When a # precedes a parameter inside a macro, the preprocessor converts that parameter into a character array. Put another way: # means "stringize"; a # appearing in a macro definition converts the parameter that follows it into a string.

Note: it can only be used in macros that take parameters, and it must be placed before the parameter name in the macro body.

For example:

#define exp(s) printf("test s is:%s\n",s)
#define exp1(s) printf("test s is:%s\n",#s)
#define exp2(s) #s 
int main() {
    exp("hello");
    exp1(hello);

    string str = exp2(   bac );
    cout<<str<<" "<<str.size()<<endl;
    /**
     * ​忽略​传入​参数​名​前面​和​后面​的​空格​。
     */
    string str1 = exp2( asda  bac );
    /**
     * ​当​传入​参数​名​间​存在​空格​时​，​编译器​将会​自动​连接​各个​子​字符串​，
     * ​用​每个​子​字符串​之间​以​一个​空格​连接​，​忽略​剩余​空格​。
     */
    cout<<str1<<" "<<str1.size()<<endl;
    return 0;
}

The code above shows the basic usage together with the whitespace handling rules, which are as follows:

  • Whitespace before and after the argument name passed in is ignored.
string str = exp2(   bac );
cout<<str<<" "<<str.size()<<endl;

Output:

bac 3
  • When there is whitespace between the words of the argument passed in, the compiler automatically joins the sub-strings, connecting each sub-string with a single space and ignoring the remaining whitespace.
string str1 = exp2( asda  bac );
cout<<str1<<" "<<str1.size()<<endl;

Output:

asda bac 8

docs.title: 1.2 The Token-Pasting Operator (##)
docs.text:
"##" is a separation-and-connection mechanism: it first separates, then forcibly joins. It turns multiple formal parameters of a macro definition into a single actual parameter name.

Points to note:

(1) When ## joins formal parameters, the whitespace before and after ## is optional.

(2) The actual parameter name produced by the join must be a name that actually exists, or a macro definition the compiler already knows.

(3) If the parameter after ## is itself a macro, ## prevents that macro from being expanded.

Example:

#define expA(s) printf("​前缀​加上​后​的​字符串​为​:%s\n",gc_##s)  //gc_s​必须​存在​
// ​注意事项​2
#define expB(s) printf("​前缀​加上​后​的​字符串​为​:%s\n",gc_  ##  s)  //gc_s​必须​存在​
// ​注意事项​1
#define gc_hello1 "I am gc_hello1"
int main() {
    // ​注意事项​1
    const char * gc_hello = "I am gc_hello";
    expA(hello);
    expB(hello1);
}

docs.title: 1.3 The Line-Continuation Operator ()
docs.text:
When a macro definition cannot be expressed completely on a single line, you can use "\" to indicate that the macro definition continues on the next line.

Note: leave a space before the .

#define MAX(a,b) ((a)>(b) ? (a) \
   :(b))  
int main() {
    int max_val = MAX(3,6);
    cout<<max_val<<endl;
}

For the code above see: sig_examp.cpp

docs.title: 2.1 Avoiding Misinterpretation
docs.text:
For example:

#define fun() f1();f2();
if(a>0)
    fun()

Once this macro is expanded, it becomes:

if(a>0)
    f1();
    f2();

The intent is that f1 and f2 execute when a>0, but in reality f2 executes every time, so this is wrong.

To solve this kind of problem, you can usually adopt a {} block when writing the code.

For example:

#define fun() {f1();f2();}
if(a>0)
    fun();
// ​宏​展开​
if(a>0)
{
    f1();
    f2();
};

But you will notice that after expansion the macro above carries an extra semicolon, which is not quite right syntactically. (Although it compiles and runs without problems, it would normally be without the semicolon.)

docs.title: 2.2 Avoiding goto Control Flow
docs.text:
In some functions we may need to do cleanup work before the return statement — for example, releasing memory allocated by malloc at the start of the function. Using goto is always a simple way to do this:

int f() {
    int *p = (int *)malloc(sizeof(int));
    *p = 10; 
    cout<<*p<<endl;
#ifndef DEBUG
    int error=1;
#endif
    if(error)
        goto END;
    // dosomething
END:
    cout<<"free"<<endl;
    free(p);
    return 0;
}

But since goto does not fit the structured approach of software engineering and can make code hard to understand, many people advocate against using it. In that case, we can use do{...}while(0) to do the same thing:

int ff() {
    int *p = (int *)malloc(sizeof(int));
    *p = 10; 
    cout<<*p<<endl;
    do{ 
#ifndef DEBUG
        int error=1;
#endif
        if(error)
            break;
        //dosomething
    }while(0);
    cout<<"free"<<endl;
    free(p);
    return 0;
}

Here the body of the function is wrapped in do{...}while(0), with break replacing goto, and the cleanup work comes after the while. Now we achieve the same effect, and the code is far more readable and maintainable than the goto version above.

docs.title: 2.3 Avoiding Warnings Caused by Macros
docs.text:
Because of the constraints of different architectures, empty macros are used a lot in the kernel. At compile time these empty macros produce warnings. To avoid such warnings, we can define empty macros with do{...}while(0):

#define EMPTYMICRO do{}while(0)

docs.title: 2.4 Defining a Single Function Block for Complex Operations
docs.text:
If you have a complex function with many variables and you do not want to add a new function, you can use do{...}while(0) and write your code inside it. Inside, you can define variables without worrying that their names clash with variables that appear before or after the block in the function.

This refers to the situation where one variable is used in several places (with a different meaning in each): we can narrow its scope inside each do-while, for example:

int fc()
{
    int k1 = 10;
    cout<<k1<<endl;
    do{
        int k1 = 100;
        cout<<k1<<endl;
    }while(0);
    cout<<k1<<endl;
}

For the code above see: do_while.cpp

Further reading: https://www.cnblogs.com/lizhenghn/p/3674430.html

docs.title: C++ Member Initializer List Pitfalls
docs.text:
In C++, correctly initializing a class is one of the key steps to ensure a program runs correctly. This is especially true when using initializer lists: we need to watch out for some potential traps to avoid unexpected results during code execution.

The initializer list is generally considered the preferred way to set up the state of a new class instance, because it provides a concise, efficient way to initialize class members. However, referring to other member variables in the initializer list can sometimes lead to confusing problems.

docs.title: Problem Example
docs.text:
Consider the following Foo class:

#include <iostream>

class Foo
{
public:
  Foo(int size) : size_(size),
                 capacity_(size_ + 2),
                 length_(capacity_)
  {}

  void print() {
    std::cout << "Size: " << size_ << " Capacity:  " << capacity_ << " Length: " << length_  << std::endl;
  }

private:
  int length_;
  int capacity_;
  int size_;
};

int main() {
  Foo foo(50);
  foo.print();
}

In this example, we try to initialize length_, capacity_, and size_ by referring to other member variables in the initializer list. However, because class members are initialized in the order in which they are declared in the class, length_ and capacity_ may not be initialized the way we expect.

docs.title: How to Solve It?
docs.text:
To avoid this kind of problem, you should follow these points:

1. Avoid referring to other member variables in the initializer list

2. Order consistency: member variables are initialized in the order in which they are declared in the class

Corrected example:

#include <iostream>

class Foo
{
public:
  Foo(int size) : size_(size),
                 capacity_(size_ + 2),
                 length_(calculateLength(size_))
  {}

  void print() {
    std::cout << "Size: " << size_ << " Capacity:  " << capacity_ << " Length: " << length_  << std::endl;
  }

private:
  int calculateLength(int size) {
    return size + 2;
  }

private:
  int size_;
  int capacity_;
  int length_;
};

int main() {
  Foo foo(50);
  foo.print();
}

docs.title: C++ Pointers vs References | C++​那些​事
docs.text: Last updated：2026-10-13

docs.title: About the Author:
docs.text: Personal WeChat official account:

docs.title: 1. References and Pointers
docs.text:
Overview:

Reference Pointer Must be initialized May be left uninitialized Cannot be null Can be null Cannot change its target Can change its target

A reference must be initialized, whereas a pointer may be left uninitialized.

When we define a reference we must give it an initial value, but a pointer does not need one.

int &r;    //​不​合法​，​没有​初始化​引用​
int *p;    //​合法​，​但​p​为野​指针​，​使用​需要​小心​

A reference cannot be null, whereas a pointer can.

Since a reference cannot be null, we do not need to validate it when using one; with a pointer, however, we must first check whether it is a null pointer, otherwise the program may crash.

void test_p(int* p)
{
    if(p != null_ptr)    //​对​p​所指​对象​赋值​时​需先​判断​p​是否​为空​指针​
        *p = 3;
    return;
}
void test_r(int& r)
{
    r = 3;    //​由于​引用​不能​为空​，​所以​此处​无需​判断​r​的​有效性​就​可以​对​r​直接​赋值​
    return;
}

A reference cannot change its target

A pointer can change what it points to at any time, but a reference can only ever refer to the object it was bound to at initialization and cannot be changed.

int a = 1;
int b = 2;

int &r = a;    //​初始化​引用​r​指向​变量​a
int *p = &a;   //​初始化​指针​p​指向​变量​a

p = &b;        //​指针​p​指向​了​变量​b
r = b;         //​引用​r​依然​指向​a，​但​a​的​值​变成​了​b

docs.title: Lvalue References
docs.text: Ordinary references, which generally represent the identity of an object.

docs.title: Rvalue References
docs.text:
An rvalue reference is a reference that must be bound to an rvalue (a temporary object, an object about to be destroyed); it generally represents the value of an object.

Rvalue references enable move semantics and perfect forwarding, and they serve two main purposes:

  • Eliminating unnecessary object copies when two objects interact, saving computation and storage resources and improving efficiency.
  • Making it simpler and clearer to define generic functions.

docs.title: Reference Collapsing
docs.text:
• X& &, X& &&, X&& & collapse into X&
  • X&& && collapses into X&&

C++ references trade some programmer freedom for greater safety in memory operations and more elegant semantics. For example, the requirement that a reference must be initialized means that when we use one we no longer have to check whether it is null, which keeps the code cleaner and more elegant and avoids pointers flying everywhere. Beyond that scenario, references are also used in the following two situations:

Reference parameters

We generally use const reference parameters for read-only arguments; in this case we both avoid copying the argument and keep the same call syntax as pass-by-value.

void test(const vector<int> &data)
{
    //...
}
int main()
{
    vector<int> data{1,2,3,4,5,6,7,8};
    test(data);
}

Reference return values

C++ lets us overload operators. When overloading certain operators, using a reference return type gives us call syntax identical to the operator's original syntax, preserving the consistency of the operator's semantics. One example is the operator [] — this operator generally needs to return a reference for the result to be correctly modifiable.

vector<int> v(10);
v[5] = 10;    //[]​操作符​返回​引用​，​然后​vector​对应​元素​才能​被​修改​
              //​如果​[]​操作符​不​返回​引用​而是​指针​的话​，​赋值​语句​则​需要​这样​写​
*v[5] = 10;   //​这种​书写​方式​，​完全​不​符合​我们​对​[]​调用​的​认知​，​容易​产生误解​

docs.title: 3. The Performance Gap Between Pointers and References
docs.text:
Is there a performance gap between pointers and references? To answer this kind of question we need to drop down to the assembly level. Let us first write a test1 function that passes its parameter by pointer:

void test1(int* p)
{
    *p = 3;    //​此处​应该​首先​判断​p​是否​为空​，​为了​测试​的​需要​，​此处​我们​没加​。
    return;
}

The assembly code corresponding to this snippet is as follows:

(gdb) disassemble 
Dump of assembler code for function test1(int*):
   0x0000000000400886 <+0>:  push   %rbp
   0x0000000000400887 <+1>:  mov    %rsp,%rbp
   0x000000000040088a <+4>:  mov    %rdi,-0x8(%rbp)
=> 0x000000000040088e <+8>:  mov    -0x8(%rbp),%rax
   0x0000000000400892 <+12>: movl   $0x3,(%rax)
   0x0000000000400898 <+18>: nop
   0x0000000000400899 <+19>: pop    %rbp
   0x000000000040089a <+20>: retq   
End of assembler dump.

In the code above, lines 1 and 2 are the parameter-passing and stack-frame setup; line 3 is parameter passing — the first argument of a call is usually placed in the rdi register, and this line writes the value of the rdi register (the value of the pointer p) onto the stack; line 4 writes the value of p from the stack into the rax register; line 5 writes the immediate value 3 into the memory pointed to by the value in the rax register. Note the parentheses around (%rax) here — they are by no means optional: (%rax) and %rax mean completely different things. (%rax) denotes the memory at the address held in the rax register, which is equivalent to *p in C++ code, whereas %rax denotes the rax register itself, equivalent to the value of p in C++ code. That is why the assembly uses (%rax) rather than %rax.

Now let us write the C++ snippet test2, which passes its parameter by reference:

void test2(int& r)
{
    r = 3;    //​赋值​前​无需​判断​reference​是否​为空​
    return;
}

The assembly code corresponding to this snippet is as follows:

(gdb) disassemble 
Dump of assembler code for function test2(int&):
   0x000000000040089b <+0>:  push   %rbp
   0x000000000040089c <+1>:  mov    %rsp,%rbp
   0x000000000040089f <+4>:  mov    %rdi,-0x8(%rbp)
=> 0x00000000004008a3 <+8>:  mov    -0x8(%rbp),%rax
   0x00000000004008a7 <+12>: movl   $0x3,(%rax)
   0x00000000004008ad <+18>: nop
   0x00000000004008ae <+19>: pop    %rbp
   0x00000000004008af <+20>: retq   
End of assembler dump.

We find that the assembly for test2 is exactly the same as the assembly for test1, which shows that the C++ compiler compiles pointers and references into exactly the same machine code. So a C++ reference is merely "syntactic sugar" over pointer operations: at the underlying implementation level, the C++ compiler implements the two operations in exactly the same way.

docs.title: 3. Summary
docs.text:
C++ introduced references so that, under more restrictive rules of use, they guarantee safety and convenience while keeping the code elegant. Using the right tool in the right situation, references can to some extent avoid the "pointers flying everywhere" situation, which also has a positive effect on program stability. Finally, pointers and references have identical underlying implementations, so there is no need to worry about any performance gap between them.

The above partly references: http://irootlee.com/juicer_pointer_reference/#

docs.title: The C++ sizeof Operator | C++​那些​事

docs.title: The C++ sizeof Operator
docs.text:
First a summary, then real examples below — hands-on time!

  • The size of an empty class is 1 byte
  • Within a class, the virtual functions themselves, member functions (both static and non-static), and static data members take up no storage space in class objects.
  • For a class containing virtual functions, no matter how many virtual functions there are, there is only one virtual pointer — the size of the vptr.
  • With ordinary inheritance, the derived class inherits all the base class's functions and members, and the size must be computed according to byte alignment
  • With virtual-function inheritance, whether single or multiple inheritance, the base class's vptr is inherited. (4 bytes on a 32-bit OS, 8 bytes on a 64-bit OS)!
  • With virtual inheritance, the base class's vptr is inherited. Note that the result is compiler-dependent: GCC merges the virtual base pointer with the virtual function table pointer (e.g. 8/8/16), while MSVC/Windows stores them separately (e.g. 8/8/32); see issue #246.

docs.title: 1. Principle 1
docs.text:
/**
 * @file blackclass.cpp
 * @brief ​空类​的​大小​为​1​字节​
 * @author ​光城​
 * @version v1
 * @date 2019-07-21
 */
#include<iostream>
using namespace std;
class A{};
int main()
{
    cout<<sizeof(A)<<endl;
    return 0;
}

docs.title: 2. Principle 2
docs.text:
/**
 * @file static.cpp
 * @brief ​静态数据​成员​
 * ​静态数据​成员​被​编译器​放在​程序​的​一个​global data members​中​，​它​是​类​的​一个​数据​成员​，​但​不​影响​类​的​大小​。​不管​这个​类​产生​了​多少​个​实例​，​还是​派生​了​多少​新​的​类​，​静态数据​成员​只有​一个​实例​。​静态数据​成员​，​一旦​被​声明​，​就​已经​存在​。 
 * @author ​光城​
 * @version v1
 * @date 2019-07-21
 */
#include<iostream>
using namespace std;
class A
{
    public:
        char b;
        virtual void fun() {};
        static int c;
        static int d;
        static int f;
};

int main()
{
    /**
     * @brief 16  ​字节​对齐​、​静态​变量​不​影响​类​的​大小​、vptr​指针​=8
     */
    cout<<sizeof(A)<<endl; 
    return 0;
}

docs.title: 3. Principle 3
docs.text:
/**
 * @file morevir.cpp
 * @brief ​对于​包含​虚​函数​的​类​，​不管​有​多少​个​虚​函数​，​只有​一个​虚​指针​,vptr​的​大小​。
 * @author ​光城​
 * @version v1
 * @date 2019-07-21
 */
#include<iostream>
using namespace std;
class A{
    virtual void fun();
    virtual void fun1();
    virtual void fun2();
    virtual void fun3();
};
int main()
{
    cout<<sizeof(A)<<endl; // 8
    return 0;
}

docs.title: 4. Principles 4 and 5
docs.text:
/**
 * @file geninhe.cpp
 * @brief 1.​普通​单​继承​,​继承​就是​基类​+​派生类​自身​的​大小​(​注意​字节​对齐​)
 * ​注意​：​类​的​数据​成员​按​其​声明​顺序​加入​内存​，​无​访问​权限​无关​，​只​看​声明​顺序​。
 * 2.​虚单​继承​，​派生类​继承​基类​vptr
 * @author ​光城​
 * @version v1
 * @date 2019-07-21
 */

#include<iostream>

using namespace std;

class A
{
    public:
        char a;
        int b;
};

/**
 * @brief ​此时​B​按照​顺序​：
 * char a
 * int b
 * short a
 * long b
 * ​根据​字节​对齐​4+4+8+8=24
 * 
 * ​或​编译器​优化​
 * char a
 * short a
 * int b
 * long b
 * ​根据​字节​对齐​2+2+4+8=16
 */
class B:A
{
    public:
        short a;
        long b;
};
/**
* ​把​A​的​成员​拆开​看​，char​为​1，int​为​4，​所以​是​1+（3）+4+1+（3）=12，（）​为​字节​补齐​
*/
class C
{
    A a;
    char c;
};

class A1
{
    virtual void fun(){}
};
class C1:public A1
{
};


int main()
{
    cout<<sizeof(A)<<endl; // 8
    cout<<sizeof(B)<<endl; // 16 ​或​ 24
    cout<<sizeof(C)<<endl; // 12

    /**
     * @brief ​对于​虚单​函数​继承​，​派生类​也​继承​了​基类​的​vptr，​所以​是​8​字节​
     */
    cout<<sizeof(C1)<<endl; // 8 
    return 0;
}

docs.title: 5. Principle 6
docs.text:
/**
 * @file virnhe.cpp
 * @brief ​虚​继承​
 * @author ​光城​

 */

#include<iostream>
using namespace std;
class A
{
    virtual void fun() {}
};
class B
{
    virtual void fun2() {}

class C : virtual public  A, virtual public B
{

     * @brief 8 8 16  ​派生类​虚​继承​多个​虚​函数​，​会​继承​所有​虚​函数​的​vptr
     */
    cout<<sizeof(A)<<" "<<sizeof(B)<<" "<<sizeof(C);

    return 0;
}

docs.title: C++ Smart Pointers as Function Parameters
C++​那些​事​: When Smart Pointers Should Be Function Parameters
docs.text:
We often see some functions that take smart pointers as parameters, while others take raw pointers. Which one should you use, and what are the rules for deciding?

This section uses tips from abseil to explain.

Take the following code — what is wrong with it?

bool CanYouPetTheDog(const std::shared_ptr<Dog>& dog,
                     absl::Duration min_delay) {
  return dog->GetLastPetTime() + min_delay < absl::Now();
}

The CanYouPetTheDog function does not affect the ownership of its dog parameter, yet its signature requires it to be stored in a std::shared_ptr. This creates an unnecessary dependency on a particular ownership model, even though the function itself does not need one. This dependency prevents callers from using other models, such as std::unique_ptr or objects constructed on the stack.

docs.title: Use Pointers/References
docs.text:
Use references or pointers when ownership is not affected. By using references/pointers, we remove the dependency on a particular ownership model and allow our function to work with any object of type Dog.

bool CanYouPetTheDog(const Dog& dog, absl::Duration min_delay) {
  return dog.GetLastPetTime() + min_delay < absl::Now();
}

With this definition, the function can be called regardless of the caller's ownership model:

Dog stack_dog;
if (CanYouPetTheDog(stack_dog, delay)) { ... }

auto heap_dog = std::make_unique<Dog>();
if (CanYouPetTheDog(*heap_dog, delay)) { ... }

CustomPetPtr<Dog> custom_dog = CreateDog();
if (CanYouPetTheDog(*custom_dog, delay)) { ... }

If the function modifies the value being passed, pass a mutable reference or a raw pointer, using the same approach as above.

docs.title: Use Smart Pointers
docs.text:
Use a smart pointer when the function modifies ownership. The code below provides several overloads for different smart pointer parameters. The first overload assumes ownership of the passed object; the second adds a shared reference to the passed object. Which of these operations applies depends on how the caller wants to handle ownership of the Dog. Ownership of a Dog that lives on the stack cannot be taken, because ownership cannot be taken away from the stack.

class Human {
 public:
  ...
  void Adopt(std::unique_ptr<Dog> dog) {
    pets_.push_back(std::move(dog));
  }
  void Adopt(std::shared_ptr<Cat> cat) {
    pets_.push_back(std::move(cat));
  }

 private:
  std::vector<std::shared_ptr<Pet>> pets_;
  ...
};

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
If ownership is not being transferred or modified, you should avoid taking smart pointers as function parameters.

docs.title: C++ static Members and Lifetime | C++​那些​事
docs.text: Last updated：2026-10-13

docs.title: About the Author
docs.text:
WeChat official account:

When used with different kinds of entities, the static keyword has different meanings. We can use the static keyword:

Static variables: variables in a function, variables in a class

Static class members: class objects and functions in a class

Now let's look at these uses of static in detail:

Static variables

  • Static variables in a function

When a variable is declared static, space is allocated for the lifetime of the program. Even if the function is called multiple times, space for the static variable is allocated only once, and the value of the variable from the previous call is carried over to the next function call. This is very useful in C / C++ or any other application that needs to store the previous state of a function.

#include <iostream> 
#include <string> 
using namespace std; 

void demo() 
{ 
    // static variable 
    static int count = 0; 
    cout << count << " "; 

    // value is updated and 
    // will be carried to next 
    // function calls 
    count++; 
} 

int main() 
{ 
    for (int i=0; i<5; i++)  
        demo(); 
    return 0; 
}

Output:

0 1 2 3 4

You can see in the program above that the variable count is declared static. Therefore, its value is carried across function calls. Each time the function is called, the count variable is not initialized again.

  • Static variables in a class

Since variables declared static are initialized only once — because they are allocated space in separate static storage — static variables in a class are shared by objects. There cannot be multiple copies of the same static variable for different objects. It is also for this reason that static variables cannot be initialized using a constructor.

#include<iostream> 
using namespace std; 

class Apple 
{ 
public: 
    static int i; 

    Apple() 
    { 
        // Do nothing 
    }; 
}; 

int main() 
{ 
Apple obj1; 
Apple obj2; 
obj1.i =2; 
obj2.i = 3; 

// prints value of i 
cout << obj1.i<<" "<<obj2.i; 
}

You can see in the program above that we tried to create multiple copies of the static variable i for multiple objects. But that did not happen. Therefore, a static variable in a class should be explicitly initialized by the user outside the class, using the class name and the scope resolution operator, as follows:

#include<iostream> 
using namespace std; 

class Apple 
{ 
public: 
    static int i; 

    Apple() 
    { 
        // Do nothing 
    }; 
}; 

int Apple::i = 1; 

int main() 
{ 
    Apple obj; 
    // prints value of i 
    cout << obj.i; 
}

Output:

1

Static members

  • Class objects as static

Just like variables, objects declared static also have a scope that lasts until the end of the program's lifetime.

Consider the following program, in which the object is non-static.

#include<iostream> 
using namespace std; 

class Apple 
{ 
    int i; 
    public: 
        Apple() 
        { 
            i = 0; 
            cout << "Inside Constructor\n"; 
        } 
        ~Apple() 
        { 
            cout << "Inside Destructor\n"; 
        } 
}; 

int main() 
{ 
    int x = 0; 
    if (x==0) 
    { 
        Apple obj; 
    } 
    cout << "End of main\n"; 
}

Output:

Inside Constructor
Inside Destructor
End of main

In the program above, the object is declared non-static inside the if block. Therefore, the variable's scope is only within the if block. Hence, when the object is created the constructor is called, and the destructor is called at the same moment the control of the if block passes it, because the object's scope is limited to the if block in which it is declared.

If we declare the object as static, let's now see how the output changes.

#include<iostream> 
using namespace std; 

class Apple 
{ 
    int i; 
    public: 
        Apple() 
        { 
            i = 0; 
            cout << "Inside Constructor\n"; 
        } 
        ~Apple() 
        { 
            cout << "Inside Destructor\n"; 
        } 
}; 

int main() 
{ 
    int x = 0; 
    if (x==0) 
    { 
        static Apple obj; 
    } 
    cout << "End of main\n"; 
}

Output:

Inside Constructor
End of main
Inside Destructor

You can clearly see the change in the output. Now, the destructor is called after the end of main. This is because the scope of a static object spans the entire lifetime of the program.

  • Static functions in a class

Just like static data members or static variables in a class, static member functions do not depend on objects of the class. We are allowed to invoke a static member function using an object and '.'. However, it is recommended to invoke static members using the class name and the scope resolution operator.

Static member functions are allowed to access only static data members or other static member functions; they cannot access the class's non-static data members or member functions.

#include<iostream> 
using namespace std; 

class Apple 
{ 
    public: 
        // static member function 
        static void printMsg() 
        {
            cout<<"Welcome to Apple!"; 
        }
}; 

// main function 
int main() 
{ 
    // invoking a static member function 
    Apple::printMsg(); 
}

Output:

Welcome to Apple!

Restricting the scope of access

static also serves to restrict the scope of access (similar to an anonymous namespace). From issue: https://github.com/Light-City/CPlusPlusThings/issues/142

// source1.cpp
extern void sayHello();
const char* msg = "Hello World!\n";
int main()
{
    sayHello();
    return 0;
}

// source2.cpp
#include <cstdio>
extern char* msg;
void sayHello()
{
    printf("%s", msg);
}

g++ compiles the two code files above normally and prints Hello World!, but if you add static to msg in source1.cpp, it causes an 'undefined reference to msg' compilation error:

// source1.cpp
extern void sayHello();
static const char* msg = "Hello World!\n";
int main()
{
    sayHello();
    return 0;
}

docs.title: Internal Linkage of static (Restricting the Scope of Access)
docs.text:
Thanks to issue #142 for pointing this out: when static qualifies a global variable/function, it also serves to restrict the scope of access — it changes its linkage from external linkage to internal linkage, with an effect similar to an anonymous namespace:

  • A global variable that is not static: other translation units can access it through an extern declaration;
  • A static global variable/function: visible only within the current translation unit; even an extern declaration cannot link to it (undefined reference).

In modern C++ it is preferable to use an anonymous namespace to express "visible only in this file" (it also works for types), but understanding this aspect of static is very important when reading older code.

// file1.cpp
static int hidden = 42;          // ​内部​链接​：​其他​文件​ extern ​不​可见​
int visible = 1;                 // ​外部​链接​：​其他​文件​可​ extern ​访问​

namespace {                      // ​匿名​命名​空间​：​等价​且​更​现代​的​写法​
    int also_hidden = 7;
}

docs.title: C++ std::function in Depth
docs.text:
While writing C++ code recently I used is_function, and took the opportunity to look at how it is implemented in the standard library, which raised some questions. We all learned about the three dots ..., but do you know what six dots ...... mean?

Likewise, given a piece of code like this:

template<typename... Args>
struct foo(Args......);

Do you know what it means?

Let's dig into the details together!

docs.title: 1. Six Dots
docs.text:
Six dots are usually called two ellipsis operators. We can split the six dots apart and get the following three cases

template <typename... Args> void foo1(Args......)
template <typename... Args> void foo2(Args... ...)
template <typename... Args> void foo3(Args..., ...)

Now it is easier to read. Let's look at the code of std::is_function.

docs.title: 2. Implementation Details of is_function
docs.text:
The implementation of std::is_function involves a primary template and two partial specializations:

// ​主​模板​，​假设​提供​的​类型​不是​函数​类型​
template<typename T>
struct is_function : std::false_type {};

// ​偏​特化​，​用于​正常​的​函数​类型​
template<typename Ret, typename... Args>
struct is_function<Ret(Args...)> : std::true_type {};

// ​偏​特化​，​用于​变参​函数​类型​
template<typename Ret, typename... Args>
struct is_function<Ret(Args......)> : std::true_type {};
  • The primary template assumes the given type is not a function type, and yields std::false_type as the result.
  • The first partial specialization covers normal function types, where Ret denotes the return type and Args... the parameter types. If the given type matches such a function signature, std::true_type is the result.
  • The second partial specialization covers variadic function types, where the ellipsis indicates the function takes a variable number of arguments. Likewise, if the given type matches such a function signature, std::true_type is the result.

docs.title: 3. Usage Example
docs.text:
Finally, here is an example of using std::is_function:

#include <iostream>
#include <type_traits>

int func(int x, int y) { return x + y; }
int vararg_func(int x, ...) { return x; }

int main() {
    std::cout << std::boolalpha;
    std::cout << "Is func a function? " << std::is_function<decltype(func)>::value << std::endl;
    std::cout << "Is vararg_func a function? " << std::is_function<decltype(vararg_func)>::value << std::endl;
    return 0;
}

This will output:

Is func a function? true
Is vararg_func a function? true

Got it? End of this section~

docs.title: A Deep Dive into std::cref, std::ref and std::reference_wrapper in C++
docs.text:
In C++ programming, we sometimes need to pass references around without copying, or to use constant objects where a reference is required. To address these problems, the C++ standard library provides three useful tools: std::cref, std::ref and std::reference_wrapper. This article takes a deep look at the purpose of these tools, their differences, and their practical applications.

Besides, we know that in Rust an Unwrap method is often implemented. How do we do that in C++?

That brings us to a piece of Apache Arrow code:

std::optional<std::reference_wrapper<const TransportStatusDetail>>
TransportStatusDetail::Unwrap(const Status& status) {
  std::shared_ptr<StatusDetail> detail = status.detail();
  if (!detail) return std::nullopt;
  if (detail->type_id() != kTypeId) return std::nullopt;
  return std::cref(arrow::internal::checked_cast<const TransportStatusDetail&>(*detail));
}

Afterwards we can call it like this to extract the actual TransportStatusDetail from the Status.

Status status(transportDetail);
auto result = Unwrap(status);

Below we'll look at it from several angles, and finally give the complete demo code.

docs.title: 1. std::cref: Creating a Reference to a Constant
docs.text:
std::cref is a template function used to create a reference to a constant object. It returns a std::reference_wrapper object that can be used wherever a reference is needed. This is particularly useful for passing function arguments, since it lets us pass constant objects without copying while preserving reference semantics.

Example:

#include <iostream>
#include <functional>

void printValue(const int& value) {
    std::cout << "Value: " << value << std::endl;
}

int main() {
    int number = 42;
    auto crefNumber = std::cref(number);

    printValue(crefNumber);  // ​使用​常量​引用​传递​参数​

    return 0;
}

docs.title: 2. std::ref: Creating a Modifiable Reference
docs.text:
Unlike std::cref, std::ref is a template function used to create a reference to a modifiable object. It returns a std::reference_wrapper object that can be used wherever a reference is needed, while also allowing the referenced object to be modified.

Example:

#include <iostream>
#include <functional>

void modifyValue(int& value) {
    value *= 2;
}

int main() {
    int number = 42;
    auto refNumber = std::ref(number);

    modifyValue(refNumber);  // ​使用​可​修改​的​引用​作为​参数​

    std::cout << "Modified Value: " << number << std::endl;

    return 0;
}

docs.title: 3. std::reference_wrapper: A Wrapper for References
docs.text:
std::reference_wrapper is a template class used to wrap references so they can be stored in containers or passed around as references. It provides reference-like syntax and works with the standard containers, since containers cannot store references directly.

Example:

#include <iostream>
#include <vector>
#include <functional>

int main() {
    int number1 = 42;
    int number2 = 73;

    std::vector<std::reference_wrapper<int>> numbers = {std::ref(number1), std::ref(number2)};

    for (auto& num : numbers) {
        num.get() += 10;  // ​修改​原始​对象​的​值​
    }

    std::cout << "Number 1: " << number1 << std::endl;
    std::cout << "Number 2: " << number2 << std::endl;

    return 0;
}

In this example, std::reference_wrapper lets us wrap references in a container and then access and modify the original objects' values through the get() method.

docs.title: 4. Unwrap Demo
docs.text:
Here is the concrete code snippet; for the complete code see the content on Knowledge Planet (zhishixingqiu).

std::optional<std::reference_wrapper<const TransportStatusDetail>> Unwrap(const Status& status) {
    std::shared_ptr<StatusDetail> detail = status.detail();
    if (!detail) return std::nullopt;
    if (detail->type_id() != kTypeId) return std::nullopt;
    return std::cref(static_cast<const TransportStatusDetail&>(*detail));
}

int main() {
    // ​创建​ TransportStatusDetail ​对象​
    std::shared_ptr<StatusDetail> transportDetail = std::make_shared<TransportStatusDetail>();

    // ​创建​ Status ​对象​并​传入​ TransportStatusDetail ​对象​
    Status status(transportDetail);

    auto result = Unwrap(status);

    if (result) {
        const TransportStatusDetail& detail = result.value().get();
        // ​使用​ detail ​进行​操作​
        std::cout << "TransportStatusDetail found." << std::endl;
    } else {
        std::cout << "No valid TransportStatusDetail found." << std::endl;
    }

    return 0;
}

About struct in C and C++, see All About struct

Generally speaking, a struct is better seen as the implementation body of a data structure, while a class is better seen as the implementation body of an object.

Differences:

The most essential difference is the default access control

The default inheritance access permission: for a struct it is public, for a class it is private.

As the implementation body of a data structure, a struct's default data access control is public, whereas as the implementation body of an object, a class's default member variable access control is private.
