docs.title: 1. struct in C
docs.text:
• In C, a struct is used purely as a composite data type; that is, only data members can be placed in the struct declaration, not functions.
  • C struct declarations cannot use C++ access modifiers such as public, protected and private, whereas in C++ they can.
  • In C, when defining a struct variable with the definition below, you must include the struct keyword.
  • A C struct cannot be inherited (the concept does not exist).
  • If a struct's name is the same as a function's name, the program still runs and calls normally! For example: you can define void Base() {} without conflicting with struct Base.

Complete example:

#include<stdio.h>

struct Base {            // public
    int v1; 
//    public:      //error
        int v2; 
    //private:
        int v3; 
    //void print(){       // c​中​不能​在​结构​体中​嵌入​函数​
    //    printf("%s\n","hello world");
    //};    //error!
};

void Base(){
    printf("%s\n","I am Base func");
}
//struct Base base1;  //ok
//Base base2; //error
int main() {
    struct Base base;
    base.v1=1;
    //base.print();
    printf("%d\n",base.v1);
    Base();
    return 0;
}

The final output:

1
I am Base func

For the complete code see: struct_func.c

docs.title: 2. struct in C++
docs.text:
Compared with C:

  • In a C++ struct you can define not only data but also functions.
  • A C++ struct can use access modifiers such as public, protected and private.
  • A C++ struct can be used directly without the struct keyword.
  • C++ inheritance
  • If a struct's name is the same as a function's name, the program still runs and calls normally! But when defining a struct variable, you can only use the form with struct!

For example:

Case 1: defining a struct alias without typedef

Before a function of the same name is added:

struct Student {

};
//Student(){}
struct Student s; //ok
Student s;  //ok

After a function of the same name is added:

struct Student {

};
Student(){}
struct Student s; //ok
Student s;  //error

Case 2: defining a struct alias with typedef

typedef struct Base1 {         
    int v1;
    int v3;
    public:     //​显示​声明​public
    int v2;
    void print(){       
        printf("%s\n","hello world");
    };    
}B;
//void B() {}  //error! ​符号​ "B" ​已经​被​定义​为​一个​ "struct Base1" ​的​别名​

The first three cases

#include<iostream>
#include<stdio.h>

struct Base {         
    int v1;
//    private:   //error!
        int v3;
    public:     //​显示​声明​public
        int v2;

        printf("%s\n","hello world");

};

int main() {
    struct Base base1;  //ok
    Base base2; //ok
    Base base;
    base.v1=1;
    base.v3=2;
    base.print();
    printf("%d\n",base.v1);
    printf("%d\n",base.v3);
    return 0;
}

Inheritance example

Same-name function

docs.title: C++ Tail Recursion
docs.text: Tail-call optimization is a special optimization technique applicable to recursive functions that can greatly reduce the stack space consumed by recursive calls. With tail-call optimization, the compiler can avoid creating a new stack frame when executing tail recursion and instead reuse the current stack frame, reducing the risk of stack overflow and improving performance.

docs.title: What Is Tail Recursion?
docs.text: When a recursive call returns and no other operations remain to be performed, the recursion is called tail recursion. In this situation, the compiler can replace the recursion with a loop structure, avoiding the overhead of repeated function calls.

docs.title: An Example of Non-Tail Recursion (Fibonacci)
docs.text:
Your fibonacci_non_tail() function is a standard non-tail-recursive implementation:

int fibonacci_non_tail(int n) {
    if (n <= 1) {
        return n;
    }
    return fibonacci_non_tail(n - 1) + fibonacci_non_tail(n - 2);
}

In this implementation, after the recursive calls fibonacci_non_tail(n - 1) and fibonacci_non_tail(n - 2) return, their results still have to be added together, so this is not tail recursion. Every call must save context information so that computation can resume after the recursion returns, causing the stack space to grow rapidly.

docs.title: Example of Tail-Call Optimization
docs.text:
fibonacci_tail() takes the tail-recursive approach:

int fibonacci_tail_helper(int n, int a, int b) {
    if (n == 0) {
        return a;
    }
    return fibonacci_tail_helper(n - 1, b, a + b);
}

int fibonacci_tail(int n) {
    return fibonacci_tail_helper(n, 0, 1);
}

Here fibonacci_tail_helper() is tail recursive. As you can see, after the recursive call fibonacci_tail_helper(n - 1, b, a + b), the function has nothing left to do: it directly returns the result of the recursive call. The recursive call is therefore in the "tail" of the function, with no additional operations to perform after it.

docs.title: Advantages of Tail-Call Optimization
docs.text:
• Less stack space usage: since the context of recursive calls does not need to be saved, the compiler can reuse stack frames and avoid stack bloat.
  • Prevents stack overflow: tail-call optimization allows the recursion depth to reach very large values without a stack overflow.
  • More efficient: on compilers that support tail-call optimization, tail recursion performs close to an iterative implementation, eliminating the overhead of recursive function calls.

docs.title: Performance Testing
docs.text: Finally, a benchmark of the above shows that tail-call optimization is very useful in this scenario — you can see the performance difference is huge!

docs.title: 1. The this Pointer
docs.text:
Many of you, I'm sure, are learning Python. Python has self; the C++ analogue is the this pointer. So let's dig into how the this pointer is used inside a class!

First, let's talk about what the this pointer is for:

(1) An object's this pointer is not part of the object itself and does not affect the result of sizeof(object).

(2) this lives inside the class scope: when a non-static member function accesses a non-static member of the class, the compiler automatically passes the address of the object itself to the function as an implicit argument. In other words, even if you do not write the this pointer explicitly, the compiler adds it at compile time. As an implicit formal parameter of every non-static member function, all member access goes through this.

Next, how to use the this pointer:

(1) When returning the class object itself from a non-static member function of the class, simply use return *this.

(2) When a parameter has the same name as a member variable, write this->n = n (it cannot be written as n = n).

Also, online you may see this being resolved by the compiler as A *const or A const * — which one is it? Let's find out by setting a breakpoint and debugging:

Given the following example:

#include<iostream>
#include<cstring>


using namespace std;
class Person{
public:
    typedef enum {
        BOY = 0, 
        GIRL 
    }SexType;
    Person(char *n, int a,SexType s){
        name=new char[strlen(n)+1];
        strcpy(name,n);
        age=a;
        sex=s;
    }
    int get_age() const{

        return this->age; 
    }
    Person& add_age(int a){
        age+=a;
        return *this; 
    }
    ~Person(){
        delete [] name;
    }
private:
    char * name;
    int age;
    SexType sex;
};


int main(){
    Person p("zhangsan",20,Person::BOY); 
    cout<<p.get_age()<<endl;
    cout<<p.add_age(10).get_age()<<endl;
    return 0;
}

For this simple program, surely there is no problem: a class is defined, then the constructor initializes it, and we get the person's age, set it, and get it again!

To verify which one the this pointer is, we now set a breakpoint at add_age and run:

You will find that the compiler automatically gives us A* const, not A const *this!

Next, there is also a const function above, so let's set a breakpoint on get_age, as follows:

You will find that the compiler turns the this above into const A* const. You could have guessed this: since the function is a const function, it can only access const variables and const functions and must not modify the values of other variables, so it needs a this that points to variables that cannot be modified — that is, const A*. And since this itself is a const pointer, the result is const A* const!

Summary: this is constructed before execution of a member function begins and cleared after the member's execution ends. The get_age function above gets resolved to get_age(const A * const this), and add_age gets resolved to add_age(A* const this, int a). In C++ classes and structs differ in only one way: class members are private by default, while struct members are public. this is a pointer to the class; if it were a struct, this would be a pointer to the struct.

A union is a space-saving special kind of class: a union can have multiple data members, but at any moment only one of them can have a value. When some member is assigned, the other members become undefined. Unions have the following characteristics:

  • The default access specifier is public
  • They may have constructors and destructors
  • They may not have members of reference type
  • They may not inherit from other classes and may not serve as base classes
  • They may not have virtual functions
  • The members of an anonymous union can be accessed directly in the scope where the union is defined
  • An anonymous union may not contain protected or private members
  • A global anonymous union must be static

docs.title: Changing Accessibility
docs.text:
class Base{
public:
 std::size_t size() const { return n;  }
protected:
 std::size_t n;
};
class Derived : private Base {
public:
 using Base::size;
protected:
 using Base::n;
};

Class Derived privately inherits Base, so for it the member variable n and the member function size are private. By using using declarations, their accessibility can be changed: in the example above, size can be accessed with public permission and n with protected permission. For the complete code see: derived_base.cpp

docs.title: Function Overloading
docs.text:
During inheritance, a derived class can override zero or more instances of an overloaded function; as soon as one overloaded version is defined, all the other overloaded versions become invisible.

If, for a set of overloaded functions in a base class, we need to change one of them in the derived class and keep the others visible, we would have to redefine every version, which is extremely tedious.

#include <iostream>
using namespace std;

class Base{
    public:
        void f(){ cout<<"f()"<<endl;
        }
        void f(int n){
            cout<<"Base::f(int)"<<endl;
        }
};

class Derived : private Base {
    public:
        using Base::f;
        void f(int n){
            cout<<"Derived::f(int)"<<endl;
        }
};

int main()
{
    Base b;
    Derived d;
    d.f();
    d.f(1);
    return 0;
}
In the code above, a using declaration in the derived class names a function without specifying a parameter list, so a single using declaration for a base-class member function adds all of its overloaded instances to the derived class's scope. At this point, the derived class only needs to define the functions specific to it, without redefining the other functions it inherits.

For the complete code see: using_derived.cpp

docs.title: C++ vector resize vs reserve
docs.text:
In C++, resize and reserve are two member functions of containers (for example std::vector) used to manage a vector's size and memory allocation.

For example:

std::vector<int> v1;
v1.resize(1000); //allocation + instance creation
cout <<(v1.size() == 1000)<< endl;   //prints 1
cout <<(v1.capacity()==1000)<< endl; //prints 1

std::vector<int> v2;
v2.reserve(1000); //only allocation
cout <<(v2.size() == 1000)<< endl;   //prints 0
cout <<(v2.capacity()==1000)<< endl; //prints 1

The resize function changes the size of the container; it can increase or decrease the number of elements in the container. When the container's size is increased, the newly added elements are initialized. When the size is decreased, elements beyond the new size are removed.

The reserve function pre-allocates the container's memory without changing its size. It can be used to allocate enough memory in advance, avoiding frequent reallocation and thereby improving performance. Note, though, that calling reserve does not change the container's size — it only allocates enough memory space for the container.

It is worth noting that resize and reserve differ in which container types they are available on. The resize function is available for most container types, while reserve is only valid for containers with dynamic size, such as std::vector and std::deque. For fixed-size container types (such as std::array), calling reserve has no effect.

From the source-code level:

void resize(size_type new_size, value_type value = value_type()) {
    if (new_size < size()) {
        erase(begin() + new_size, end()); // ​移除​超出​新​大小​的​元素​
    } else {
        insert(end(), new_size - size(), value); // ​添加​新元素​
    }
}
void reserve(size_type _n) {
    if (__n > max_size())
     __throw_length_error(__N("vector::reserve"));
   if (capacity() < __n)
     _M_reallocate(__n);
}

End of this section

docs.title: 1. Virtual Functions and Runtime Polymorphism
docs.text:
Corresponding code: emp.cpp

The invocation of a virtual function depends on the type of the object pointed to or referred to, not on the type of the pointer or reference itself.

docs.title: 2. vptr and vtable
docs.text: See vptr and vtable

docs.title: 3. Default Arguments in Virtual Functions
docs.text:
Corresponding code: default_arg.cpp

Default arguments are statically bound, while virtual functions are dynamically bound. Which default argument is used depends on the type of the pointer or reference itself, not on the type of the object.

docs.title: 4. Is It Allowed?
docs.text:
(1) Can a static function be declared virtual?

There are two main reasons:

A static function cannot be declared virtual, nor can it be qualified with the const or volatile keywords

A static member function does not belong to any class object or class instance, so adding virtual to such a function is meaningless.

Virtual functions rely on the vptr and the vtable. The vptr is a pointer, created in the class's constructor, and can only be accessed through the this pointer; static member functions have no this pointer, so they cannot access the vptr.

Code to study: static_error.cpp

(2) Can a constructor be virtual?

A constructor cannot be declared virtual. Moreover, apart from inline and explicit, a constructor may not use any other keyword.

Why can't a constructor be virtual?

Although the virtual function table (vtable) is built at compile time, the pointer to the virtual function table (vptr) is only generated at runtime when the object is instantiated. If a class contains virtual functions, the compiler adds code in the constructor to create the vptr. Here comes the problem: if the constructor were virtual, it would need the vptr to access the vtable, but at that moment the vptr does not exist yet. Therefore, a constructor cannot be virtual.

The reason we use virtual functions is that we need polymorphic dispatch with incomplete information. A constructor, on the other hand, is used to initialize an instance, and the type of the instance must be definite. Therefore, there is no need to declare a constructor virtual.

Code to study:

  • copy_consrtuct.cpp

  • vir_con.cpp

(3) Can a destructor be virtual?

A destructor can be declared virtual. If we need to delete a base-class pointer that points to a derived class, the destructor should be declared virtual. In fact, as long as a class might be inherited by other classes, a virtual destructor should be declared (even if that destructor does nothing).

Code to study:

  • full_virde.cpp

  • vir_de.cpp

(4) Can a virtual function be private?

  • When a base-class pointer points to a derived-class object, the derived class's function is invoked;
  • int main() must be declared a friend of the Base class, otherwise compilation fails. The compiler reports an error: ptr cannot access the private function. Of course, if the base class is declared public and the derived class private, the problem disappears.

Code to study:

  • virtual_function.cpp
  • virtual_function1.cpp

(5) Can a virtual function be inlined?

Usually the compiler considers whether to inline class member functions. But a virtual function invoked through a base-class pointer or reference can never be inlined. Of course, when a virtual function is called on an actual object or invoked statically, it can be inlined, and a statically invoked virtual destructor will certainly be expanded inline.

  • A virtual function can be an inline function; inline is allowed to qualify a virtual function, but a virtual function cannot be inlined when it exhibits polymorphic behavior.
  • Inlining is a suggestion to the compiler to inline at compile time, while the polymorphism of virtual functions happens at runtime; the compiler cannot know which code will be invoked at runtime, so a virtual function cannot be inlined when it behaves polymorphically (at runtime).
  • The only time inline virtual can be inlined is when the compiler knows which class the object being called belongs to (for example Base::who()), which only happens when the compiler has an actual object rather than a pointer or reference to the object.

Code to study:

  • virtual_inline.cpp

  • inline_virtual.cpp

docs.title: 5. RTTI and dynamic_cast
docs.text:
RTTI (Run-Time Type Identification) allows a program to use a base class's pointer or reference to check the actual derived class type of the object they point to.

In object-oriented programming, we sometimes need to query at runtime whether an object can be used as a certain polymorphic type. Similar to Java's instanceof and C#'s as and is operators, C++ provides dynamic_cast for dynamic casting. Compared with C-style casts and C++ reinterpret_cast, dynamic_cast provides type-safety checks and is a capability-query-based conversion, so dynamic_cast is the preferred choice for conversions between polymorphic types.

  • warn_rtti.cpp

docs.title: 1. volatile
docs.text: Reading or writing a variable qualified with volatile triggers some observable side effects, and those observable side effects are determined by factors outside the program.

docs.title: 2. Applications of volatile
docs.text:
(1) Hardware registers of parallel devices (such as status registers). Suppose we want to initialize a device, and one of its registers is 0xff800000.

int  *output = (unsigned  int *)0xff800000; //​定义​一个​IO​端口​；  
int   init(void)  
{  
    int i;  
    for(i=0;i< 10;i++)
    {  
    *output = i;  
    }  
}
After compiler optimization, the compiler decides the whole loop above is pointless and has no effect on the final result, because in the end the pointer output is just assigned 9 — so the code the compiler finally produces is equivalent to: 
int  init(void)  
{  
    *output = 9;  
}
If the process of initializing this external device must assign values sequentially as in the code above, the optimization clearly fails to achieve the goal. Conversely, if instead of writing to this port repeatedly you read from it repeatedly, the result is the same: after optimization, the compiler may perform your code's reads from this address only once. Yet from the code's point of view there is nothing wrong. This is when volatile should be used to tell the compiler that this variable is unstable and must not be optimized when encountered. (2) A variable accessed inside an interrupt service routine;

static int i=0;

int main()
{
    while(1)
    {
    if(i) dosomething();
    }
}

/* Interrupt service routine */
void IRS()
{
    i=1;
}
The intent of the example above is that when an interrupt occurs, the interrupt service routine IRS handles it and changes the program variable i so that main calls the dosomething function. However, since the compiler sees that i is never modified inside main, it may perform the read from i into a register only once, and then every if check uses that "copy of i" in the register, so dosomething never gets called. If the variable i is qualified with volatile, the compiler guarantees that reads and writes of i are not optimized away, ensuring that after i is changed by an external program the change is promptly visible to the original program. (3) Variables shared by multiple tasks in multi-threaded applications. When several threads share a variable whose value can be changed by any one of them, it should be declared volatile. Its purpose is to prevent the compiler's optimization from loading the variable from memory into a CPU register, where a change made by one thread might not be synchronized to the other threads in time and cause program errors. volatile means the compiler must genuinely fetch the variable from memory on every access, instead of using the value already sitting in a register. Example: 
volatile  bool bStop=false;  //bStop ​为​共享​全局变量​  
//​第一个​线程​
void threadFunc1()
{
    ...
    while(!bStop){...}
}
//​第二个​线程​终止​上面​的​线程​循环​
void threadFunc2()
{
    ...
    bStop = true;
}
To terminate the first thread's loop from the second thread, if bStop is not defined with volatile the loop becomes an infinite one, because bStop has already been read into a register, and the register's copy of bStop never becomes FALSE. With volatile, each iteration reads bStop's value from memory, and there is no infinite loop.

Knowing the application scenarios of volatile is an effective way to distinguish C/C++ programmers from embedded developers: embedded folks constantly deal with hardware, interrupts, RTOSes and so on, all of which require volatile variables. Not understanding volatile invites disaster in program design.

docs.title: 3. Common volatile Questions
docs.text:
The questions below show whether an interviewee truly understands volatile. (1) Can a parameter be both const and volatile? Why? Yes. One example is a read-only status register. It is volatile because it may be changed unexpectedly. It is const because the program should not try to modify it. (2) Can a pointer be volatile? Why? Yes, although this is not common. One example is when an interrupt service routine modifies a pointer that points to a buffer. (3) What is wrong with the following function? 

int square(volatile int *ptr) 
{ 
return *ptr * *ptr; 
}
This code is a bit devious. Its intent is to return the square of the value pointed to by ptr, but since ptr points to a volatile parameter, the compiler will produce something like the following: 
int square(volatile int *ptr) 
{ 
int a,b; 
a = *ptr; 
b = *ptr; 
return a * b; 
}
Since the value of *ptr may change unexpectedly, a and b may be different. As a result, this code may not return the square you expect! The correct code is as follows: 
long square(volatile int *ptr) 
{ 
int a=*ptr; 
return a * a; 
}

docs.title: 4. Using volatile
docs.text:
• The volatile keyword is a type modifier; a variable declared with it can be changed by factors unknown to the compiler (the operating system, hardware, other threads, etc.). Use volatile to tell the compiler not to optimize such objects.

  • A variable declared volatile must be read from memory on every access (a variable not qualified with volatile may be read from a CPU register because of compiler optimization)

  • const can be volatile (e.g. a read-only status register)
  • Pointers can be volatile

docs.title: C++ Virtual Pointer and vtable Mechanism
About the Author:
docs.text: Personal WeChat official account:

docs.title: 1. Basic Theory
docs.text:
To implement virtual functions, C++ uses a special form of late binding known as the virtual table. The virtual table is a lookup table used to resolve function calls in a dynamic/late-bound fashion. The virtual table goes by other names too, such as "vtable", "virtual function table", "virtual method table", or "dispatch table".

The virtual table is actually quite simple, even if it is a little complicated to describe in words. First, every class that uses virtual functions (or is derived from a class that uses virtual functions) has its own virtual table. This table is simply a static array the compiler sets up at compile time. The virtual table contains one entry for each virtual function that can be called by objects of the class. Each entry in this table is just a function pointer pointing to the most-derived function accessible to that class.

Second, the compiler also adds a hidden pointer to the base class, which we call vptr. The vptr is set automatically when an instance of the class is created, so that it points to the virtual table for that class. Unlike the this pointer, which is really a function parameter the compiler uses to resolve self-reference, the vptr is a real pointer.

Consequently, it makes every class object bigger by one pointer. It also means the vptr is inherited by derived classes, which is important.

docs.title: 2. Implementation and Internal Structure
docs.text:
Now let's look at automatically and manually manipulating the vptr to obtain addresses and invoke virtual functions!

Before looking at the code, here is a call diagram to make things easier to understand:

The code all follows the standard commenting style; you will understand it at a glance, and if not, feel free to leave a comment!

/**
 * @file vptr1.cpp
 * @brief C++​虚​函数​vptr​和​vtable
 * ​编译​：g++ -g -o vptr vptr1.cpp -std=c++11
 * @author ​光城​
 * @version v1
 * @date 2019-07-20
 */

#include <iostream>
#include <stdio.h>
using namespace std;

/**
 * @brief ​函数指针​
 */
typedef void (*Fun)();

/**
 * @brief ​基类​
 */
class Base
{
    public:
        Base(){};
        virtual void fun1()
        {
            cout << "Base::fun1()" << endl;
        }
        virtual void fun2()
        {
            cout << "Base::fun2()" << endl;
        }
        virtual void fun3(){}
        ~Base(){};
};

/**
 * @brief ​派生类​
 */
class Derived: public Base
{
    public:
        Derived(){};
        void fun1()
        {
            cout << "Derived::fun1()" << endl;
        }
        void fun2()
        {
            cout << "DerivedClass::fun2()" << endl;
        }
        ~Derived(){};
};
/**
 * @brief ​获取​vptr​地址​与​func​地址​,vptr​指向​的​是​一块​内存​，​这块​内存​存放​的​是​虚​函数​地址​，​这块​内存​就是​我们​所说​的​虚表​
 *
 * @param obj
 * @param offset
 *
 * @return 
 */
Fun getAddr(void* obj,unsigned int offset)
{
    cout<<"======================="<<endl;
    void* vptr_addr = (void *)*(unsigned long *)obj;  //64​位​操作系统​，​占​8​字节​，​通过​*(unsigned long *)obj​取出​前​8​字节​，​即​vptr​指针​
    printf("vptr_addr:%p\n",vptr_addr);

    /**
     * @brief ​通过​vptr​指针​访问​virtual table，​因为​虚表​中​每个​元素​(​虚​函数指针​)​在​64​位​编译器​下​是​8​个​字节​，​因此​通过​*(unsigned long *)vptr_addr​取出​前​8​字节​，
     * ​后面​加上​偏移量​就是​每个​函数​的​地址​！
     */
    void* func_addr = (void *)*((unsigned long *)vptr_addr+offset);
    printf("func_addr:%p\n",func_addr);
    return (Fun)func_addr;
}
int main(void)
{
    Base ptr;
    Derived d;
    Base *pt = new Derived(); // ​基类​指针​指向​派生类​实例​
    Base &pp = ptr; // ​基类​引用​指向​基类​实例​
    Base &p = d; // ​基类​引用​指向​派生类​实例​
    cout<<"​基类​对象​直接​调用​"<<endl;
    ptr.fun1();
    cout<<"​基类​引用​指向​基类​实例​"<<endl;
    pp.fun1(); 
    cout<<"​基类​指针​指向​派生类​实例​并​调用​虚​函数​"<<endl;
    pt->fun1();
    cout<<"​基类​引用​指向​派生类​实例​并​调用​虚​函数​"<<endl;
    p.fun1();

    // ​手动​查找​vptr ​和​ vtable
    Fun f1 = getAddr(pt, 0);
    (*f1)();
    Fun f2 = getAddr(pt, 1);
    (*f2)();
    delete pt;
    return 0;
}

Run result:

​基类​对象​直接​调用​
Base::fun1()
​基类​引用​指向​基类​实例​
Base::fun1()
​基类​指针​指向​派生类​实例​并​调用​虚​函数​
Derived::fun1()
​基类​引用​指向​派生类​实例​并​调用​虚​函数​
Derived::fun1()
=======================

func_addr:0x400ea8
Derived::fun1()
=======================
vptr_addr:0x401130
func_addr:0x400ed4
DerivedClass::fun2()

We observe that C++'s dynamic polymorphism is achieved through virtual functions. Simply put, via the virtual mechanism, a base-class pointer pointing to a subclass can call the subclass's functions. For example, above, a base-class pointer points to a derived-class instance and calls a virtual function; let's simplify the code above to:

Base *pt = new Derived(); // ​基类​指针​指向​派生类​实例​
cout<<"​基类​指针​指向​派生类​实例​并​调用​虚​函数​"<<endl;
pt->fun1();

The process is as follows: first, the program recognizes that fun1() is a virtual function; second, it uses pt->vptr to fetch Derived's virtual table; third, it looks up which version of fun1() to call in Derived's virtual table. Here we can see that Derived::fun1() is the one called. Therefore pt->fun1() is resolved to Derived::fun1()!

Beyond that, as you can see in the code above, it also includes manually obtaining the vptr address and calling a function in the vtable. So let's verify together whether the address above matches the one really used when the vtable's virtual function is invoked automatically — for example, when pt->fun1() runs above!

Here we use gdb debugging; remember to add -g when compiling.

Enter the gdb debugging screen with gdb vptr, then type b Derived::fun1 to set a breakpoint on fun1, and then type r to run the program to the breakpoint. At this point we need to inspect the memory addresses in the call stack: disassemable fun1 shows the relevant assembly code for fun1, where we see 0x0000000000400ea8; comparing this with the result above, we find it matches the manually invoked fun1, and fun2 is similar, proving the code is correct!

docs.title: Building C++ Projects with Bazel
docs.text: This site's projects (including CPlusPlusThings) have switched to Bazel builds. Here I record the complete process, from a fresh install to a successful build — every step actually run through.

docs.title: 1. Installation
docs.text:
Taking Linux as an example, the official recommendation is to install a user-level version with the installer script (no root required): gpadmin@gpadmin:~$ ./bazel-6.1.1-installer-linux-x86_64.sh --user Bazel installer

Bazel is bundled with software licensed under the GPLv2 with Classpath exception. You can find the sources next to the installer on our release page: https://github.com/bazelbuild/bazel/releases

docs.title: Building C++ Projects with Bazel | C++​那些​事
Build information
docs.text:
• Commit Uncompressing......WARNING: Invoking Bazel in batch mode since it is not invoked from within a workspace (below a directory having a WORKSPACE file). Extracting Bazel installation... .

Bazel is now installed!

Make sure you have "/home/gpadmin/bin" in your path.

For bash completion, add the following line to your : source /home/gpadmin/.bazel/bin/bazel-complete.bash

For fish shell completion, link this file into your /home/gpadmin/.config/fish/completions/ directory: ln -s /home/gpadmin/.bazel/bin/bazel.fish /home/gpadmin/.config/fish/completions/bazel.fish

See http://bazel.build/docs/getting-started.html to start a new project! 

​安装​完​默认​放在​ `~/bin`，​可以​先​确认​一下​：
gpadmin@gpadmin:~$ ls ~/bin/ bazel 
## 2.​配置​ PATH

​安装​器会​提醒​你​把​ `~/bin` ​加进​ PATH。​编辑​ `~/.bashrc`，​在​文件​末尾​加​一行​：
export PATH="\(PATH:\)HOME/bin" 
​然后​重新​加载​使​其​生效​：
source ~/.bashrc 
## 3.​验证​与​第一个​构建​
bazel --version 
​能​打印​版本号​就​说明​装好​了​。​接着​到​任意​一个​带​ WORKSPACE/MODULE.bazel ​的​项目​目录​里​跑​：
bazel build //... ```

Bazel automatically fetches dependencies and caches build artifacts, so the second build is basically instant — this is the core of why it beats traditional Make: content-hash-based remote/local caching + a strict dependency closure.

For a complete hands-on walkthrough of building this site's project, watch the Bilibili video: Episode 1: Step By Step — Building This Project; it pairs best with this post. Questions are welcome in the comments~

docs.title: Debugging Bazel Builds with LLDB
docs.text:
Today, while debugging, I found that files compiled by Bazel could no longer be debugged on my Mac — all I got was assembly.

* thread #1, queue = 'com.apple.main-thread', stop reason = breakpoint 1.1
    frame #0: 0x0000000100000fd0 hello_world`main
hello_world`main:
->  0x100000fd0 <+0>: pushq  %rbp
    0x100000fd1 <+1>: movq   %rsp, %rbp
    0x100000fd4 <+4>: subq   $0x60, %rsp
    0x100000fd8 <+8>: movl   $0x0, -0x4(%rbp)
(lldb) quit

How to solve it?

The default is standalone, and we need to disable it; here we use local, which means the output will be linked against its dependencies instead of using the default standalone strategy.

build --spawn_strategy=local

With this, the code becomes visible.

* thread #1, queue = 'com.apple.main-thread', stop reason = breakpoint 1.1
    frame #0: 0x0000000100000fdf hello_world`main at hello_world.cc:14:21
   11  
   12   int main() {
   13     // Create a thread pool
-> 14     auto threadPool = GetCpuThreadPool();
   15     if (!threadPool) {

docs.title: Why This Happens
docs.text:
Why is that? Bazel's default standalone spawn strategy runs compile actions inside a sandbox; on macOS the sandbox implementation (sandbox-exec) skews debug info paths and dSYM generation, and the binary ends up with a broken symbol table — so LLDB can only show you assembly.

Switch to:

build --spawn_strategy=local

This means compile actions run directly on the local machine without entering the sandbox; symbol information is fully preserved, and breakpoints land on the correct source lines. I recommend writing it straight into the project's .bazelrc, once and for all:

build --spawn_strategy=local
build --compilation_mode=dbg   # ​调试​构建​记得​带​ -c dbg

(1) when debugging, use bazel build -c dbg //... or bazel run -c dbg to make sure -O0 -g is on;

(2) on Linux the default sandbox generally does not affect debug symbols; this problem mainly shows up on macOS;

(3) if you still cannot see the source code, check the dSYM: dsymutil ./hello_world && lldb ./hello_world.

With that, Bazel + LLDB work happily together. If you have hit other pitfalls, feel free to add them in the comments~

docs.title: 1.Setting Compiler Flags
docs.text:
For example: setting the C++ standard and showing all warnings.

set(CMAKE_CXX_FLAGS "-std=c++0x -Wall")
set(CMAKE_CXX_FLAGS "${CMAKE_CXX_FLAGS} -std=c++0x -Wall")
add_compile_options("$<$<STREQUAL:$<TARGET_PROPERTY:LINKER_LANGUAGE>,CXX>:-std=c++11>")

You can also set some optimization flags.

Official documentation: https://gcc.gnu.org/onlinedocs/gcc/Optimize-Options.html

For example:

-O0, -O1, -O2, -O3

If you use LLVM, you can refer to this:

https://clang.llvm.org/docs/DiagnosticsReference.html

docs.title: 2.Setting Source File Properties
docs.text:
This is one of CMake's more complex features: when multiple targets exist, you may need to change the behavior of only one target. For example, if you want to build main.cpp with C++11 while building the library itself as C++14, you can use the set_source_files_properties command to configure the properties of specific source files, as shown below:

cmakeCopy code
set_source_files_properties(${CMAKE_CURRENT_SOURCE_DIR}/*.cpp PROPERTIES COMPILE_FLAGS "-std=c++11")

You can browse a large number of properties in the following manual; each of them can be used to meet your specific needs.

  • CMake properties

https://cmake.org/cmake/help/v3.3/manual/cmake-properties.7.html#source-file-properties

docs.title: 3.Linker Flags
docs.text:
The following is a list of linker flags for the GNU GCC linker.

GNU GCC link options

https://gcc.gnu.org/onlinedocs/gcc/Link-Options.html

By default, the GCC linker can search the directories defined in environment variables (/usr/lib; /usr/local/lib) and then links the standard libraries by default.

One of the most common flags is -l, used to link the required libraries, such as -lzlib, -lboost, and so on.

There are also additional flags that help you change the linking-option behavior of your executable.

The following are the variables to which you can add linker flags:

  • CMAKE_EXE_LINKER_FLAGS: flags used by the linker when creating executables
  • CMAKE_EXE_LINKER_FLAGS_RELEASE: flags used by the linker when creating release executables
  • CMAKE_EXE_LINKER_FLAGS_DEBUG: flags used by the linker when creating debug executables
  • CMAKE_STATIC_LINKER_FLAGS: flags used by the linker when creating static libraries (.a, .lib)
  • CMAKE_SHARED_LINKER_FLAGS: flags used by the linker when creating shared libraries (.so, .dll)
  • CMAKE_MODULE_LINKER_FLAGS: flags used by the linker when creating module libraries

For example, you can add linker flags with the following code:

set(CMAKE_EXE_LINKER_FLAGS "${CMAKE_EXE_LINKER_FLAGS} -fsanitize=address")
set(CMAKE_EXE_LINKER_FLAGS "${CMAKE_EXE_LINKER_FLAGS} -Wl")

Knowing how to use these flags helps you better control the linking behavior of your executables.

docs.title: 4.Debug and Release Builds
docs.text:
Inside the CMakeLists.txt file, you can access CMAKE_BUILD_TYPE. You can easily check the build type in CMakeLists.txt:

if(${CMAKE_BUILD_TYPE} MATCHES Debug)
    message("Debug Build")
elseif(${CMAKE_BUILD_TYPE} MATCHES Release)
    message("Release Build")
endif()

You can also use the configuration variables shown in the previous section to set compiler and linker flags separately for the different build types:

  • CMAKE_EXE_LINKER_FLAGS_RELEASE: flags used to create release executables
  • CMAKE_EXE_LINKER_FLAGS_DEBUG: flags used to create debug executables
  • CMAKE_CXX_FLAGS_RELEASE
  • CMAKE_CXX_FLAGS_DEBUG

docs.title: 2.Installing Third-Party Libraries
docs.text:
When installing third-party libraries, we usually need to know the version of the library to install, so Conan provides a corresponding search command that lists the available versions of a library.

conan search gtest --remote=conancenter

Searching directly will fail because conancenter cannot be found, so the first step is to set up the remote.

conan remote add conancenter https://center.conan.io

Then, when we retry the search command above, we get an error:

Unable to connect to conancenter=https://center.conan.io
1. Make sure the remote is reachable or,
2. Disable it by using conan remote disable,
Then try again.

At this point, we need to configure certificates.

conan config install https://github.com/conan-io/conanclientcert.git

docs.title: 3.Writing a Project
docs.text:
Next, let's write a project using Conan.

Project background: during development we need unit tests — for example, for division we need assertions covering boundary cases such as dividing by 0 versus non-zero — so we need to pull in a third-party library; here we use gtest.

1.Write the code

#include <gtest/gtest.h>
double divide(double a, double b) { return b == 0 ? 0 : a / b; }

TEST(Div, NonZero) {
  double expected = 1.5;
  double actual = divide(3, 2);
  ASSERT_EQ(expected, actual);
}

TEST(Div, Zero) {
  double expected = 0;
  double actual = divide(3, 0);
  ASSERT_EQ(expected, actual);
}

2.Write conanfile.txt, specifying a gtest version.

[requires]
gtest/1.13.0

[generators]
cmake

3.Add CMakeLists.txt. The content is very simple — pay attention to the exclamation-mark parts.

cmake_minimum_required(VERSION 3.16)
project(MultiplyTest LANGUAGES CXX)

enable_testing()

// !!!
find_package(GTest REQUIRED)

add_executable(div_test div_test.cpp)

// !!!
target_link_libraries(div_test
 PRIVATE
  GTest::GTest)

add_test(div_gtest div_test)

docs.title: C++ Insights Compile-Time Observation
docs.text: Readers often ask me: what does a range-for actually compile into? Are lambda captures really just member variables? What if I cannot memorize the auto deduction rules? The answers to all of these questions are written in the compiler's eyes, but we normally cannot see them. Today I am introducing a tool that translates this "compiler-view" code straight out for you: C++ Insights.

docs.title: 1. What It Is
docs.text: C++ Insights is an open-source tool by Andreas Fertig (GitHub); at heart it is a modified Clang: after semantic analysis of your C++ source, it "decompiles" it back into equivalent but fully explicit C++. It does not optimize and does not generate assembly — it exists solely to answer "what did the compiler write for me".

docs.title: 2. What You Can See
docs.text:
Take a few of the most-frequently-asked scenarios; I suggest opening the site and pasting the code below in to compare.

(1) the true face of range-for:

std::vector<int> v{1, 2, 3};
for (auto x : v) {
  std::cout << x;
}

Insights will tell you it actually is:

{
  auto&& __range = v;
  for (auto __begin = __range.begin(), __end = __range.end();
       __begin != __end; ++__begin) {
    auto x = *__begin;
    std::cout << x;
  }
}

This also explains why the loop has undefined behavior once __range dangles.

(2) a lambda is just an anonymous class's operator():

int base = 10;
auto add = [base](int x) { return base + x; };

After expansion you can see the compiler-generated closure type and the captured members; the difference between mutable, capture-by-reference, and capture-by-value is plain at a glance.

(3) auto/decltype, structured bindings, the real types after template instantiation — all made explicit.

docs.title: 3. How to Use
docs.text:
Online version: cppinsights.io, paste code on the left and get the result on the right, with a choice of C++ standard (11/14/17/20/23).

The command-line version can be installed locally:

git clone https://github.com/andreasfertig/cppinsights
cd cppinsights && mkdir build && cd build
cmake .. -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release
make -j8

The compiled insights binary works directly on files: insights hello.cpp -- -std=c++20.

docs.title: C++ string to int
docs.text:
My WeChat official account:

First, here are the candidate solutions:

  • atoi
  • strtol
  • stoi

What are the differences between these? Let's compare them with tests below.

C-style functions

Comparing atoi and strtol:

string str = "16s";
int a = atoi(str.c_str());
int b = strtol(str.c_str(), nullptr, 10);

Output:

atoi​的​结果​为​:16
strtol​的​结果​为​:16

Both of these functions start scanning the string for digits, a sign, or a decimal point, and stop when an invalid character is encountered.

That is why scanning stops early at the "s" character above — in other words, when your string is not a number, or contains a decimal point or other non-digit characters, no exception is thrown! It simply outputs 0.

For example:

string str = "asdsa";
int a = atoi(str.c_str());
int b = strtol(str.c_str(), nullptr, 10);

Output:

0
0

Compared with atoi, strtol supports conversion with multiple bases, such as base 8.

For example:

int b = strtol(str.c_str(), nullptr, 8);

C++ style

In C++, you can use stoi to convert to int. The single biggest characteristic of this function compared with the previous two is: exceptions!

As we know, C++ adds exceptions compared to the C language, and this is the most prominent capability this function gains in C++.

For example:

string str1 = "asq,";
//    int c = stoi(str1);    // ​报​异常​
string str2 = "12312";
int c = stoi(str2);     // ok
cout << c << endl;

The exception is as follows:

terminate called after throwing an instance of 'std::invalid_argument'
what():  stoi

Roll your own

That is, write it yourself, as follows:

int stringToInt(const string &s) {
    int v;
    stringstream ss;
    ss << s;
    ss >> v;
    return v;
}
int main() {
    int i = stringToInt("2.3");
    cout<<i<<endl;
}

docs.title: The C++ dbg-macro Debugging Macro
docs.text:
Logging is an indispensable way of debugging in C++ development. Inspired by the dbg macro in Rust, dbg-macro provides a better macro function than printf and std::cout. Its main features are as follows:

  • Beautiful colored output (colors are automatically disabled when the output is not an interactive terminal)
  • C++11 compatible and header-only
  • Supports printing both fundamental types and STL container types
  • Can print the file name, line number, function name, and the original expression

For example, the following code:

#include <vector>
#include <dbg.h>

// You can use "dbg(..)" in expressions:
int factorial(int n) {
  if (dbg(n <= 1)) {
    return dbg(1);
  } else {
    return dbg(n * factorial(n - 1));
  }
}

int main() {
  std::string message = "hello";
  dbg(message);  // [example.cpp:15 (main)] message = "hello" (std::string)

  const int a = 2;
  const int b = dbg(3 * a) + 1;  // [example.cpp:18 (main)] 3 * a = 6 (int)

  std::vector<int> numbers{b, 13, 42};
  dbg(numbers);  // [example.cpp:21 (main)] numbers = {7, 13, 42} (size: 3) (std::vector<int>)

  dbg("this line is executed");  // [example.cpp:23 (main)] this line is executed

  factorial(4);

  return 0;
}

The result looks like this:

git clone https://github.com/sharkdp/dbg-macro
sudo ln -s $(readlink -f dbg-macro/dbg.h) /usr/include/dbg.h

Now you can use dbg.h anywhere.

For more, see the official documentation.

docs.title: GCC Compilation Flags Explained
docs.text: People usually pass some gcc flags when compiling code; this article walks through some of the more important gcc flags.

docs.title: 1.Optimization Flags
docs.text:
Optimization flags are used to improve the performance of the compiled code. They can speed up the compilation process and produce efficient programs.

Some commonly used optimization flags include:

-O1, -O2, -O3, -Os: these flags control the level of optimization applied.

-O1 applies basic optimizations, while -O2 and -O3 provide more advanced optimization. -Os optimizes for code size.

-finline-functions, -funroll-loops: these flags control function inlining and loop unrolling optimizations respectively, aiming to eliminate function-call overhead and reduce loop iterations.

docs.title: 2.Debugging Flags
docs.text:
Debugging flags help provide extra information so that debugging tools can trace and analyze the code.

Some commonly used debugging flags include:

-g: this flag includes debugging symbols in the compiled executable.

-ggdb: this flag makes GCC produce debugging information in a format suitable for the GNU Debugger (GDB).

docs.title: 3.Warning Flags
docs.text:
Warning flags help identify potential problems, coding errors, or problematic practices in the code. By enabling warning flags, the compiler warns about these situations, allowing developers to improve code quality.

Some commonly used warning flags include:

-Wall: this flag enables a comprehensive set of warnings covering a wide range of potential problems.

-Werror: this flag treats warnings as errors, stopping the compilation process whenever a warning is encountered.

docs.title: 4.Preprocessor Flags
docs.text:
Preprocessor flags deal with the directives in source code that start with #. These flags define macros and control compilation.

Some commonly used preprocessor flags include:

-D: this flag is used to define macros during compilation. For example, -DDEBUG can be used to define the DEBUG macro, enabling conditional compilation based on whether it exists.

-I: this flag is used to specify additional directories where header files are located. It helps the preprocessor find the necessary header files when compiling code.

docs.title: 5.Linker Flags
docs.text:
Linker flags control the linking process, which takes place after compilation, combining object files and libraries to produce the final executable.

Some commonly used linker flags include:

-l: this flag is used to link external libraries. For example, -lpthread links the POSIX threads library.

-L: this flag is used to specify additional directories where libraries are located. It helps the linker find the required libraries during linking.

docs.title: 6.Platform-Specific Flags
docs.text:
GCC provides flags targeted at specific platforms, allowing developers to target a particular architecture or enable specific platform features. These flags are very useful when developing code for specific hardware or operating systems.

Platform-specific flags include:

-march: this flag specifies the target architecture. For example, -march=native tells GCC to optimize for the architecture of the host machine.

-m32 and -m64: these flags specify whether to compile for a 32-bit or 64-bit target.

docs.title: 7.Miscellaneous Flags
docs.text:
Besides the categories mentioned above, there are also some other flags.

Some commonly used miscellaneous flags include:

-std: this flag specifies the version of the C language standard to use. For example, -std=c99 selects the C99 standard. -pedantic: this flag enables strict adherence to the selected C language standard, issuing extra warnings for non-standard or questionable code constructs. -Wextra: this flag enables additional warnings beyond those enabled by -Wall, providing a more thorough analysis of the code.

Note that the availability and behavior of flags may vary across GCC versions and platforms. It is therefore recommended to consult the GCC documentation and related resources for detailed information about specific flags and their usage.

Full documentation address:

https://gcc.gnu.org/onlinedocs/gcc/

docs.text: Last updated：2026-10-13

docs.title: Debugging C++ Programs with GDB
docs.text:
When debugging C code with the GNU Debugger (GDB), you will find that it is the most popular debugger on UNIX systems for debugging C and C++ programs. Here is a concise, easy-to-understand explanation of debugging C code with GDB:

First, switch to the current folder containing your code on the command line and run the following command:

gcc -g -Wall code.c -o output

Here, the -g option is necessary for using the GDB tool. The -Wall option is used to display warning messages. This will create an executable file named "output".

Then, run the following command to open the GDB dialog and load the symbol information from the output file (or simply put, set up the whole environment to debug code.c):

gdb output

The following commands can help you debug:

  • list: lists the source code.
  • b x: sets a breakpoint at x. x can be the name of a module or a line number. For example, x can be a function name such as main.
  • r: runs the program (until a breakpoint) and provides the result; that is, it runs the code up to the breakpoint and produces the result. [With arguments, it is: r arg1 arg2 arg3 ...]
  • info breakpoints x: gives detailed information about breakpoint x.
  • info breakpoints: gives detailed information about all breakpoints.
  • delete x: deletes breakpoint x.
  • disable x and enable x: disable and enable breakpoint x.
  • print p: prints the value of the variable p.
  • display p: displays the value of the variable p after each run (automating the whole process).
  • c: continues executing the program (skipping iterations such as for loops). Use c-iter1 to skip the first iteration, type c again to skip the second iteration, and so on.
  • You can also use extra conditions, such as b x if (y > m), which means: set a breakpoint at line x if the value of y is greater than m.
  • GDB can also set breakpoints across multiple files. For example, if a function defined in function.c is called from program.c, you can use b function.c:x to set a breakpoint at line x of function.c.
  • bt: used to backtrace the path of code execution. bt gives an indexed list showing the frames the code passed through, for example: #0 a description of frame 0, #1 a description of frame 1, and so on, where 0 is the most recent frame.
  • Typing f x jumps to frame x (f 0 jumps to frame 0) and shows the values of the variables when the corresponding function was executing.
  • s: used to step into a function and get more details.
  • next: used to execute the code line by line.

docs.title: GDB Python Extension Debugging | C++​那些​事
docs.text: Last updated：2026-10-13

docs.title: 0.Introduction
docs.text:
Debugging is an indispensable part of software development, and GDB (the GNU Debugger), as a powerful debugging tool, is widely used among developers. Besides the traditional command-line debugging features, GDB also provides a Python GDB library that allows developers to extend and enhance their debugging capabilities using the Python language. This article introduces how to use the Python GDB library inside GDB, demonstrating its powerful debugging features and use cases.

Before starting, make sure Python and GDB are correctly installed and that the Python version is compatible with GDB. Then, install the Python GDB library by following these steps:

a. Run gdb on the command line to open GDB.

b. Type the python command to enter GDB's Python interpreter.

c. Run import gdb; if no error is reported, the Python GDB library is correctly installed.

(gdb) python
>import gdb
>end

While debugging with gdb, we often want to inspect variables with complex structures, such as the List structure in PostgreSQL, which can hold anything — what exactly is inside it is hard to print directly. That is where Python scripts come in for our daily development, as in the example below:

(gdb) tl
TargetEntry [resno=1 resname="sum"]
    Aggref [aggfnoid=2107 aggtype=1700 aggtranstype=2281 aggstar=false aggvariadic=false aggkind=110 'n' agglevelsup=0 aggsplit=AGGSPLIT_FINAL_DESERIAL aggno=0 aggtransno=0 agg_expr_id=0]

docs.title: 1.Hello python gdb
docs.text:
We can run some Python operations inside gdb, for example: print, as shown below:

scssCopy code
(gdb) python
> print(1+2)
> end
3
(gdb) end
This command cannot be used at the top level.

In this example, we entered GDB's Python interpreter and executed a simple Python statement, print(1+2), whose result is 3.

Another example is that we can directly type python xxxx to run it.

scssCopy code
(gdb) python f = 2
(gdb) python print(f)
2

In this example, we defined a variable f with a Python statement inside GDB and printed its value, with the result 2.

docs.title: 2.In Practice: How to Write One?
docs.text:
The key point is how do we write these scripts, so that we can conveniently print our own data? What follows is the hands-on part. The code and materials related to this section will be published in the Knowledge Planet community — stay tuned:

struct Point {
    int x;
    int y;
};

Now, given a Point struct, I want to print it out with a script — how do we do that?

The logic is very simple: read the struct, then print it.

import gdb

def print_point(point):
    print(f"Point: x={point['x']}, y={point['y']}")

def print_person(person):
    age = person['age']
    print(f"Person: age={age}")

class PrintCppStruct(gdb.Command):
    def __init__(self):
        super(PrintCppStruct, self).__init__("print_cpp_struct", gdb.COMMAND_USER)

    def invoke(self, arg, from_tty):
        try:
            cl = gdb.parse_and_eval(arg)
            if cl.type.code == gdb.TYPE_CODE_STRUCT and str(cl.type) == 'Point':
                print_point(cl)
            elif cl.type.code == gdb.TYPE_CODE_STRUCT and str(cl.type) == 'Person':
                print_person(cl)
            else:
                print("Unknown C++ structure type.")
        except gdb.error as e:
            print(f"Error: {e}")

PrintCppStruct()

How to use it?

Just source it:

(gdb) source print.py

In this example, we used the source command to load a Python script named print.py into GDB.

(gdb) print_cpp_struct myPoint
Point: x=10, y=20

In this example, we used a custom command print_cpp_struct inside GDB, which printed the value of a C++ struct named myPoint via the Python GDB library.

By using the Python GDB library inside GDB, developers can leverage the power of Python to extend and enhance their debugging capabilities. It provides a rich API and flexible scripting, making the debugging process more efficient and convenient. Whether it is automating debugging tasks, data analysis and visualization, or dynamically modifying program behavior, the Python GDB library offers developers abundant choices and flexibility. I hope this article helps you better understand and apply the Python GDB library, and improves your debugging skills and development efficiency.

docs.title: Debugging C++ Programs with LLDB
docs.text:
This article introduces how to use the LLDB debugger to debug a simple C++ program. Our example code is named test.cpp.

#include <iostream>
#include <string>

struct MyStruct {
    int myInt;
    std::string myString;
};

int main() {
    MyStruct myStruct;
    myStruct.myInt = 42;
    myStruct.myString = "Hello, world!";

    int sum = 0;
    for (int i = 1; i <= 5; ++i) {
        sum += i;
    }

    return 0;
}

docs.title: Compile
docs.text:
First, we need to compile the code with the -g flag to enable extra debugging information.

clang++ -g test.cpp -o test

docs.title: Start Debugging
docs.text:
Next, we attach the debugger.

lldb test

docs.title: Breakpoints
docs.text:
We set a breakpoint at the main() function.

(lldb) b main

Output:

Breakpoint 1: where = test`main + 19 at test.cpp:10:14, address = 0x0000000100003be3

docs.title: Run
docs.text:
Then, we start the process.

(lldb) run

Output:

Process 11333 launched: '/Users/light/test' (x86_64)
Process 11333 stopped
* thread #1, queue = 'com.apple.main-thread', stop reason = breakpoint 1.1
    frame #0: 0x0000000100003be3 test`main at test.cpp:10:14
   7    };
   8    
   9    int main() {
-> 10       MyStruct myStruct;
   11       myStruct.myInt = 42;
   12       myStruct.myString = "Hello, world!";
   13

docs.title: Inspecting Breakpoints
docs.text:
We have now stopped at the beginning of the main() function. We can set a breakpoint on a specific line.

(lldb) b 16

Output: Breakpoint 2: where = test`main + 76 at test.cpp:16:16, address = 0x0000000100003c1c

To list the currently set breakpoints, use the following command.

(lldb) breakpoint list

Output:

(lldb) breakpoint list
Current breakpoints:
1: name = 'main', locations = 1, resolved = 1, hit count = 1
  1.1: where = test`main + 19 at test.cpp:10:14, address = 0x0000000100003be3, resolved, hit count = 1 

2: file = '/Users/zhangxing/test.cpp', line = 16, exact_match = 0, locations = 1, resolved = 1, hit count = 0
  2.1: where = test`main + 76 at test.cpp:16:16, address = 0x0000000100003c1c, resolved, hit count = 0

docs.title: Continuing Execution
docs.text:
We can continue executing the program until the next breakpoint.

(lldb) c

Output:

Process 11823 resuming
Process 11823 stopped
* thread #1, queue = 'com.apple.main-thread', stop reason = breakpoint 2.1
    frame #0: 0x0000000100003c1c test`main at test.cpp:16:16
   13   
   14       int sum = 0;
   15       for (int i = 1; i <= 5; ++i) {
-> 16           sum += i;
   17       }
   18   
   19       return 0;

docs.title: Printing Variables
docs.text:
To get the value of a current local variable, you can use the following command:

(lldb) p myStruct

Output:

(MyStruct) $0 = (myInt = 42, myString = "Hello, world!")

docs.title: Watchpoints
docs.text:
To monitor changes in the value of a specific variable, we can use a watchpoint.

(lldb) watch set variable sum

Output:

Watchpoint created: Watchpoint 1: addr = 0x7ffeefbff1e8 size = 4 state = enabled type = w
    declare @ '/Users/zhangxing/test.cpp:14'
    watchpoint spec = 'sum'
    new value: 0

After stepping with next, you will see the watchpoint change.

(lldb) n

Watchpoint 1 hit:
old value: 3
new value: 6
Process 11823 stopped
* thread #1, queue = 'com.apple.main-thread', stop reason = watchpoint 1
    frame #0: 0x0000000100003c25 test`main at test.cpp:15:29
   12       myStruct.myString = "Hello, world!";
   13   
   14       int sum = 0;
-> 15       for (int i = 1; i <= 5; ++i) {
   16           sum += i;
   17       }
   18

If you want execution to stop based on a condition, you can set a stop condition.

(lldb) watch modify -c '(sum > 5)'

Output:

Watchpoint 1 hit:
new value: 6
Process 12848 stopped
* thread #1, queue = 'com.apple.main-thread', stop reason = watchpoint 1
    frame #0: 0x0000000100003c25 test`main at test.cpp:15:29

docs.title: Hands-On Memory Leak Troubleshooting in C++
docs.text:
While investigating a memory problem in a database kernel (Greenplum/PostgreSQL family) recently, I got a string of very classic WARNINGs: problem in alloc set ExecutorState: bad single-chunk. What this log means: the memory pool (alloc set) found, during validation, that a chunk's header had been corrupted — nine times out of ten, some code wrote out of bounds and trampled the neighboring chunk's metadata.

The hard part of such problems is: where the error surfaces is not where the bug lives. The WARNING is only printed when the memory is freed and validated, while the out-of-bounds write could have happened in any piece of code long before. Below is the complete investigation process from that session — let us see how to recover the "crime scene" with gdb.

Read the scene information first:

regression=# SELECT t1.a, t1.c, t2.b, t2.c FROM prt1_e t1, prt2_e t2 WHERE (t1.a + t1.b)/2 = (t2.b + t2.a)/2 AND t1.c = 0 ORDER BY t1.a, t2.b;
WARNING:  problem in alloc set ExecutorState: bad single-chunk 0x7cfdd48 in block 0x7cfc580  (seg1 slice1 127.0.1.1:7003 pid=4295)
WARNING:  problem in alloc set ExecutorState: found inconsistent memory block 0x7cfc580  (seg1 slice1 127.0.1.1:7003 pid=4295)
WARNING:  problem in alloc set ExecutorState: bad single-chunk 0x7cfdd48 in block 0x7cfc580  (seg1 slice1 127.0.1.1:7003 pid=4295)
WARNING:  problem in alloc set ExecutorState: found inconsistent memory block 0x7cfc580  (seg1 slice1 127.0.1.1:7003 pid=4295)
WARNING:  problem in alloc set ExecutorState: bad single-chunk 0x87f85c8 in block 0x87f6e00  (seg0 slice1 127.0.1.1:7002 pid=4294)
WARNING:  problem in alloc set ExecutorState: found inconsistent memory block 0x87f6e00  (seg0 slice1 127.0.1.1:7002 pid=4294)
WARNING:  problem in alloc set ExecutorState: bad single-chunk 0x7d3c5c8 in block 0x7d3ae00  (seg2 slice1 127.0.1.1:7004 pid=4296)
WARNING:  problem in alloc set ExecutorState: found inconsistent memory block 0x7d3ae00  (seg2 slice1 127.0.1.1:7004 pid=4296)
WARNING:  problem in alloc set ExecutorState: bad single-chunk 0x87f85c8 in block 0x87f6e00  (seg0 slice1 127.0.1.1:7002 pid=4294)
WARNING:  problem in alloc set ExecutorState: bad single-chunk 0x7d3c5c8 in block 0x7d3ae00  (seg2 slice1 127.0.1.1:7004 pid=4296)
WARNING:  problem in alloc set ExecutorState: found inconsistent memory block 0x87f6e00  (seg0 slice1 127.0.1.1:7002 pid=4294)
WARNING:  problem in alloc set ExecutorState: found inconsistent memory block 0x7d3ae00  (seg2 slice1 127.0.1.1:7004 pid=4296)

From the WARNINGs we can extract several key pieces of information:

(1) the bad chunk's address is known: 0x7cfdd48 (bad single-chunk points at it);

(2) the block it lives in is 0x7cfc580, and the same block's "found inconsistent memory block" means the whole block's chain validation also failed;

(3) multiple segments (seg0/seg1/seg2) report it at the same time, so this is not environment flakiness but a deterministic logic bug.

With an exact address in hand, the plan is very direct: set a conditional breakpoint on the memory allocator (aset.c's AllocSetAlloc) to intercept the one call that "returns this address on allocation", then put a hardware watchpoint on that address — whoever writes it is the culprit.

The gdb session:

Debugging:

(gdb) b aset.c:1109 if chunk=0x7cfdd48
Breakpoint 1 at 0x105d420: file aset.c, line 1109.
(gdb) c
Continuing.

Thread 1 "postgres" hit Breakpoint 1, AllocSetAlloc (context=0x787ac50, size=4096) at aset.c:1109
1109        block->freeptr += (chunk_size + ALLOC_CHUNKHDRSZ);
(gdb) p chunk
$1 = (AllocChunk) 0x7cfdd48
(gdb) p chunk->size
$2 = 9187201950435737471
(gdb) p &chunk->size
$3 = (Size *) 0x7cfdd48
(gdb) watch (*((Size *) 0x7cfdd48))
Hardware watchpoint 2: (*((Size *) 0x7cfdd48))
(gdb) i b
Num     Type           Disp Enb Address            What
1       breakpoint     keep y   0x000000000105d420 in AllocSetAlloc at aset.c:1109
    stop only if chunk=0x7cfdd48
    breakpoint already hit 1 time
2       hw watchpoint  keep y                      (*((Size *) 0x7cfdd48))
(gdb) d 1
(gdb) c

docs.title: Retrospective
docs.text:
The playbook of this case transfers directly to memory-corruption investigations in any C/C++ project:

(1) first extract the exact address from the error log — it is the only reliable anchor;

(2) the conditional breakpoint b aset.c:1109 if chunk=0x7cfdd48 catches the allocation site and confirms who got this address;

(3) watch (*(Size*)0x7cfdd48), a hardware watchpoint, waits for the culprit to show up — hardware breakpoints do not rewrite memory and do not affect program behavior, which makes them the most reliable tool for memory-corruption problems;

(4) once running, the call stack at the moment the watchpoint hits is the complete scene of the out-of-bounds write.

Note that in step one, p chunk->size printed 9187201950435737471 (0x7F7F7F7F7F7F7F7F) — a pile of 0x7F, the classic signature of scribbled memory: the trampling code was writing a bunch of flags/fill values. Globally searching the codebase for this value often finds the culprit directly.

One question to leave you: if the out-of-bounds write happens in a forked child process while you are debugging the parent, how should the flow above be adjusted? Feel free to discuss in the comments.

docs.title: Building C++ Projects with Meson
docs.text:
Recently, while using some open-source projects, I noticed that they all adopted the meson+ninja build approach, abandoning CMake and Makefiles. This article introduces Meson, from getting it installed to writing a complete Meson project.

Now, let's get into the main content.

docs.title: 1.Installing Meson
docs.text:
https://github.com/mesonbuild/meson

Meson is available from PyPI, so you can install it with pip3 install meson. Make sure you use the correct pip command on different systems — it must be the Python 3 version of pip.

If you prefer, you can also install it locally with the standard Python command:

python3 -m pip install meson

If you build with Ninja, you can download Ninja directly from the Ninja GitHub releases page or via PyPI:

python3 -m pip install ninja

For more information about installing the Meson build system, read the official Meson website below.

https://mesonbuild.com/Getting-meson.html

docs.title: 2.Meson vs CMake
docs.text:
Since everyone uses CMake, why bother with Meson — and what are their respective strengths and weaknesses?

In terms of performance, Meson is generally known for its fast build speed. Meson is designed to optimize build speed and performs especially well on incremental builds. Meson uses the Ninja build system as its default backend, and Ninja itself is also known for being fast and efficient.

By comparison, CMake's build speed can be affected by project size, especially in larger projects. CMake uses various generators (such as Makefiles), and different generators may also perform differently.

Of course, you can also use CMake + Ninja to speed up compilation.

Looking at Meson from the open-source project perspective, it is used in a great many places, for example: PostgreSQL, QEMU, GNOME Software, GTK+, and so on.

https://mesonbuild.com/Users.html

docs.title: 2.1 Meson's Advantages and Disadvantages
docs.text:
1.Advantages

  • Python-based and easy to use
  • Supports cross compilation
  • All objects are strongly typed: since objects are entities such as 'dependency' and 'include directory', it is hard to make string-substitution errors.
  • Extremely convenient for pulling in third-party libraries
  • Very, very fast, especially on incremental builds.
  • Documentation is n times better than CMake's.

http://mesonbuild.com

2.Disadvantages

  • May not be as mature as CMake
  • Has Python 3 + Ninja dependencies
  • Project generators and IDE support for Meson lag behind CMake
  • VS Code support
  • https://github.com/mesonbuild/vscode-meson
  • Limited modules available
  • You need to submit non-Meson projects to WrapDB yourself
  • https://mesonbuild.com/Wrapdb-projects.html

docs.title: 2.2 CMake's Advantages and Disadvantages
docs.text:
1.Advantages

  • Friendly IDE support and comfortable team collaboration
  • Mature; it has practically become the standard for C++ projects

2.Disadvantages

  • Cross compilation is difficult
  • Compilation is relatively slow

docs.title: 3.Meson WrapDB
docs.text:
Since googletest is not a Meson project, how do we depend on it from Meson?

Likewise, grpc and abseil-cpp are used in a similar way.

This is where WrapDB comes in. Meson WrapDB is a component of the Meson build system that manages and provides build description files for third-party projects, commonly called "wrap" files. These wrap files contain the information needed to configure and build third-party projects so that they can be easily integrated into other projects using the Meson build system.

You can look up third-party libraries with the search command or on the website below.

https://mesonbuild.com/Wrapdb-projects.html#meson-wrapdb-packages

Let's take gtest as an example:

  • Search for gtest
meson wrap search gtest

If the command returns the name of the wrapped project, you can move on to the next step:

  • Create a subprojects directory in your own project and install gtest via install
mkdir -p subprojects
meson wrap install gtest

At this point, the third-party libraries your project depends on are all installed in the subprojects directory.

➜  gtest_div tree -L 1 subprojects
subprojects
├── gtest.wrap

This generates gtest.wrap, whose content includes the following.

Note: this file is generated by the install step above; it is recommended that you do not modify it.

[wrap-file]
directory = googletest-1.14.0
source_url = https://github.com/google/googletest/archive/refs/tags/v1.14.0.tar.gz
source_filename = gtest-1.14.0.tar.gz
source_hash = 8ad598c73ad796e0d8280b082cebd82a630d73e73cd3c70057938a6501bba5d7
patch_filename = gtest_1.14.0-1_patch.zip
patch_url = https://wrapdb.mesonbuild.com/v2/gtest_1.14.0-1/get_patch
patch_hash = 2e693c7d3f9370a7aa6dac802bada0874d3198ad4cfdf75647b818f691182b50
source_fallback_url = https://github.com/mesonbuild/wrapdb/releases/download/gtest_1.14.0-1/gtest-1.14.0.tar.gz
wrapdb_version = 1.14.0-1

[provide]
gtest = gtest_dep
gtest_main = gtest_main_dep
gmock = gmock_dep
gmock_main = gmock_main_dep

docs.title: 4.How Do You Write a Meson Project?
docs.text:
Next comes the hands-on part: how do you write a Meson project?

Below is a small project that uses gtest for unit testing, taking a/b division tests as an example.

docs.title: 4.1 Write the Code
docs.text:
double divide(double a, double b);

Put the .h and .cc files in the src directory:

src
├── division.cc
└── division.h

Then create a test directory at the same level.

test
└── division_test.cc

docs.title: 4.2 Meson Project Management
docs.text:
Add a meson.build file at the project root with the following content:

project('gtest_div', 'cpp')
gtest_proj = subproject('gtest')
gtest_dep = gtest_proj.get_variable('gtest_main_dep') 
div_src = files('src/division.cc')
tests_src = files('test/division_test.cc')
e = executable(
    'division_test',
    tests_src + div_src, 
    dependencies : [ gtest_dep],
    override_options : ['cpp_std=c++14']
)
# https://mesonbuild.com/Unit-tests.html#testing-tool
test('this is a division test', e)

As you can see, this is essentially the same as Python syntax, so anyone familiar with Python will find this code very easy to read. Here we will focus on the more important parts above.

  • Pulling in third-party libraries

For example, suppose the third-party library you pull in is a project called gtest, like this:

project('gtest', 'cpp',
  version : '1.14.0',
  default_options : ['cpp_std=c++14'],
  license : 'bsd')

You can then obtain this project via subproject, and gtest_proj.get_variable gives you gtest's dependency information. For example, this is how it is declared inside googletest:

gtest_main_dep = declare_dependency(
    include_directories : gtest_incdir,
    sources : [gtest_libsources, gtest_mainsources],
    dependencies : dependency('threads')
)
  • executable

executable is very similar to add_executable in CMake; it produces the division_test executable.

  • test

Unit test syntax:

e = executable('prog', 'testprog.c')
test('name of test', e)

You can use meson test or ninja test; after the run a test log is produced, located at:

build/meson-logs/testlog.txt

docs.title: 4.3 Building and Running a Meson Project
docs.text: With the steps above, a Meson project is ready. Next, let's build and run this project.

docs.title: 4.3.1 Configure the Build Directory
docs.text:
This is similar to CMake's mkdir build && cmake ...

meson setup build

It runs as follows:

➜  gtest_div meson setup build               
The Meson build system

At this point, we can see the cached gtest project under subprojects.

subprojects
├── googletest-1.14.0  # here
├── gtest.wrap
└── packagecache # here

docs.title: 4.3.2 Compile
docs.text:
We can use either of the following two commands. The first:

meson compile -C build/

Run log:

➜  gtest_div meson compile -C build/            
INFO: autodetecting backend as ninja
INFO: calculating backend command to run: /usr/local/bin/ninja -C /Users/light/work/practice/gtest_div/build
ninja: Entering directory `/Users/light/work/practice/gtest_div/build'
[5/5] Linking target division_test

The second:

➜  gtest_div ninja -C build
ninja: Entering directory `build'
[5/5] Linking target division_test

These two commands are essentially the same — both compile with ninja. Of course, you can also skip -C to specify the directory, in which case you need cd build && ninja or cd build && meson compile.

docs.title: 4.3.3 Run and Test
docs.text:
This produces the division_test executable, which runs as follows:

➜  gtest_div ./build/division_test

or

docs.title: Quick STL Container Output in C++
docs.text:
I made some modifications to Mr. Wu's code — click here to go straight to the code

Input:

map<int, int> mp{
            {1, 1},
            {2, 4},
            {3, 9}};
    cout << mp << endl;

The output shows:

{ 1 => 1, 2 => 4, 3 => 9 }

docs.title: Quick STL Container Output in C++ | C++​那些​事
How to Integrate
docs.text:
Download output_container.h into your project and include it:

#include "output_container.h"

int main() {
    std::vector<int> vec{1, 2, 3, 4, 5};
    std::set<std::string> names{"light", "city"};
    std::cout << vec << std::endl;   // { 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 }
    std::cout << names << std::endl; // { city, light }
    return 0;
}

docs.title: Which Containers Are Supported
docs.text: vector, list, set, map, multiset, multimap, the unordered family, pair — plus any custom type that is iterable (anything implementing begin/end); nested containers print directly too.

docs.title: The Principle in One Sentence
docs.text:
The core is specializing operator<< for containers: use SFINAE (void_t detecting begin()/end()) to decide "is it iterable" — if yes, do element-wise output; if not, fall back to the original output stream. If you are interested, read the source directly: under two hundred lines, great material for learning the expression-detection idiom.

Printing containers while debugging is a real necessity; this little tool saves you countless hand-written for loops. Questions are welcome in the comments~

docs.title: The Problem
docs.text: During the Project stage, the fields in the schema changed. fields is a vector node whose members are std::shared_ptr<arrow::Field>; comparing the vector pointers before and after, I found that the _M_start position of _M_impl had changed, so I needed to set a gdb watch on it to see where it was modified.

docs.title: The Vector Structure
docs.text:
The vector code:

https://github.com/gcc-mirror/gcc/blob/master/libstdc%2B%2B-v3/include/bits/stl_vector.h

typedef typename __gnu_cxx::__alloc_traits<_Tp_alloc_type>::pointer
        pointer;
struct _Vector_impl_data
{
    pointer _M_start;
    pointer _M_finish;
    pointer _M_end_of_storage;
}

A few important pieces of information:

  • _M_start, _M_finish, and so on are all of pointer type
  • The pointer type is a raw pointer type

With this information, we can use watch to conveniently observe what changed about _M_start. Note that it is the pointer _M_start itself that changed, not its value.

docs.title: Watch
docs.text:
First, print its address:

(gdb) p &((arrow::Schema::Impl *)this->output_schema_->impl_)->fields_._M_impl._M_start
$10 = (std::_Vector_base<std::shared_ptr<arrow::Field>, std::allocator<std::shared_ptr<arrow::Field> > >::pointer *) 0xb11dd0

We obtained the address of the pointer*; now watch it.

(gdb) watch *((std::_Vector_base<std::shared_ptr<arrow::Field>, std::allocator<std::shared_ptr<arrow::Field> > >::pointer *) 0xb11dd0)
Hardware watchpoint 2: *((std::_Vector_base<std::shared_ptr<arrow::Field>, std::allocator<std::shared_ptr<arrow::Field> > >::pointer *) 0xb11dd0)

Then we continue, and we land at the point of the change:

(gdb) c
Continuing.


Thread 1 "postgres" hit Hardware watchpoint 2: *((std::_Vector_base<std::shared_ptr<arrow::Field>, std::allocator<std::shared_ptr<arrow::Field> > >::pointer *) 0xb11dd0)

Old value = (std::_Vector_base<std::shared_ptr<arrow::Field>, std::allocator<std::shared_ptr<arrow::Field> > >::pointer) 0x979470
New value = (std::_Vector_base<std::shared_ptr<arrow::Field>, std::allocator<std::shared_ptr<arrow::Field> > >::pointer) 0x9fe1e0
VecSeqNext (node=0x9fdc40) at src/backend/vecexecutor/nodeSeqscan.c:210
210     if (table_scan_getnextslot(scandesc, direction, slot))
(gdb) bt

    (node=0x9fdc40, accessMtd=0x7f45994e6335 <VecSeqNext>, recheckMtd=0x7f45994e6430 <VecSeqRecheck>) at src/backend/vecexecutor/execScan.c:146

    at src/backend/vecexecutor/execScan.c:40

    (node=0x9fdc40, vestate=0x9fdd48, accessMtd=0x7f45994e6335 <VecSeqNext>, recheckMtd=0x7f45994e6430 <VecSeqRecheck>)
    at src/backend/vecexecutor/execScan.c:200

docs.title: Formatting C++ Code in VS Code
C++​那些​事​: Formatting Your Code Style Step by Step
0.Introduction
docs.text: This section explains from scratch how to format your own code style; everything shown uses a VS Code plugin.

docs.title: 1.Prerequisites
docs.text:
This guide uses the clang-format plugin; installation is straightforward:

On macOS:

brew install clang-format  #Mac OS

On Ubuntu:

apt install clang-format

For the Windows version, you can download it here:

https://llvm.org/builds/

Once installed, verify it:

clang-format --version

If you prefer not to use VS Code, you can also use the bare clang-format command directly!

Then install the following two plugins in VS Code:

  • c/c++
  • clang-format

Both can be downloaded from the extension marketplace.

After installation, some configuration is needed — see below.

docs.title: 2.Configuration
docs.text:
In the VS Code settings you can search for Clang_format_style; the default is file, and you do not need to change it here — though you can set it to something else. Let me show you that the default value here is file, which means formatting reads the .clang-format file in the current folder or a parent directory.

So all we need to do is generate this file; go to your code directory and run:

clang-format -style=google -dump-config > .clang-format

This generates the file using the Google style, and you can modify the file as you like.

Following the screenshot below, set up the clang-format plugin format in VS Code; then, inside a file, alt+shift+f will format the file. To avoid pressing this shortcut every time, you can check format on save so that the file is formatted whenever it is saved.
