docs.title: The C++ Singleton Pattern | C++​那些​事
docs.text: Last updated：2026-10-13

docs.title: 0. Introduction
docs.text: Design patterns are an inescapable interview topic. This section covers the design pattern most frequently asked in interviews — the singleton pattern — including its classifications, thread safety, and thread-safe singleton solutions both from a pre-C++11 perspective and from a C++11-based perspective. Read this article carefully and you won't need to worry about it in future interviews.

docs.title: 1. The Well-Known Singleton
docs.text:
In most books, or as commonly known, the singleton pattern looks like this:

class singleton {
private:
    singleton() {}
    static singleton *p;
public:
    static singleton *instance();
};

singleton *singleton::p = nullptr;

singleton* singleton::instance() {
    if (p == nullptr)
        p = new singleton();
    return p;
}

This is a very simple implementation: the constructor is declared private or protected to prevent external functions from instantiating the class; inside, a static class pointer holds the unique instance; the instantiation is realized by a public method, which returns the sole instance of the class.

Of course this code is only suitable for single-threaded use; with multiple threads it is unsafe. Consider two threads calling instance for the first time at the same moment and both observing p as nullptr: both threads would construct an instance for p at the same time, which violates the rule of the singleton.

docs.title: 2. Lazy and Eager Initialization
docs.text:
Singletons come in two implementation styles:

  • Lazy initialization
  • The instance is created the first time it is needed; the code above is the lazy implementation.
  • Eager initialization
  • The instance is created at the time the singleton class is defined.

Here is the eager implementation as well:

class singleton {
private:
    singleton() {}
    static singleton *p;
public:
    static singleton *instance();
};

singleton *singleton::p = new singleton();
singleton* singleton::instance() {
    return p;
}

This one is of course thread-safe. The thread-unsafe variant we usually speak of is the lazy style; below we will go through thread-safe code optimizations for the lazy pattern.

docs.title: 3. Locking for Multiple Threads
docs.text:
In C++ there is a class for locking whose implementation principle is RAII, so you don't have to manage unlock manually — lock_guard; we use it here to lock.

class singleton {
private:
    singleton() {}
    static singleton *p;
    static mutex lock_;
public:
    static singleton *instance();
};

singleton *singleton::p = nullptr;

singleton* singleton::instance() {
    lock_guard<mutex> guard(lock_);
    if (p == nullptr)
        p = new singleton();
    return p;
}

With this version, the situation above — both threads executing into the p == nullptr branch — cannot happen. While thread A executes p = new Singleton(), if thread B calls instance(), it will definitely block at the lock and wait until thread A finishes and releases the lock. Hence it is thread-safe.

But this version performs very poorly, because every call to instance() acquires and releases the lock, while that step is only necessary for the first new Singleton(). Once p has been created, no matter how many threads access it concurrently, judging with if (p == nullptr) is enough (it is only a read operation, no lock needed); there is no thread-safety problem, and after adding the lock there is instead a performance problem.

This leads to DCL.

docs.title: 4. Double-Checked Locking Pattern
docs.text:
The version above always acquires the lock and then releases it no matter what, while for read operations there is no thread-safety concern, so locking is needed only when the instance is first created, and never afterwards. First, let's look at the DCLP implementation:

singleton* singleton::instance() {
    if(p == nullptr) {  // ​第一次​检查​
        Lock lock;
        if(p == nullptr){ // ​第二次​检查​
            p = new singleton;
        }
    }
    return p;
}

Building on the above, we can write double-checked locking + automatic reclamation

class singleton {
private:
    singleton() {}

    static singleton *p;
    static mutex lock_;
public:
    static singleton *instance();

    // ​实现​一个​内嵌​垃圾​回收​类​
    class CGarbo
    {
    public:
        ~CGarbo()
        {
            if(singleton::p)
                delete singleton::p;
        }
    };
    static CGarbo Garbo; // ​定义​一个​静态​成员​变量​，​程序​结束​时​，​系统​会​自动​调用​它​的​析构​函数​从而​释放​单例​对象​
};

singleton *singleton::p = nullptr;
singleton::CGarbo Garbo;
std::mutex singleton::lock_;

singleton* singleton::instance() {
    if (p == nullptr) {
        lock_guard<mutex> guard(lock_);
        if (p == nullptr)
            p = new singleton();
    }
    return p;
}

The key point of DCLP is that most calls to instance will see p as non-null, so they don't even try to initialize it. DCLP therefore checks whether p is null before attempting to acquire the lock. Only when that check succeeds (that is, p has not yet been initialized) does it acquire the lock, and then checks again whether p is still null (hence the name double-checked locking). The second check is necessary because, as we have just seen, another thread may well have initialized p after the first check and before the lock is successfully acquired.

The code above looks wonderful, yet quite some time passed before this flaw was discovered. The reason: out-of-order memory reads/writes (a compiler issue).

Consider again the line that initializes p:

p = new singleton;

This statement causes three things to happen:

  1. Allocate memory able to store the singleton object;
  2. Construct a singleton object in that allocated memory;
  3. Make p point to that allocated memory.

You might think these three steps execute in order, but in reality only step 1 is guaranteed to run first; steps 2 and 3 are not. That's where the problem lies.

  • Thread A calls instance, performs the first test of p, acquires the lock, executes steps 1 and 3, and is then suspended. At this moment p is non-null, but no Singleton object has been constructed yet in the memory p points to.
  • Thread B calls instance, sees p as non-null, and returns it to instance's caller. The caller dereferences the pointer to get the singleton — oops, an object that has not been constructed yet. There's the bug.

DCLP works well only when steps one and two are executed before step three, but there is no way to express that constraint in C or C++. It's like a dagger stuck in DCLP's heart: we need to define constraints on the relative order of instructions, but our language gives no way to express such constraints.

docs.title: 5. The memory barrier Instruction
docs.text:
The DCLP problem was solved in C++11.

Because the new C++11 specifies a new memory model, it is guaranteed that no thread switch happens while the three steps above execute — the initialization is effectively an "atomic" operation — and DCL can be used correctly again. However, under C++11 there is an even more concise way to write a multithreaded singleton, which we will introduce later.

Before C++11 the solution was the barrier instruction. To make it execute correctly, a memory barrier has to be inserted between steps 2 and 3, forcing the CPU to run in the order 1, 2, 3.

First implementation:

Based on operator new + placement new, written following the 1, 2, 3 execution order.

// method 1 operator new + placement new
singleton *instance() {
    if (p == nullptr) {
        lock_guard<mutex> guard(lock_);
        if (p == nullptr) {
            singleton *tmp = static_cast<singleton *>(operator new(sizeof(singleton)));
            new(tmp)singleton();
            p = tmp;
        }
    }
    return p;
}

Second implementation:

Based on directly embedding the ASM instruction mfence; Unix's barrier macro is also implemented through this instruction.

#define barrier() __asm__ volatile ("lwsync")
singleton *singleton::instance() {
    if (p == nullptr) {
        lock_guard<mutex> guard(lock_);
        barrier();
        if (p == nullptr) {
            p = new singleton();
        }
    }
    return p;
}

Usually this is an instruction provided by the CPU, and its role is to prevent the CPU from swapping instructions that come before it to after it; such an instruction is commonly called a barrier. In the code above, asm marks this as an assembly instruction; volatile is optional — if used, it declares to the compiler that this assembly instruction must not be optimized. lwsync is the barrier instruction provided by POWERPC.

docs.title: 6. Static Local Variables
docs.text:
Scott Meyers proposed a concise singleton writing style in Effective C++

singleton &singleton::instance() {
    static singleton p;
    return p;
}
  • In single-threaded use, correct.
  • Under multithreading in C++11 and later versions (e.g. C++14), correct.
  • Under multithreading before C++11, not necessarily correct.

The reason is that the standards before C++11 did not specify a memory model for local static variables, so it was not thread-safe. In C++11, however, it is thread-safe, because the new C++ standard stipulates that while one thread is initializing a variable, other threads must wait until that initialization completes before they can access it.

The memory orders used above:

  • memory_order_relaxed: relaxed memory order; only guarantees that operations on the atomic object are atomic
  • memory_order_acquire: an acquire operation; when reading an atomic object, no later reads or writes of the current thread may be reordered before this operation, and all memory writes by other threads before releasing the same atomic object become visible to the current thread
  • memory_order_release: a release operation; when writing an atomic object, no earlier reads or writes of the current thread may be reordered after this operation, and all memory writes of the current thread become visible to other threads that acquire the same atomic object

docs.title: 7. Atomic
docs.text:
In versions before C++11, besides implementing a thread-safe Singleton with locks, you can also make use of the atomic operations built into various compilers.

After discovering the reordering problem, java and c# added a keyword volatile: when declaring the variable p, it must be qualified with volatile, and once the compiler sees that, it knows this place must not be reordered (memory must be allocated first, then the constructor executed, and the assignment made only after everything is done).

The c++ standard, however, was never fixed, so VC++ also added this keyword in its 2005 release, but this is not portable (it only supports Microsoft platforms).

Then, with c++ 11, a memory model suitable for multithreading was introduced to eliminate these holes at the root. Finally there is such a mechanism to help us implement a portable solution.

mutex singleton::lock_;
atomic<singleton *> singleton::p;

/*
* std::atomic_thread_fence(std::memory_order_acquire); 
* std::atomic_thread_fence(std::memory_order_release);
* ​这​两句话​可以​保证​他们​之间​的​语句​不会​发生​乱序执行​。
*/
singleton *singleton::instance() {
    singleton *tmp = p.load(memory_order_relaxed);
    atomic_thread_fence(memory_order_acquire);
    if (tmp == nullptr) {
        lock_guard<mutex> guard(lock_);
        tmp = p.load(memory_order_relaxed);
        if (tmp == nullptr) {
            tmp = new singleton();
            atomic_thread_fence(memory_order_release);
            p.store(tmp, memory_order_relaxed);
        }
    }
    return p;
}

Notably, the code above uses two fairly key terms, acquire and release:

  • Acquire is a read operation on memory; no later reads or writes of the current thread may be reordered before it.
  • Release is a write operation on memory; no earlier reads or writes of the current thread may be reordered after it.

acquire and release usually appear in pairs, with the goal of guaranteeing that if a release on the same atomic object happens before an acquire, the memory modifications that happened before the release can all be seen by the memory reads after the acquire.

docs.title: 8. pthread_once
docs.text:
On Unix platforms, besides using atomic operations, if C++11 is not an option you can also implement the Singleton through pthread_once.

The prototype is as follows:

int pthread_once(pthread_once_t once_control, void (init_routine) (void))；

Implementation:

class singleton {
private:
    singleton(); //​私有​构造函数​，​不​允许​使用者​自己​生成​对象​
    singleton(const singleton &other);

    //​要​写成​静态方法​的​原因​：​类​成员​函数​隐含​传递​this​指针​（​第一个​参数​）
    static void init() {
        p = new singleton();
    }

    static pthread_once_t ponce_;
    static singleton *p; //​静态​成员​变量​ 
public:
    singleton *instance() {
        // init​函数​只会​执行​一次​
        pthread_once(&ponce_, &singleton::init);
        return p;
    }
};

docs.title: 9. Summary
docs.text:
This article covered several singleton patterns, explained thread-safe singleton patterns, and covered several thread-safe singleton implementations that do not use C++11: memory barrier, static local variables, the pthread_once approach, the C++11 atomic implementation, and so on.

Finally, note that for the destructor of the singleton classes above, refer to the double-checked locking + automatic reclamation implementation: you must declare a static local variable inside the class. A static local variable can be understood as a global variable; when the program ends, the destructor of that static local variable is called automatically. This is why a nested class is declared and defined inside the class instead of directly writing the singleton's destructor.

docs.title: A Reusable Thread-Safe Singleton Template Class
docs.text:
Answering the request in issue #303: following the idea of boost::container::singleton_default, a CRTP template base class can turn any class into a thread-safe singleton in a single line (see singleton_default.hpp for the complete code, which includes concurrency tests):

template <class T>
class SingletonDefault {
public:
    static T& instance() {
        static T inst;   // C++11 ​起​局部​静态​变量​初始化​线程​安全​
        return inst;
    }
    SingletonDefault(const SingletonDefault&) = delete;
    SingletonDefault& operator=(const SingletonDefault&) = delete;
protected:
    SingletonDefault() = default;
};

// ​用法​：​继承​即可​
class MyConfig : public SingletonDefault<MyConfig> {
    friend class SingletonDefault<MyConfig>;
private:
    MyConfig() = default;   // ​构造​私有​，​交由​基类​创建​
public:
    int value = 42;
};

// MyConfig::instance().value

docs.title: How C++ std::move Works and How to Use It
docs.text:
std::move is a very important function: it provides a way to mark an lvalue object as a special kind of rvalue object, namely an xvalue. This transformation is what allows move semantics to be applied instead of the usual copy semantics.

  • Why use std::move
  • Practical use cases

docs.title: 1.Why use std::move
docs.text:
Normally, only rvalue objects can be moved, because the move constructor takes an rvalue reference as its parameter, and an rvalue reference can only bind to an rvalue. Therefore, if you want to perform a move operation on an object represented by an lvalue expression, you need to use std::move to convert it into an xvalue (a special kind of rvalue).

Use std::move with care, because a move operation leaves the object in a state where typically only destruction is allowed. Therefore, it is best to move an object only at its last use.

std::move does not actually perform a move. To be clear, std::move does not execute the move operation itself. It merely converts the given lvalue object into an rvalue reference. Here is one possible implementation of std::move:

template <typename T>
typename remove_reference<T>::type&& move(T&& t)
{
    return static_cast<typename remove_reference<T>::type&&>(t);
}

docs.title: 2.1 Move construction instead of copy construction
docs.text:
In the function f1, the parameter a is an lvalue that has an rvalue reference type, not an rvalue itself, because it has a name. Therefore, to force the move constructor of Foo to be invoked, we must convert it into an rvalue, and std::move does exactly that.

struct Foo { 
    ... 
    Foo(const Foo&) {} 
    Foo(Foo&&) {} 
}; 

void f1(Foo&& a) { 
    Foo b(a); // ​调用​拷贝​构造函数​，​而​非​移动​构造函数​
} 

void f2(Foo&& a) { 
    Foo b(std::move(a)); // right
}

docs.title: 2.2 Ownership management
docs.text:
Suppose we have the following code:

Foo* p = new Foo();
data.push_back(p);

The code above works, but you cannot tell who owns the pointer. Who should delete the pointer? And when should the pointer be deleted? Will it be deleted when the container is destroyed?

In C++11, the statement std::unique_ptr<Foo> p(new Foo()); produces a compilation error. The reason is that the unique ownership rule kicks in.

However, you can use std::move to transfer ownership of the pointer:

data.push_back(std::move(p));

Now ownership of the pointer has been transferred to the container, and it will be deleted when the lifetime of the container ends. Although the object p still exists, any attempt to dereference it will result in a null pointer exception.

In fact, after the move operation, the internal pointer held by p has been set to nullptr.

In summary, the purpose of std::move is to provide a means of safely enabling move semantics for objects, converting their lvalue nature into an rvalue so that they can be consumed by move constructors or the move assignment operator. Using std::move correctly can improve performance and ensure proper ownership transfer.

So the next question is: when do you not need to use std::move?

docs.title: C++ std::bind vs lambda
docs.text:
Interviews often ask: both std::bind and lambda can package a function plus its arguments into a callable object — which one should you use? Everyone can recite the answer, "use lambda", but why? Beyond readability, how big is the performance difference really? Talk is cheap, so I wrote a benchmark and measured it.

(1) Test subject: the same member function Calculator::calculate, packaged with std::bind and with a lambda respectively, then passed to the same template function f and called repeatedly;

(2) For fairness, f receives the callable as a template parameter (so the type-erasure overhead of std::function does not pollute the conclusion);

(3) Code and results: https://quick-bench.com/q/CEnR_XUuIwnZxaP4KJNSlpYG38c

#include <functional>
#include <numeric>
#include <vector>



struct Calculator {
    int count{1};
    int total{0};

    auto calculate() -> void {
        using std::iota, std::vector;

        // Random math
        vector<int> u(8), v(Calculator::count * u.size());

        iota(v.begin(), v.end(), *u.begin());

        int sum{*v.begin() + *u.begin()};

        for (size_t pos{0}; pos < v.size(); ++pos) {
            sum += u[pos % u.size()] * v[pos];
        }

        Calculator::total += sum;
        ++Calculator::count;
    }
};

// auto f(std::function<void(int)> g) -> void { g(rand()); }

template<typename FN> auto f(FN g) -> void { g(rand()); }


static auto BM_bind(benchmark::State& state) -> void {
    Calculator calculator;
    for (auto _ : state) {
        f(std::bind(&Calculator::calculate, &calculator));
    }
}

static auto BM_lambda(benchmark::State& state) -> void {
    Calculator calculator;
    for (auto _ : state) {
        f([&calculator]([[maybe_unused]] int x) { calculator.calculate(); });
    }
}

BENCHMARK(BM_bind);
BENCHMARK(BM_lambda);

docs.title: How to Read the Results
docs.text:
The lambda version comes out clearly faster than the bind version, for two main reasons:

(1) The binder type returned by std::bind stores "the bound callable + every placeholder argument" as members; a call has to go through a long chain of forwarding inside the standard library, and in early implementations bind objects had heavy copy semantics and were hard to inline. A lambda is just a closure object: it stores exactly what it captures, and the compiler inlines it without any obstacle.

(2) A subtler point: std::bind differs from lambda in how it handles argument evaluation order, overload resolution, and default arguments, and in C++11 times implementations even disagreed (the standard later tightened the behavior). Effective Modern C++ Item 34 has the full summary: prefer lambda over bind whenever you can.

The only remaining real use case for bind is basically this: before C++14 there were no generic lambdas and no init-capture, and std::bind's placeholders could do "argument reordering / partially pre-binding arguments". Today lambda can do all of that, and more intuitively.

A question to leave: change f above from a template to taking a std::function<void(int)> — how would the gap between the two benchmarks change, and why?

docs.title: Variadic Templates from C++​那些​事
docs.text:
Recently, while reading the Arrow source code, I came across an interesting design: multiple nodes, such as proj and agg, can be added to a single plan.

Today let's talk about the design and implementation behind this.

docs.title: 1.Adding nodes
docs.text:
A plan usually needs a whole bunch of nodes added to it, and this is done by calling EmplaceNode.

return plan->EmplaceNode<ScalarAggregateNode>(
    plan, std::move(inputs), schema(std::move(fields)), std::move(target_field_ids),
    std::move(aggregates), std::move(kernels), std::move(states),
    std::move(owned_options));

Similarly, adding a proj node looks like this:

return plan->EmplaceNode<ProjectNode>(plan, std::move(inputs),
                schema(std::move(fields)), std::move(exprs),
                project_options.async_mode);

So what is the magic that makes the code this smooth?

Here is a simplified version of Plan:

class ARROW_EXPORT ExecPlan
{
    public:
    template <typename Node, typename... Args>
      Node* EmplaceNode(Args&&... args) {
        std::unique_ptr<Node> node{new Node{std::forward<Args>(args)...}};
        auto out = node.get();
        AddNode(std::move(node));
        return out;
      }
 }

This syntax looks very complicated, and indeed it is - it is the variadic template introduced after C++11. To explain what this code means: it forwards the parameter pack to the corresponding Node constructor. This example may look a bit complicated, so next let's move on to the demo.

docs.title: 2.Demo
docs.text:
Next we create a graph containing two different nodes, node A and node B. For simplicity, a function template EmplaceNode is used here.

NodeA* nodeA = EmplaceNode<NodeA>("Node A", 10, 3.14);
NodeB* nodeB = EmplaceNode<NodeB>(1, "Node B");

The complete code is as follows:

#include <iostream>
#include <vector>
#include <memory>

class NodeA {
public:
    NodeA(const std::string& name, int value, double weight)
        : name_(name), value_(value), weight_(weight) {}

    const std::string& GetName() const {
        return name_;
    }

private:
    std::string name_;
    int value_;
    double weight_;
};

class NodeB {
public:
    NodeB(int id, const std::string& desc)
        : id_(id), desc_(desc) {}

    int GetID() const {
        return id_;
    }

private:
    int id_;
    std::string desc_;
};
template<typename Node, typename... Args>
Node* EmplaceNode(Args&&... args) {
    std::unique_ptr<Node> node{new Node{std::forward<Args>(args)...}};
    auto out = node.get();
    // AddNode(std::move(node));
    return out;
}

int main() {
    NodeA* nodeA = EmplaceNode<NodeA>("Node A", 10, 3.14);
    NodeB* nodeB = EmplaceNode<NodeB>(1, "Node B");
    std::cout << "Node A name: " << nodeA->GetName() << std::endl;
    std::cout << "Node B ID: " << nodeB->GetID() << std::endl;
    return 0;
}

docs.title: 3.Extension: implementing a print function that can print data of any type
docs.text:
A simple implementation:

It can be implemented with variadic template parameters plus recursion.

Each call peels off one element plus the rest of the pack, until only a single element is left. Hence there is one function that handles a single element and one function that handles one element plus the rest, corresponding to the first print_impl and the second print_impl respectively.

#include <iostream>
#include <utility>

template <typename T>
void print_impl(T&& t) {
    std::cout << t;
}

template <typename T, typename... Args>
void print_impl(T&& t, Args&&... args) {
    std::cout << t;
    print_impl(std::forward<Args>(args)...);
}

template <typename... Args>
void print(Args&&... args) {
    print_impl(std::forward<Args>(args)...);
}

int main() {
    int x = 1;
    const char* str = "Hello, world!";
    print("The value of x is ", x, ", and the string is ", str, ".\n");
    return 0;
}

docs.title: C++17 [[nodiscard]] Attribute
docs.text: Since the [[nodiscard]] attribute was introduced in C++17, we have had a more powerful tool for marking function return values that should not be ignored at the call site. In this article we will take a deep dive into how to use [[nodiscard]] and watch out for some potential pitfalls.

docs.title: What is [[nodiscard]]?
docs.text: [[nodiscard]] is a function attribute that tells the compiler that the return value of a function should not be ignored. This is especially useful for functions that rely on their return value, such as predicate functions or factory functions.

docs.title: How to use [[nodiscard]]?
docs.text:
It is possible to use [[nodiscard]] on classes, constructors, and enums. Here are some examples:

class [[nodiscard]] A {};

class B {
public:
    [[nodiscard]] B() = default;
};

enum class [[nodiscard]] State {
    Default,
    Foo,
    Bar
};

In the examples above, the compiler will issue a warning whenever the return value is ignored, which helps us catch potential bugs early.

docs.title: Watch out: pitfalls of [[nodiscard]]
docs.text:
Although [[nodiscard]] can effectively prevent return values from being ignored unintentionally, we need to be aware of some potential pitfalls. A common pitfall is a [[nodiscard]] function that returns a scope-guard-like object in order to perform cleanup at the end of the scope (for example, committing a transaction).

[[nodiscard]] ScopeGuard createScopeGuard() {
    // Implementation of a scope guard
}

// ​在​这里​，​用户​可以​选择​忽略​返回值​，​导致​作用域​立即​销毁​，​从而​失去​清理​效果​
std::ignore = createScopeGuard();

Although [[nodiscard]] indicates that the return value of the function should not be ignored, the user can still explicitly discard the return value by means such as std::ignore, thereby bypassing the cleanup.

docs.title: Complete example
docs.text:
#include <tuple> // std::ignore

class [[nodiscard]] A {};
class B {
public:
    [[nodiscard]] bool isOk() const { return true; }
};

// no need for nodiscard, A is nodiscard
A foo() {
    return A();
}

// B is not nodiscard, mark it explicitly
[[nodiscard]] B bar() {
    return B();
}

int main()
{    
    foo(); // warning: ignoring temporary created by a constructor declared with 'nodiscard' attribute
    bar(); // warning

    std::ignore = foo(); // ok
    auto b = bar(); // ok
    b.isOk(); // warning
    if (b.isOk()) {} // ok
}

docs.title: C++17 std::string_view | C++​那些​事
docs.text: Last updated：2026-10-13

docs.title: 0.The problem
docs.text:
string_view was introduced after C++17; it is essentially the slice in leveldb, and its purpose is to solve memory copying and provide an efficient substr.

However, it also introduces problems with pointers and references. Since a string_view does not own the content it points to, compared with Rust it is merely a borrow: if the object that owns the content is released early, a dangling reference problem arises. Rust analyzes variable lifetimes at compile time to guarantee that borrowed resources are not released while still in use. C++, however, performs no such checking, so it must be guaranteed manually.

docs.title: 1.Internal implementation
docs.text:
string_view is a basic_string_view type. As you can see, _Traits uses the default char_traits, which is important: several of the functions below rely on member functions of char_traits to perform their core operations.

template<class _CharT, class _Traits = char_traits<_CharT> >
    class _LIBCPP_TEMPLATE_VIS basic_string_view;

typedef basic_string_view<char>     string_view;

Members of basic_string_view:

private:
    const   value_type* __data;
    size_type           __size;

Construction is compatible with string and const char*:

constexpr basic_string_view() noexcept;
constexpr basic_string_view(const basic_string_view&) noexcept = default;
basic_string_view& operator=(const basic_string_view&) noexcept = default;
template<class Allocator>
constexpr basic_string_view(const charT* str);
constexpr basic_string_view(const charT* str, size_type len);

Iterator support:

constexpr const_iterator begin() const noexcept;
constexpr const_iterator end() const noexcept;
constexpr const_iterator cbegin() const noexcept;
constexpr const_iterator cend() const noexcept;
const_reverse_iterator rbegin() const noexcept;
const_reverse_iterator rend() const noexcept;
const_reverse_iterator crbegin() const noexcept;
const_reverse_iterator crend() const noexcept;

Other core functions:

  • substr
  • remove_prefix
  • compare
  • find
  • ...

Since C++20 it also supports starts_with, ends_with, and contains; these three were supported in leveldb's slice from the very beginning.

A string_view literal for char*:

constexpr basic_string_view<char>     operator "" sv( const char *str,     size_t len ) noexcept;
constexpr basic_string_view<wchar_t>  operator "" sv( const wchar_t *str,  size_t len ) noexcept;
constexpr basic_string_view<char16_t> operator "" sv( const char16_t *str, size_t len ) noexcept;
constexpr basic_string_view<char32_t> operator "" sv( const char32_t *str, size_t len ) noexcept;

docs.title: 2.1 \0
docs.text:
string_view does not care about \0; it cares about the actual number of characters.

std::string_view s = "abc\0\0def"sv;
std::cout << "s: " << s.size() << " \"" << s << "\"\n";

Output: s: 8 "abcdef"

std::string_view str{"hello", 1};
std::cout << str.data() << std::endl; // ​输出​ hello，​而​不是​h

Here hello is expected to be printed, but h is printed instead.

docs.title: 2.2 Lifetime
docs.text:
string_view foo() {
    std::string s{"hello world"};
    return string_view{s};
}

In this example, once s goes out of scope, the string_view becomes a dangling reference.

Lifetime

std::string_view does not own the underlying character storage; make sure the lifetime of the referenced object covers the entire period of use.

docs.title: 1.Introduction
docs.text:
Before C++17, the standard library provided std::allocator, and in C++17 this facility was strengthened with the introduction of polymorphic_allocator.

Before C++17, if we wanted to use std::allocator to build a custom memory pool, we could not use the traditional approach of virtual polymorphism, because std::allocator does not provide virtual functions. Inheritance is therefore clearly not a good choice, but we can use it as a class member instead, as shown below:

template <typename Allocator = std::allocator<uint8_t>>
class MemoryPool {
 public:
  explicit STLMemoryPool(const Allocator& alloc) : alloc_(alloc) {}

  Status Allocate(int64_t size, uint8_t** out) {
    try {
      *out = alloc_.allocate(size);
    } catch (std::bad_alloc& e) {
      return Status::OutOfMemory(e.what());
    }
    return Status::OK();
  }

  void Free(uint8_t* buffer, int64_t size) {
    alloc_.deallocate(buffer, size);
  }

 private:
  Allocator alloc_;
};

Before C++17, if we wanted to print something, or perform some custom operations, when memory is allocated/freed, there were two ways to do it:

  • Custom global new/delete
void* operator new(std::size_t size) {
  void* ptr = malloc(size);
  std::cout << "Allocated: " << size << " bytes at address " << ptr << std::endl;
  return ptr;
}

void operator delete(void* ptr, std::size_t n) noexcept {
  std::cout << "Deallocated: " << n << " bytes at address " << ptr << std::endl;
  free(ptr);
}
  • A custom allocator
class allocator {
 public:
  using value_type = T;
  value_type* allocate(std::size_t n) {
    value_type* p = static_cast<value_type*>(::operator new(n * sizeof(value_type)));
    std::cout << "Allocated: " << n * sizeof(value_type) << " bytes at address "
              << static_cast<void*>(p) << std::endl;
    return p;
  }

  void deallocate(value_type* p, std::size_t n) noexcept {
    std::cout << "Deallocated: " << n * sizeof(value_type) << " bytes at address "
              << static_cast<void*>(p) << std::endl;
    ::operator delete(p);
  }
};

std::vector<int, allocator<int>> vec;

So, besides these, what other options are there?

Since C++17, we can use the polymorphic memory management tools, polymorphic memory resources (pmr). Usage:

#include <memory_resources>

pmr::monotonic_buffer_resource res(10);
pmr::vector<vector<int>> vec1(&res);

For the problem above, we can inherit from memory_resource; for an explanation of the code below, see memory_resource further down.

class TrackAllocator : public std::pmr::memory_resource {
    void* do_allocate(std::size_t bytes, std::size_t alignment) override {
        void* p = std::pmr::new_delete_resource()->allocate(bytes, alignment);
        std::cout << "do_allocate: " << bytes << " bytes at " << p
                  << " alignment: " << alignment << std::endl;
        return p;
    }

    void do_deallocate(void* p, std::size_t bytes, std::size_t alignment) override {
      std::cout << "do_deallocate: " << bytes << " bytes at "
                << " alignment: " << alignment << std::endl;
      return std::pmr::new_delete_resource()->deallocate(p, bytes, alignment);
    }

    bool do_is_equal(const std::pmr::memory_resource& other) const noexcept override {
        return std::pmr::new_delete_resource()->is_equal(other);
    }
};

With this, we have achieved the effect shown above.

docs.title: 2.memory_resource
docs.text:
The implementation of the std::par::memory_resource class in the STL is fairly simple; here is a pseudo-code implementation:

class memory_resource {
  static const size_t __max_align = alignof(max_align_t);

public:
  virtual ~memory_resource();

  void* allocate(size_t __bytes, size_t __align = __max_align) {
    return do_allocate(__bytes, __align);
  }

  void deallocate(void* __p, size_t __bytes, size_t __align = __max_align) {
    do_deallocate(__p, __bytes, __align);
  }

  bool is_equal(const memory_resource& __other) const noexcept { 
    return do_is_equal(__other); 
  }

private:
  virtual void* do_allocate(size_t, size_t)                       = 0;
  virtual void do_deallocate(void*, size_t, size_t)               = 0;
  virtual bool do_is_equal(memory_resource const&) const noexcept = 0;
};

Unlike the default std::allocator, memory_resource provides polymorphic capabilities, allowing users to override the following three interfaces through inheritance:

  • do_allocate
  • Allocates memory of a given size and with a given alignment requirement.
  • do_deallocate
  • Frees memory previously allocated via do_allocate.
  • do_is_equal
  • Checks whether this memory resource object is equal to another memory resource object.

Therefore, our TrackAllocator above simply overrides these three function interfaces.

Careful readers will have noticed that besides these interfaces, memory_resource also exposes three public interfaces. In addition, it provides these global interfaces:

memory_resource* new_delete_resource() noexcept;
memory_resource* null_memory_resource() noexcept;
memory_resource* get_default_resource() noexcept;
memory_resource* set_default_resource(memory_resource* __r) noexcept;
  • new_delete_resource

Returns a memory_resource pointer that allocates and deallocates memory using the new and delete operators. This resource is implemented with the global new and delete operators, which makes it the default memory resource manager. This memory_resource subclass is __resource_adaptor_imp, which is responsible for overriding the three interfaces above.

  • null_memory_resource

Returns a memory_resource pointer representing a null memory resource that does nothing. You can use this resource when you want to test or stub things out without performing actual memory allocation. The implementation in the STL source defines a

inline memory_resource*
null_memory_resource() noexcept {
    class type final : public memory_resource {};
}

type, as a subclass, overrides the three interfaces above; the do_allocate interface throws an allocation-failure exception, because semantically allocation is simply not allowed.

do_allocate(size_t, size_t) override
    { std::__throw_bad_alloc(); }

So when we use null_memory_resource, we need a try/catch. For example: a string whose character count is less than 16 is allocated on the stack, in which case our memory_resource here is not used, so things run normally; once the length is greater than or equal to 16, a std::bad_alloc exception is thrown.

std::pmr::memory_resource* default_resource = std::pmr::null_memory_resource();

std::pmr::set_default_resource(default_resource);

try {
  std::pmr::vector<int> data{1};
} catch (std::bad_alloc e) {
  std::cerr << "bad_alloc is thrown vector" << std::endl;
}

std::pmr::string str1{"hello world hel"};
std::cerr << str1 << " length:" << str1.size() << std::endl;

try {
  std::pmr::string str1{"hello world hel0"};
} catch (std::bad_alloc e) {
  std::cerr << "bad_alloc is thrown string" << std::endl;
}
  • get_default_resource

Returns the current default global memory resource manager. By default it is the same resource returned by new_delete_resource(), but the default resource can be changed via the set_default_resource function.

  • set_default_resource

Sets the memory resource manager. The argument may be null (restoring the default resource); otherwise it is set to the passed resource, and the previous default resource is returned.

docs.title: 3.Memory reuse
docs.text:
std::pmr::monotonic_buffer_resource is a buffer with significant advantages for memory reuse. monotonic_buffer_resource inherits from memory_resource and overrides the three interfaces above; internally it holds an upstream memory_resource, and when its current memory is insufficient it fetches more from the upstream. This helps reduce memory fragmentation and improve memory utilization.

Below are some ways to use std::pmr::monotonic.

Usage 1 - Create a monotonic_buffer_resource with a fixed buffer:

char buf1[30] = {};
std::fill_n(std::begin(buf1), std::size(buf1) - 1, '_');
std::pmr::monotonic_buffer_resource pool1{std::data(buf1), std::size(buf1)};
std::pmr::vector<int> myVec1{&pool1};

Usage 2 - Create a monotonic_buffer_resource with an upstream resource:

std::pmr::memory_resource* upstreamResource2 = std::pmr::get_default_resource();
std::pmr::monotonic_buffer_resource pool2(upstreamResource2);
{
    std::pmr::vector<double> numbers(&pool2);
    for (double d = 0.1; d < 1.0; d += 0.1) {
        numbers.push_back(d);
    }
}

Usage 3 - Inherit from std::pmr::monotonic_buffer_resource:

class MyMonotonicBufferResource : public std::pmr::monotonic_buffer_resource {
public:
    using std::pmr::monotonic_buffer_resource::monotonic_buffer_resource; // Inherit constructors

    // Public function to access do_allocate
    void* allocate(std::size_t bytes, std::size_t alignment) {
        return do_allocate(bytes, alignment);
    }

    // Public function to access do_deallocate
    void deallocate(void* p, std::size_t bytes, std::size_t alignment) {
        do_deallocate(p, bytes, alignment);
    }
};

MyMonotonicBufferResource pool3;
// Allocate memory
void* mem = pool3.allocate(100, alignof(int));

// Use the allocated memory (this is just an example)
std::pmr::vector<int> numbers({1, 2, 3}, &pool3);

// Deallocate memory
pool3.deallocate(mem, 100, alignof(int));

std::cout << "Usage 3 - Inherit: \n\n";

docs.title: 4.pool resource
docs.text:
synchronized_pool_resource is a thread-safe memory pool resource class. It is designed to make memory allocation and deallocation safe in multi-threaded environments. When multiple threads concurrently attempt to allocate or free memory, synchronized_pool_resource uses synchronization mechanisms to ensure thread safety. This usually incurs some performance overhead, because locking is required to protect the shared memory pool.

Its counterpart is unsynchronized_pool_resource, where the user is responsible for guaranteeing thread safety.

The source implementation of synchronized_pool_resource is really just mutex + unsynchronized_pool_resource.

class synchronized_pool_resource : public memory_resource {

public:
    // some interface
private:
  mutex __mut_;
  unsynchronized_pool_resource __unsync_;
};

pool_options can be used to configure these memory pools.

struct pool_options {
  size_t max_blocks_per_chunk        = 0;
  size_t largest_required_pool_block = 0;
};
  • max_blocks_per_chunk

The maximum number of blocks a chunk may contain. It limits how much memory the pool fetches from the upstream memory resource at one time. If set to 0, the kernel modifies pool_options through the munge_options function.

  • largest_required_pool_block

The largest block size the memory pool can handle.

docs.title: C++17 Seventeen Advanced Features | C++​那些​事
docs.text: Last updated：2026-10-13

docs.title: A complete rundown of 17 advanced C++17 features
docs.text: C++17 is one of the most commonly used versions today. This time I spent some effort sorting out 17 important features - and there are more features than just these.

docs.title: 1. Parallel algorithms
docs.text:
C++17 introduced parallel versions of many algorithms in the standard library. These algorithms can execute in parallel, so they may bring significant performance improvements on multi-core systems.

I previously wrote an article that covers this feature in depth; you can read that one:

Example:

#include <algorithm>
#include <vector>
#include <execution>
int main() {
    std::vector<int> v = {1, 2, 3, 4, 5};
    std::sort(std::execution::par, v.begin(), v.end());
}

In this example, std::sort executes in parallel, sorting the elements of the vector v in a parallel fashion.

docs.title: 2. If Initializers
docs.text:
The if initializer in C++17 is a feature that allows variables to be initialized directly in an if statement. This style of initialization can, to some extent, improve the readability and conciseness of the code.

In traditional C++, we would usually initialize the variable like this:

int x;
if (condition) {
    x = 42;
} else {
    x = 24;
}

In C++17, however, an if initializer can be used to simplify this process and make the code more compact:

if (bool condition = /* some condition */) {
    int x = 42;
} else {
    int x = 24;
}

In this example, we put the initialization of the variable x directly in the if statement. The variable condition is defined and initialized in the if statement and is then usable inside the if block. This style is more intuitive and concise, especially for simple conditional initialization.

docs.title: 3. Class Template Argument Deduction (CTAD)
docs.text:
CTAD lets the compiler deduce template arguments automatically from function arguments. This makes templates easier to use without having to specify template arguments explicitly.

A previous article covered this feature in depth:

Example:

template <typename T>
void foo(T t) {
    // ...
}

int main() {
    foo(42);  // ​编译器​推导​出​T​的​类型​为​int
}

In this example, when foo(42) is called, the compiler deduces that the type of T is int.

docs.title: 4. template <auto>
docs.text:
The template keyword was introduced as a placeholder for non-type template parameters. It allows values of any type to be represented in a template.

Example:

template<auto value>
struct constant {
    static constexpr auto get_value() { return value; }
};

// ​用法​
static_assert(constant<42>::get_value() == 42);

docs.title: 5. std::optional and std::variant
docs.text:
std::optional and std::variant are two new types introduced in C++17. std::optional represents a value that may or may not exist, while std::variant is a type-safe union that can hold values of different types.

Example:

#include <optional>
#include <variant>

int main() {
    std::optional<int> opt = 42;
    std::variant<int, double> var = 3.14;
}

In this example, opt is an optional integer holding the value 42, and var is a variant holding the value 3.14.

docs.title: 6. Fold expressions
docs.text:
In C++17, fold expressions provide a concise way to apply binary operations to a parameter pack. They allow operations such as summing, multiplying, or concatenating the elements of a parameter pack without explicit recursion or iteration.

For example:

#include <iostream>

template<typename T>
T sum(T t) {
    return t;
}

// ​使用​折叠​表达式​的​递归​情况​
template<typename T, typename... Args>
T sum(T first, Args... args) {
    return first + sum(args...);
}

int main() {
    int total = sum(1, 2, 3, 4, 5);
    std::cout << "​总和​: " << total << std::endl;

    return 0;
}

The fold expression (first + ... + args) in the recursive sum function applies the addition operation to every element of the parameter pack.

docs.title: 7. Structured bindings
docs.text:
Structured bindings allow you to decompose an object into its constituent elements, similar to the tuple unpacking you may already be familiar with.

Previous article:

Example:

#include <tuple>
#include <string>
int main() {
    std::tuple<int, std::string, double> t(42, "hello", 3.14);
    auto [i, s, d] = t;  // i = 42, s = "hello", d = 3.14
}

In this example, the structured binding [i, s, d] decomposes the tuple t into its constituent elements.

docs.title: 8. Template template parameters
docs.text:
For example: in C++17, the syntax template<template<class...>typename bob> struct foo {} declares a template named foo that accepts a template template parameter named bob. The template template parameter bob itself accepts any number of template type parameters.

template <template<class...> typename bob>
struct foo {
    template<typename T>
    void bar(const bob<T>& arg) {
        std::cout << "size: " << arg.size() << std::endl;
    }
};

int main() {
    foo<std::vector> f;
    std::vector<int> vec = {1, 2, 3, 4, 5};
    f.bar(vec);

    return 0;
}

In the main function, we instantiate foo with std::vector as the template argument for bob. This lets us create a generic structure foo that can work with any template accepting any number of type parameters, such as std::vector, std::list, or user-defined templates.

docs.title: 9. Inline variables
docs.text:
C++17 allows variables to be defined as inline inside the class definition, which can help reduce binary size and may improve performance by preventing duplicate copies of the variable across multiple translation units.

Example:

class MyClass {
public:
    inline static int inlineVar = 42;
};

int main() {
    int localVar = MyClass::inlineVar;
}

Here, inlineVar is an inline static member variable of MyClass.

docs.title: 10. Attribute improvements
docs.text:
C++17 provides new attributes and improves existing ones, allowing developers to give the compiler more information about how the code behaves.

Example:

[[nodiscard]] int get_sum(int a, int b) {
    return a + b;
}

int main() {
    auto result = get_sum(1, 2);
    // ​编译器​可能​会​警告​‘result’​未​使用​
}

In this example, [[nodiscard]] is an attribute that can be applied to a function, indicating that its return value should not be discarded by the caller.

docs.title: 11. Nested namespaces
docs.text:
C++17 enhanced variadic templates with fold expressions, making code that handles parameter packs more concise and expressive.

Example:

// ​外部​命名​空间​
namespace outer {
    // ​内部​命名​空间​
    namespace inner {
        void foo() {
            std::cout << "​在​内部​命名​空间​中​" << std::endl;
        }
    }
}

outer::inner::foo();

Nested namespace definitions provide a way to organize code hierarchically, improving readability and maintainability, especially in large projects. They also help avoid naming conflicts by providing a more structured namespace hierarchy.

docs.title: 12. Literal improvements
docs.text:
C++17 enhanced literals, including improvements to integer and floating-point literals, as well as support for the true and false literals.

Example:

auto num = 123_456; // Underscore in integer literals  
auto pi = 3.1415_f; // Suffix for floating-point literals

docs.title: 13. constexpr Lambda
docs.text:
C++17 allows lambda functions to be constexpr; if they satisfy the requirements, they can be used in contexts that require compile-time evaluation, for example:

constexpr auto lambda = [](int x) { return x * 2; };
static_assert(lambda(5) == 10);

In this example, lambda is a constexpr lambda that takes an integer x as its parameter and returns twice x. The static_assert checks at compile time whether the value of lambda(5) equals 10.

docs.title: 14. Capturing *this
docs.text:
Capturing *this in a lambda has become simpler, allowing direct access to the members of the containing object.

class Foo {
    int data = 42;
public:
    auto member_lambda() {
        return [*this] { std::cout << data << std::endl; };
    }
};

// ​使用​
Foo f;
f.member_lambda()(); // ​输出​ "42"

docs.title: 15. Extended if and switch statements
docs.text:
The condition of an if or switch statement can now be any expression, not just a boolean condition. This makes control flow more flexible, for example when using structured bindings:

if (const auto [it, inserted] = map.insert({"foo", bar}); inserted) {
    // ...
}

In this example, the if statement checks whether the variable inserted is true, but the condition also includes the assignment of a structured binding.

docs.title: 16. Generalized range-based for loops
docs.text:
This improvement supports sentinels, or end iterators, whose type differs from the begin iterator, which helps when dealing with null-terminated loops and other similar cases. For example:

for (auto it = my_container.begin(); it != my_container.end(); ++it) {
   // ...
}

In this example, my_container might be a container that uses a different type for its end iterator, but the loop still works correctly.

docs.title: 17. if constexpr
docs.text:
This feature allows the compiler to evaluate conditions at compile time, enabling more generic code. If the condition is true, the code inside the if block is included in the compiled code; otherwise it is discarded. This can simplify code by eliminating unnecessary branches at run time. For example:

if constexpr (std::is_same_v<T, int>) {
   // ​用于​int​的​特定​代码​
} else {
   // ​用于​其他​类型​的​代码​
}

In this example, the if constexpr statement checks whether the type T is int and includes the appropriate code accordingly.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: That is all for this section; the remaining content will be covered in the next one.

docs.title: C++17 Class Template Argument Deduction CTAD
Introduction
docs.text:
C++ template metaprogramming has long been a well-known capability among C++ developers: newcomers and advanced developers alike can use it to write generic code with type parameters. With class template argument deduction (CTAD) introduced in C++17, working with class templates has become more intuitive and flexible.

All the code in this section will also be updated in the community.

CTAD, introduced in C++17, brings the following benefits:

For example, with such complicated code

std::vector<FooBar<int, const char*>> obj{a, b, c};

we only need:

 std::vector obj{a, b, c};

Or again:

std::tuple<int>

can be simplified to:

std::tuple t1{1};

So today let's take a look at CTAD.

CTAD stands for Class template argument deduction (CTAD), that is, class template argument deduction. Once you give the compiler a deduction guide, we can use this feature.

If we do not provide one, as in the example below:

#include <iostream>
template <typename T, typename U>
struct MyPair {
  T first{};
  U second{};
};

int main() {
  MyPair<int, int> p1{1, 2};
  MyPair p2{1, 2};
  std::cout << p1.first << ", " << p1.second << std::endl;
  std::cout << p2.first << ", " << p2.second << std::endl;
  return 0;
}

For p2 we get an error:

no viable constructor or deduction guide for deduction of template arguments of 'MyPair'

So how do we fix it?

We only need to add a deduction guide, written as follows.

template <typename T, typename U>
MyPair(T, U) -> MyPair<T, U>;

Class template argument deduction (CTAD) simplifies the instantiation of class templates by allowing the compiler to deduce template arguments from constructor arguments. Before CTAD was introduced, developers had to specify template arguments explicitly when instantiating. With CTAD, such explicit specification is no longer necessary, making the code easier to read and maintain.

template <typename T>
class Add{
    private:
        T first;
        T second;
    public:
        Add() = default;
        Add(T first, T second): first_{first}, second_{second} {}
        T result() const { return first + second; }
};

int main(){
    Add one(1,2);               // T​被​推导​为​int
    Add two{1.245, 3.1415};     // T​被​推导​为​double
    Add three = {0.24f, 0.34f}; // T​被​推导​为​float
}

In the examples above, CTAD allows the type T to be deduced based on the constructor arguments, eliminating the need for explicit type specification.

docs.title: Non-static member initialization
docs.text:
But there is one scenario where CTAD cannot be used: non-static member initialization. For example, to use the outer MyPair inside a Test class, you must write the template arguments out in full.

template <typename T = int, typename U = int>
struct MyPair {
  T first{};
  U second{};
};

template <typename T, typename U>
MyPair(T, U) -> MyPair<T, U>;

class Test {
  MyPair p4;   // use of class template 'MyPair' requires template arguments; argument
               // deduction not allowed in non-static class member
};

In the example above, we defined a template class MyPair and used CTAD with it. However, when we try to use MyPair as a non-static member of the class Test, CTAD no longer works because of the non-static member initialization context, resulting in a compilation error. In this case, we must explicitly specify the template arguments of MyPair.

As we can see, in the context of non-static member initialization CTAD cannot deduce template arguments. Therefore, when a class template is used as a non-static member, developers must explicitly specify all the template arguments. This is something to pay special attention to in real-world development, to ensure the correctness and maintainability of the code.

docs.title: C++17 optional_ref
docs.text: This post retells foonathan's blog optional_ref discussion; the original is the single best discussion of why std::optional<T&> (an optional reference) never made it into the standard. The topic was dug up again right before C++26, so it is worth walking through the core arguments.

docs.title:
1. The Problem: Why Doesn't std::optional Compile?

std::optional<int>, std::optional<std::string> are both fine, but std::optional<int&> fails to compile outright. The reason is a bit of "historical baggage": when the standard was drawn up, no consensus was reached on its assignment semantics, so the standard simply states that behavior is undefined when T is a reference type.

So what is so hard about a "possibly empty reference"? The author distilled four questions:

(1) Is optional<T&> the same thing as a pointer?

(2) Do we really need optional<T&>?

(3) On assignment, should it rebind (rebind to the new object) or assign-through (write to the referred object)?

(4) Should it even have an assignment operator at all?

The author's tl;dr answers: no, we do not, rebind, and it should not. Let us see why.

2. An optional Reference Is Not a Pointer

Intuitively, a "possibly empty reference" is just a pointer, but the author points out a more essential difference:

  • creation of and access to a T& are both implicit: once you have the reference you just use it, no dereference needed;
  • creation of and access to a T* are both explicit: you need &x to take the address and *p to dereference.

This explicitness difference has value: a pointer reminds you "this may be null, there may be aliasing problems here". Making optional<T&> an "easier pointer" with implicit conversions everywhere throws away exactly this layer of protection. The author's conclusion: if you want to express "may be empty", an explicit T* is actually better documentation.

4. Summary

(1) optional<T&> is not syntactic sugar for a pointer; the two have an essential division of labor in explicitness;

(2) what blocked it is the ambiguity of assignment semantics: both rebind and assign-through make sense;

(3) when you need a "nullable reference", an explicit pointer or an optional_ref is a safer choice than a "legalized optional".

Finally, a question to ponder: should optional<T&>'s value() and *opt return T& or const T&? And if you also want to express captured-as-const semantics, how should the template parameter be designed?

docs.title: C++17 Structured Bindings
docs.text:
Before talking about structured bindings, here are a few interview questions - can you answer them?

  • How do you access the private members of a custom class using structured bindings?

  • How do you modify the members of a custom class using structured bindings?

Few people can answer these questions, and neither the questions nor the answers can be found online. Based on these questions, this article introduces its topic: how to support structured bindings for custom types, and what pitfalls lie along the way.

Note: for the lazy, the answers and code are already available in the members' community.

To make this article flow more smoothly, let's start from an example.

docs.title: 1.Custom types
docs.text:
Given a class:

struct Foo {
  Foo(int64_t id, std::string data) : id_(id), data_(std::move(data)) {}
  void Print() { std::cout << "id = " << id_ << ", data = " << data_ << std::endl; }

 private:
  int64_t id_;
  std::string data_;
};

To make the following code run:

int main() {
  Foo f{12, "hello world"};
  const auto& [id, data] = f;
  std::cout << "id = " << id << ", data = " << data << std::endl;
  f.Print();
}

If you run it directly, it fails to compile:

 cannot decompose inaccessible member 'Foo::id_' of 'const Foo'
   42 |   const auto& [id, data] = f;

So what do we do?

docs.title: 2.Supporting structured bindings
docs.text:
We solve this problem in two steps:

Step 1: specialize std::tuple_size and std::tuple_element

namespace std {
  template <>
  struct tuple_size<Foo> : std::integral_constant<std::size_t, 2> {};

  template <>
  struct tuple_element<0, Foo> {
    using type = int64_t;
  };

  template <>
  struct tuple_element<1, Foo> {
    using type = std::string;
  };
}

Step 2: add a friend get function for the struct above, then implement it:

template <std::size_t Index>
decltype(auto) get(const Foo& f);

template <>
decltype(auto) get<0>(const Foo& f) {
  return f.id_;
}

template <>
decltype(auto) get<1>(const Foo& f) {
  return f.data_;
}

Now it works correctly, producing the output:

id = 12, data = hello world
id = 12, data = hello world

Finally, here are a few questions to leave you with:

  • Above we provided read-only access; what happens if the bound objects are modified when accessing via const auto&?

For example:

auto& [id, data] = f;
  • How do you support modifying access to class members?

That is, make this statement work:

auto& [id, data] = f;

That's all for this section; feel free to discuss in the comments.

docs.title: Everything in C++ can be auto
docs.text:
C++17 introduced many features aimed at making code more expressive and reducing template boilerplate. One notable enhancement is the ability to declare non-type template parameters with the auto keyword. In certain scenarios this feature is particularly convenient, because it removes the need for explicit type declarations. Below I will introduce how I used this feature at work, that is, in a database!

Learning from practice: the complete source code of this section will be uploaded to the members' community; see the QR code at the end of the page if you are interested.

docs.title: Using auto for non-type template parameters in C++17
Sorting in a database scenario
docs.text:
Consider a database-related class Foo that you want to sort according to a specific order represented by an enum:

enum class SortOrder { Ascending, Descending };

You have Foo instances with different sort orders:

Foo<SortOrder::Ascending> f1;
Foo<SortOrder::Descending> f2;

docs.title: The previous way of implementing it
docs.text:
Before C++17, we might have implemented it like this:

template <typename U, template <U> class T, U K>
auto GetSortOrder(const T<K>&) {
  return K;
}

However, this can cause errors, because the compiler cannot infer the template parameter 'U'.

docs.title: The simplified way now
docs.text:
Since C++17, for non-type template parameters we can use the auto keyword instead:

template <template <auto> class T, auto K>
auto GetSortOrder(const T<K>&) {
  return K;
}

This approach is simpler, letting us use non-type template parameters without explicitly specifying the type.

docs.title: Simplifying integral_constant
docs.text:
Previously, we might have implemented integral_constant in the following way:

template <typename _Tp, _Tp __v>
struct integral_constant {}

And now all we need is:

template <auto __v>
struct integral_constant {}

This simplification makes the code clearer and easier to read.

docs.title: Conclusion
docs.text: The use of the auto keyword for declaring non-type template parameters introduced in C++17 greatly simplifies template code. By eliminating tedious type declarations, we can express the intent of the code more directly, improving its readability and maintainability. When dealing with scenarios such as sorting, this feature is especially useful, letting us focus on the essence of the problem rather than the details of template parameters.

docs.title: Variable Templates from C++​那些​事
docs.text:
When writing template code, we often need to define and use various type traits. These traits are usually used to reason about types at compile time; the std::is_const, std::is_same, and std::is_reference provided by the STL are examples of exactly that. With these traits, developers can make compile-time decisions based on type properties.

This article introduces how to use C++14 variable templates to simplify writing type traits, together with a simple example.

docs.title: C++11
docs.text:
In C++11, writing a type trait usually involves using a struct or std::integral_constant to encapsulate a boolean value. For example, to write a trait is_float that checks whether a type is float, we can implement it as follows:

template <typename T>
struct is_float {
    static constexpr bool value = std::is_same<T, float>::value;
};

Or, slightly more concisely, using a type alias and std::integral_constant:

template <typename T>
using is_float = std::integral_constant<bool, std::is_same<T, float>::value>;

Although this is more concise than using a struct directly, in the end we are still defining a type rather than getting a boolean value directly. To use this trait, the boolean value has to be obtained through the ::value member:

template <typename T>
void test(T t){
    if (is_float<T>::value){
        std::cout << "I'm a float" << std::endl;
    } else {
        std::cout << "I'm not a float" << std::endl;
    }
}

This works, but there are still two shortcomings: 1. Every use of the trait requires accessing ::value. 2. Defining a new trait requires declaring a new type or type alias, which adds code redundancy.

docs.title: The introduction of C++14 variable templates
docs.text:
C++14 introduced variable templates, allowing us to define variables that depend on types directly. This feature simplifies writing type traits: instead of wrapping boolean values in type aliases or structs, we can define the boolean value directly.

The rewritten is_float trait looks like this:

template <typename T>
constexpr bool is_float = std::is_same<T, float>::value;

This form is clearer and more concise, removing unnecessary code. It is also more convenient to use:

template <typename T>
void test(T t){
    if (is_float<T>){
        std::cout << "I'm a float" << std::endl;
    } else {
        std::cout << "I'm not a float" << std::endl;
    }
}

Compared with the previous way of writing it, with variable templates there is no longer any need to access the boolean value through ::value, and the code is more concise and intuitive.

docs.title: Advantages of variable templates
docs.text:
1. Less redundant code: variable templates allow us to define variables based on types directly, avoiding the redundant code of encapsulating boolean values in a struct or std::integral_constant.
  2. Better readability: by simplifying the syntax, variable templates make the code clearer, especially when writing a large number of type traits.
  3. Template specialization support: unlike type alias templates, variable templates can be specialized, both fully and partially. We can define dedicated logic for specific types without worrying about extensibility.

docs.title: Further improvements in C++17
docs.text:
C++17 further extended the application of variable templates by providing a variable template helper for every type trait. For example, std::is_same gained the std::is_same_v variable template, which simplifies accessing the value of a type trait:

template <typename T>
constexpr bool is_float = std::is_same_v<T, float>;

In this way, using type traits becomes more concise: developers can take advantage of variable templates directly without accessing ::value every time.

docs.title: A real-world case
docs.text:
This feature is used quite a lot in practice. For example, when allocating memory blocks of different sizes in a database, we can initialize the block size for different types via templates.

template <typename T>
constexpr size_t block_size = 1024;  // ​默认​大小​

template <>
constexpr size_t block_size<double> = 2048;  // double ​类型​需要​更​多​内存​

docs.title: 1. What Are Coroutines
docs.text:
Since C++20, C++ finally supports coroutines; C++23 is expected to bring additional support that at least covers the most common use cases.

A coroutine is a kind of program component that generalizes the subroutine of cooperative multitasking, allowing execution to be suspended and resumed. Compared with subroutines, coroutines are more general and more flexible, but in practice they are not used as widely as subroutines. Coroutines are a better fit for implementing familiar program components such as cooperative multitasking, exception handling, event loops, iterators, infinite lists, and pipes.

This passage from Wikipedia describes the basic idea of coroutines.

From the C++ perspective, you can simply understand a coroutine as any function that contains co_return, co_yield, or co_await.

C++20 coroutines are currently syntactic sugar over function objects: the compiler generates a code framework around the coroutine. This code relies on user-defined promise types. That may change after C++23, but until then we play by the C++20 rules and write these types ourselves.

co_return, co_yield, and co_await were mentioned above; they will be explained in later sections.

docs.title: 2. Step By Step Coroutine
docs.text:
Next, let's start with a simple coroutine example. The following coroutine does nothing at all — let's call it the HelloTask coroutine.

#include <coroutine>
struct HelloTask {
    struct promise_type {
        HelloTask get_return_object() { return {}; }
        std::suspend_never initial_suspend() { return {}; }
        std::suspend_never final_suspend() noexcept { return {}; }
        void return_void() {}
        void unhandled_exception() {}
    };
};
HelloTask myCoroutine() {
    co_return; // make it a coroutine
}
int main() {
    HelloTask x = myCoroutine();
}

Compile and run this code:

g++ hello.cpp -fcoroutines -std=c++20

Your compiler needs to support C++20 features.

Let's walk through this HelloWorld program from top to bottom and see how it differs from everyday development.

docs.title: 2.1 Header
docs.text:
First, the header introduces coroutine. Here I went straight to the gcc-10 source code to see what it actually does.

https://github.com/gcc-mirror/gcc/blob/releases/gcc-10/libstdc++-v3/include/std/coroutine

Its contents include the following:

// ​用于​发现​协程​promise_type​的​特征​类型​
// ​核心​代码​:using promise_type = typename _Result::promise_type;
1.coroutine_traits

// ​协程​句柄​，​用于​管理​暂停​或​执行​的​协程​以及​Promise
2.coroutine_handle
  // coroutine_handle​全​特化​版本​  ​是​其他​特化​的​公开​基类​。​它​保有​handle​的​底层​     ​地址​。
  2.1 coroutine_handle<void>

  // coroutine_handle​泛化​版本​
  2.2 template <typename _Promise>
      struct coroutine_handle : coroutine_handle<>


  // coroutine_handle​全​特化​版本​ ​处理​无​操作​协程​
  2.3 template <>
      struct coroutine_handle<noop_coroutine_promise> : public          coroutine_handle<>
3.​平凡​多​可​等待​对象​ Trivial awaitables
  // await​表达式​应该​暂停​
  3.1 suspend_always
  // await​表达式​不​应该​暂停​
  3.2 suspend_never

You can see it contains quite a few specific terms:

  • coroutine_handle
  • Promise
  • awaitable

and so on.

The coroutine material in the rest of this article is built around these.

docs.title: 2.2 Promise
docs.text:
Continuing with the HelloTask above, you will find it contains this snippet:

struct HelloTask {
    struct promise_type {
        HelloTask get_return_object() { return {}; }
        std::suspend_never initial_suspend() { return {}; }
        std::suspend_never final_suspend() noexcept { return {}; }
        void return_void() {}
        void unhandled_exception() {}
    };
};

So the question is: why do we need to write promise_type here?

The reason for writing promise_type is the handle mentioned in section 2.1 above: when the compiler creates the coroutine's handle, it needs to know the promise_type of that coroutine object, so basically every coroutine object has a HelloTask::promise_type structure. Careful readers will have already figured it out: the promise_type is passed over, parsed inside the Handle, and used to determine the behavior of the user-defined coroutine object.

Let's take a closer look at what goes inside promise_type. Its contents are fixed, and as the later material grows richer, more and more functions get involved. For example, return_void is used here; later, when co_return returns an object, a different function will be used instead.

get_return_object can return the current user-defined object. Here it does nothing; picking up from section 2.1 above, we can use a coroutine_handle instead.

struct promise_type {
    using Handle = std::coroutine_handle<promise_type>;
    HelloTask get_return_object() {
        return HelloTask{Handle::from_promise(*this)};
    }
  // other member function
}

You can see it uses the coroutine_handle's from_promise member to construct an object.

initial_suspend: tells the compiler whether the coroutine should stay suspended the first time it executes, i.e. whether it stays suspended when the coroutine is instantiated.

final_suspend: the opposite of initial_suspend. After the coroutine body completes, there is a final_suspend at the end of the coroutine. This gives you a chance to do additional cleanup.

Both of these return an awaitable; here the suspend_always from the header file is used — of course a user-defined awaitable works too, which will be covered in a later article.

The source code of suspend_always and suspend_never is as follows:

struct suspend_always
{
  constexpr bool await_ready() const noexcept { return false; }

  constexpr void await_suspend(coroutine_handle<>) const noexcept {}

  constexpr void await_resume() const noexcept {}
};

struct suspend_never
{
  constexpr bool await_ready() const noexcept { return true; }

  constexpr void await_suspend(coroutine_handle<>) const noexcept {}

  constexpr void await_resume() const noexcept {}
};

These contain several members:

  • await_ready
  • If you already know the result is ready, can it complete synchronously?
  • await_suspend
  • The return value can be bool, void, or a coroutine handle.
  • Here it returns void, which immediately returns control to the current coroutine's caller/resumer (this coroutine remains suspended); if await_suspend returns bool instead, true means control goes to the caller/resumer and false means the current coroutine is resumed. Returning a coroutine handle will be covered in a later article.
  • await_resume
  • Its result is the result of the whole co_await expression. So the return value does not have to be void — it can also be a custom object and so on.

return_void: when co_return; is used, return_void is called.

unhandled_exception: used to catch exceptions.

Finally, one step is still missing: creating the coroutine. According to the definition at the beginning, a coroutine is any function containing co_return, co_yield, or co_await. Hence:

HelloTask myCoroutine() {
    co_return; // make it a coroutine
}

docs.title: 2.3 The Overall Flow
docs.text:
What does the whole call flow look like? This section walks through the execution logic of the code above in detail. Before starting, let's modify the code and add some print statements:

#include <iostream>
#include <coroutine>
struct HelloTask {
    struct promise_type {
        HelloTask get_return_object() { std::cout << "get_return_object" << std::endl; return { }; }
        std::suspend_never initial_suspend() { std::cout << "initial_suspend" << std::endl; return {}; }
        std::suspend_never final_suspend() noexcept { std::cout << "final_suspend" << std::endl;return {}; }
        void return_void() { std::cout << "return_void" << std::endl; }
        void unhandled_exception() { std::cout << "unhandled_exception" << std::endl; }
    };
};
HelloTask myCoroutine() {
    std::cout << "create coroutine" << std::endl;
    co_return; // make it a coroutine
}
int main() {
    std::cout << "start main" << std::endl;
    HelloTask x = myCoroutine();
    std::cout << "end main" << std::endl;
}

The output is then:

start main
get_return_object
initial_suspend
create coroutine
return_void
final_suspend
end main

The flow is as follows:

  • start main
  • The coroutine object is allocated on the heap, the promise is constructed, and promise.get_return_object is called to return the current object (this is where get_return_object is printed); the point of doing this is to save the result in a local variable.
  • promise.initial_suspend, which prints initial_suspend; this triggers co_await, prints create coroutine, and after the coroutine body runs, co_return is called.
  • co_return calls promise.return_void, printing return_void.
  • Finally, promise.final_suspend prints final_suspend.
  • end main

There is a great deal more to coroutines; this section is the opening chapter, and more will keep coming~

docs.title: C++20 in Practice: channel
docs.text:
In the previous two live streams we covered the usage and underlying implementation of thread, jthread, stop_token, stop_source, stop_callback, cv, cv_any, and more. So how can we turn this knowledge into a small project?

Which brings us to this article: writing a channel.

docs.title: 1.1 Interface Design
docs.text:
At the interface level we expect the same as a general-purpose channel: creating a sending and a receiving channel in one shot.

For example:

auto [sender, receiver] = make_channel<int>();

The implementation can expose an outward-facing interface similar to make_unique; the return values are obtained via C++17 structured bindings, and at that point we have two channels.

The two most essential interfaces: send and receive.

  • Send
 sender.send(counter++);
  • Receive
auto value = receiver.recv();

Besides that, a shutdown interface can be provided at destruction time, so that blocked send/recv calls can be woken up and released.

For example:

bool shutdown() {
    if (!state_) {
        return false;
    }

    light_city_lock lk(state_->mutex);
    if (source_.stop_requested()) {
        return false;
    }
    source_.request_stop();
    state_->cv.notify_all();
    return true;
}

docs.title: 1.2 Internal Queue Design
docs.text:
For the internal queue, refer to the article published a few days ago on designing a thread-safe multi-producer multi-consumer queue: here we can maintain a state internally that carries a queue, a mutex, and a cv_any.

struct State {
    std::queue<T> queue;
    std::mutex mutex;
    // C++11 condition_variable_any
    std::condition_variable_any cv;
};

docs.title: 2. Usage
docs.text:
It is very easy to use: just make the two channels, then send and recv.

Here I used jthread + stop_token to do the work, for example:

std::jthread sender_thread(
    [](Channel<int> sender, std::stop_token token) {
      int counter = 0;
      while (!token.stop_requested()) {
        sender.send(counter++);
        std::this_thread::sleep_for(std::chrono::milliseconds(100));
      }
    },
    std::move(sender), token);

The receiving thread is similar. Once things have run about long enough, we can use

stop_source.request_stop();

At this point a channel has been simulated: the sending side sends data, and the receiving side just receives it.

Sample run:

➜  channel ./a.out                  
Received: 0
Received: 1
Received: 2
Received: 3
Received: 4
Received: 5
Received: 6
Received: 7
Received: 8
Received: 9
