docs.title: C++20 Concepts
docs.text:
C++20 introduced concepts: a set of constraints on template parameters (evaluated at compile time). You can use them with class templates and function templates to control function overloading and specialization. Some of the benefits include:

  • Enforcing type constraints on template parameters
  • Improving code readability (replacing long SFINAE code)
  • Providing friendlier error messages
  • Preventing unintended template instantiations by restricting which types can be used

Let's start with a fairly simple addition example.

#include <iostream>

struct Foo {};

template <typename T>
T Add(T a, T b) {
  return a + b;
}

int main() {
  std::cout << Add(1, 2) << std::endl;
  Foo f1, f2;
  std::cout << Add(f1, f2) << std::endl;
  return 0;
}

Foo does not support addition, and at the same time it cannot be used with std::cout << directly, so compilation spits out a pile of errors involving operator<< and operator+. But these are not the error messages we want; what we would like is the most direct message the compiler can give us, namely: can this struct be added or not?

add.cc: In function 'int main()':
add.cc:13:13: error: no match for 'operator<<' (operand types are 'std::ostream' {aka 'std::basic_ostream<char>'} and 'Foo')
   13 |   std::cout << Add(f1, f2) << std::endl;
      |   ~~~~~~~~~ ^~ ~~~~~~~~~~~
      |        |          |
      |        |          Foo
      |        std::ostream {aka std::basic_ostream<char>}
In file included from /usr/local/Cellar/gcc/13.2.0/include/c++/13/iostream:41,
                 from add.cc:1:
/usr/local/Cellar/gcc/13.2.0/include/c++/13/ostream:110:7: note: candidate: 'std::basic_ostream<_CharT, _Traits>::__ostream_type& std::basic_ostream<_CharT, _Traits>::operator<<(__ostream_type& (*)(__ostream_type&)) [with _CharT = char; _Traits = std::char_traits<char>; __ostream_type = std::basic_ostream<char>]'
  110 |       operator<<(__ostream_type& (*__pf)(__ostream_type&))

/usr/local/Cellar/gcc/13.2.0/include/c++/13/ostream:801:5: note:   template argument deduction/substitution failed:
/usr/local/Cellar/gcc/13.2.0/include/c++/13/ostream: In substitution of 'template<class _Ostream, class _Tp> _Ostream&& std::operator<<(_Ostream&&, const _Tp&) [with _Ostream = std::basic_ostream<char>&; _Tp = Foo]':
add.cc:13:26:   required from here
/usr/local/Cellar/gcc/13.2.0/include/c++/13/ostream:801:5: error: no type named 'type' in 'struct std::enable_if<false, void>'
add.cc: In instantiation of 'T Add(T, T) [with T = Foo]':
add.cc:13:19:   required from here
add.cc:7:12: error: no match for 'operator+' (operand types are 'Foo' and 'Foo')
    7 |   return a + b;
      |          ~~^~~

After implementing it with a concept:

template <typename T>
concept Addable = requires(T a, T b) { a + b; };

template <typename T>
  requires Addable<T>
T Add(T a, T b) {
  return a + b;
}

we get exactly the compile error we care about:

add_concept.cc: In function 'int main()':
add_concept.cc:17:19: error: no matching function for call to 'Add(Foo&, Foo&)'
   17 |   std::cout << Add(f1, f2) << std::endl;
      |                ~~~^~~~~~~~
add_concept.cc:10:3: note: candidate: 'template<class T>  requires  Addable<T> T Add(T, T)'
   10 | T Add(T a, T b) {
      |   ^~~
add_concept.cc:10:3: note:   template argument deduction/substitution failed:
add_concept.cc:10:3: note: constraints not satisfied
add_concept.cc: In substitution of 'template<class T>  requires  Addable<T> T Add(T, T) [with T = Foo]':
add_concept.cc:17:19:   required from here
add_concept.cc:6:9:   required for the satisfaction of 'Addable<T>' [with T = Foo]
add_concept.cc:6:19:   in requirements with 'T a', 'T b' [with T = Foo]
add_concept.cc:6:42: note: the required expression '(a + b)' is invalid
    6 | concept Addable = requires(T a, T b) { a + b; };
      |                                        ~~^~~

Now let's dive into concept syntax using the example above.

docs.title: 1. Concept Syntax
docs.text:
Syntax:

template <template-parameter-list>
concept concept-name = constraint-expression;

Mapping that onto the real example: Addable is the concept-name, and the constraint-expression is requires(T a, T b) { a + b; }.

template <typename T>
concept Addable = requires(T a, T b) { a + b; };

To use it:

#include <concepts>

The concept can be placed in several positions, as follows:

  • Where typename goes
  • After requires
  • In front of auto

docs.title: 1.1 Replacing typename
docs.text:
Constrain the template parameter by replacing typename.

// template <typename T>  typename->Addable
template <Addable T>
T Add(T a, T b) {
  return a + b;
}

docs.title: 1.2 The requires Keyword
docs.text:
We use the requires keyword in function templates. It can check whether our template T is addable; if the template can handle addition, it returns true.

requires can be placed with the template or after the function, but not after a class. Meanwhile, it comes in two forms:

  • requires with a condition

For example:

template <typename T>
  requires Addable<T>
T Add(T a, T b) { ... }
  • a requires expression

For example:

template <typename T>
concept Addable = requires(T a, T b) { a + b; };

docs.title: 1.2.1 Placed with the Template
docs.text:
Function:

template <typename T>
  requires Addable<T>
T Add(T a, T b) {
  return a + b;
}

Class:

template <typename T>
    requires Addable<T> 
class Bar {
 public:
  T Add(T a, T b) { return a + b; }
};

docs.title: 1.2.2 Trailing Requires Clause for Functions
docs.text:
Function:

template <typename T>
T Add(T a, T b)
  requires Addable<T>
{
  return a + b;
}

Classes do not support this form; it fails with: error: expected unqualified-id before 'requires' 28 | requires Addable 

template <typename T>
class Bar requires Addable<T> 
{
 public:
  T Add(T a, T b) { return a + b; }
};

docs.title: 1.2.3 Basic requires Examples
docs.text:
Take the types in a database as an example. A database has various types, which we can classify as null, binary, number, and so on. Suppose we want to perform a print operation on the type being passed in, which gives us the following example:

#include <concepts>

class NumberType {};
class BaseBinaryType {};
class NullType {};
class FloatingPointType : public NumberType {};
class IntegerType : public NumberType {};
class BinaryType: public BaseBinaryType {};

template <typename T>
  requires std::is_base_of_v<NumberType, T> || std::is_base_of_v<BaseBinaryType, T>
void PrintValue(T v) {}

int main() {
  PrintValue(FloatingPointType{});
  PrintValue(NullType{});
  return 0;
}

requires lets us use ||. NullType appears in the example above; it does not satisfy the requires clause, so compilation fails with:

concept_requires.cc:16:13: error: no matching function for call to 'PrintValue(NullType)'
   16 |   PrintValue(NullType{});
      |   ~~~~~~~~~~^~~~~~~~~~~~
concept_requires.cc:12:6: note: candidate: 'template<class T>  requires (is_base_of_v<NumberType, T>) || (is_base_of_v<BaseBinaryType, T>) void PrintValue(T)'
   12 | void PrintValue(T v) {}
      |      ^~~~~~~~~~
concept_requires.cc:12:6: note:   template argument deduction/substitution failed:
concept_requires.cc:12:6: note: constraints not satisfied
concept_requires.cc: In substitution of 'template<class T>  requires (is_base_of_v<NumberType, T>) || (is_base_of_v<BaseBinaryType, T>) void PrintValue(T) [with T = NullType]':
concept_requires.cc:16:13:   required from here
concept_requires.cc:12:6:   required by the constraints of 'template<class T>  requires (is_base_of_v<NumberType, T>) || (is_base_of_v<BaseBinaryType, T>) void PrintValue(T)'
concept_requires.cc:11:45: note: no operand of the disjunction is satisfied
   11 |   requires std::is_base_of_v<NumberType, T> || std::is_base_of_v<BaseBinaryType, T>
      |            ~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~^~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~

docs.title: 1.3 concept and auto
docs.text:
Wherever auto appears, we can use it together with a concept, for example:

auto add(auto x, auto y) {
  return x + y;
}

We can change it to:

template <typename T>
concept Addable = requires(T a, T b) { a + b; };

auto add2(Addable auto x, Addable auto y) {
  return x + y;
}

At compile time we get:

concept_auto.cc:17:20: error: no matching function for call to 'add2(Foo&, Foo&)'
   17 |   std::cout << add2(f1, f2) << std::endl;
      |                ~~~~^~~~~~~~
concept_auto.cc:10:6: note: candidate: 'template<class auto:18, class auto:19>  requires (Addable<auto:18>) && (Addable<auto:19>) auto add2(auto:18, auto:19)'
   10 | auto add2(Addable auto x, Addable auto y) {
      |      ^~~~
concept_auto.cc:10:6: note:   template argument deduction/substitution failed:
concept_auto.cc:10:6: note: constraints not satisfied
concept_auto.cc: In substitution of 'template<class auto:18, class auto:19>  requires (Addable<auto:18>) && (Addable<auto:19>) auto add2(auto:18, auto:19) [with auto:18 = Foo; auto:19 = Foo]':
concept_auto.cc:17:20:   required from here
concept_auto.cc:8:9:   required for the satisfaction of 'Addable<auto:18>' [with auto:18 = Foo]
concept_auto.cc:8:19:   in requirements with 'T a', 'T b' [with T = Foo]
concept_auto.cc:8:42: note: the required expression '(a + b)' is invalid
    8 | concept Addable = requires(T a, T b) { a + b; };

docs.title: 2. Compiler Support
docs.text:
Requires GCC (10.0+) or Clang (10.0+), with the compile options -std=c++20/-std=c++2a

https://en.cppreference.com/w/cpp/compiler_support

docs.title: 3. Summary
docs.text: With concepts provided as of C++20, we no longer need the enable_if/SFINAE machinery or function overloading to perform template constraint checks — concepts handle that for you. They offer a clearer and more powerful mechanism for constraining template parameters, making template code easier to write, understand, and maintain. By performing type checking at compile time, they help improve the robustness and readability of code.

docs.title: C++20 constexpr and the Comma Expression
C++​那些​事​: constexpr and comma expr
docs.text:
C++20 introduced a number of new features that further strengthen compile-time capabilities and code safety. This article takes a deep dive into two important changes: exception handling in constexpr functions and the deprecation of the comma operator in subscripts.

Note: for the lazy version, the code examples and related documentation for this section have been updated in the Knowledge Planet — join if you are interested.

docs.title: 1. The Change Supporting try-catch Exception Handling in constexpr Functions
docs.text:
Before C++20, try-catch blocks could not be used inside constexpr functions, a restriction that held back the compile-time capabilities of some standard library containers such as std::array. C++20 improved this by allowing try-catch blocks in constexpr functions and ignoring these exception-handling structures in constant-expression contexts. If an exception is thrown during constant-expression evaluation, the compiler reports an error.

The main purpose of this change is to let containers in the standard library support constexpr — std::array for example — while laying the groundwork for more compile-time exception handling in the future.

Example:

constexpr int SafeDivide(int a, int b) {
    if (b == 0) {
        throw std::runtime_error("Division by zero!");  // ​当​除数​为​0​时​抛出​异常​
    }
    return a / b;
}

constexpr int ComputeQuotient(int x) {
    try {
        return SafeDivide(100, x);  // ​尝试​除法​运算​
    } catch (const std::runtime_error&) {
        return -1;  // ​捕获​除​零​异常​并​返回​ -1
    }
}

The code above does not compile before C++20. So what does C++20 make of this behavior? Try to guess the outcomes of these two:

static_assert(ComputeQuotient(25) == 4); 
static_assert(ComputeQuotient(0) == -1);

docs.title: 2. Deprecation of the Comma Operator in Subscripts
docs.text:
Another change in C++20 is deprecating the use of the comma operator inside subscripts. In earlier C++ versions, in the expression array[x, y] the comma operator makes y the subscript passed to the array or container, while x is ignored. This usage, however, makes code hard to understand and gets in the way of future multidimensional arrays. Therefore, as of C++20, the comma operator in subscripts is deprecated, unless parentheses are used to spell out the precedence explicitly, as in array[(x, y)].

Sample code:

// arr[i, j] = 10;  // C++17 ​中​合法​，C++20 ​中弃​用​
arr[(i, j)] = 10;  // ​使用​括号​以​明确​逗号​的​优先级​

In this example, arr[(i, j)] uses parentheses to make the precedence of the comma operator explicit, ensuring j is the subscript passed to the array. In C++17, arr[i, j] was allowed, but in C++20 such usage triggers a deprecation warning. Doing it this way keeps the code's behavior consistent and in line with the new C++20 standard.

If you do use the comma operator, the compiler will warn:

common.cc:9:10: warning: top-level comma expression in array subscript is deprecated [-Wcomma-subscript]
    9 |     arr[i, j] = 10;  // C++17 ​中​合法​，C++20 ​中弃​用​
      |          ^

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: These changes in C++20 — the support for exception handling in constexpr functions and the deprecation of the comma operator in subscripts — are all about improving compile-time capabilities and code readability. If your code relies on these old behaviors, it is a good idea to adjust it in time to meet the new C++20 standard.

docs.title: C++20 Byte Order (endian)
docs.text:
In interviews, byte order is usually a very important topic. Interviewers will check:

  • The concepts of big-endian and little-endian
  • How to detect big-endian vs little-endian
  • Host byte order
  • Network byte order
  • And so on

There are actually many ways to detect it, for example:

  • C++20's endian
  • union
  • Address casting
  • htons

So this section covers the usage of and the fundamentals behind big-endian/little-endian in C++20.

Note: for the lazy version, the source code detecting endianness in 4 ways has been put in the Knowledge Planet — grab it there if you are interested.

docs.title: 1. Byte-Order Basics
docs.text:
A system's byte order refers to the order in which bytes are stored in memory or transmitted over a network. Big-endian systems store the most significant byte (MSB) at the lowest memory address. This is what various network protocols use to send data over the network, and it is also called network byte order. In little-endian systems, the least significant byte (LSB) is stored at the lowest memory address. For example, the hexadecimal number 0x12345678 is stored as follows:

  • Big-endian:
​地址​     | ​值​

n       | 0x12
n + 1   | 0x34
n + 2   | 0x56
n + 3   | 0x78
  • Little-endian
​地址​    | ​值​

n       | 0x78
n + 1   | 0x56
n + 2   | 0x34
n + 3   | 0x12

Depending on the architecture, different systems may have either big-endian or little-endian host byte order.

docs.title: 2. Why Byte Order Matters
docs.text: So why does this matter? If you need to send data over a network, you must make sure it is transmitted in network byte order. In most cases your host byte order will be little-endian, which means you need to reverse the order of the bytes before transmitting the data.

docs.title: 3. Checking Byte Order
docs.text:
C++20 introduced a simpler and more portable way to check the byte order: std::endian. You can use std::endian::native to check the system's host byte order. Here is a simple example:

void checkEndianness() {
  if constexpr (std::endian::native == std::endian::little) {
    std::cout << "​小端​" << std::endl;
  } else if constexpr (std::endian::native == std::endian::big) {
    std::cout << "​大​端​" << std::endl;
  } else {
    std::cout << "​未知​" << std::endl;
  }
}

docs.title: C++20: Lambda Templates
docs.text:
C++14 supports generic lambda expressions, which lets a lambda accept parameters of any type, for example:

auto func = [](auto a, auto b) {
    return a + b;
};

which gets expanded into:

struct Func {
    template <typename T1, typename T2>
    auto operator()(T1 a, T2 b) const {
        return a + b;
    }
};

But it cannot produce the following kinds of expansions:

First: the same type

template <class T>
auto operator()(T t1, T t2) const;

Second: only std::array

template <class T, std::size_t N>
auto operator()(std::array<T, N> const &) const;

Third: no deduction

template <class T>
auto operator()() const;

C++14 lambdas are nice, but C++20 lets us achieve these cases easily. C++20 allows lambda expressions to use template type parameters in their definition; here is the basic syntax:

[]<typename T>(){}

The following examples show its benefits.

docs.title: 1. Type Constraints
docs.text:
In an example like the one below, C++14 lets us write this code, but what gets passed in at the call site is not necessarily a vector, so the behavior deviates from what was intended and errors follow.

auto print = [](auto vec) {
  for (auto x : vec) {
    std::cout << x << std::endl;
  }
};

With C++20 and later, we can constrain the type:

auto print2 = []<typename T>(std::vector<T>& vec){
    //​使用​ std::vector<T> ​执行​操作​
};

So here comes an interview question: in C++14, how would you constrain this to a vector safely?

docs.title: 2. Perfect Forwarding
docs.text:
In C++20 you can use perfect forwarding very easily, for example:

auto lambdaFunc = []<typename T>(T&& number) {
  processFunction(std::forward<T>(number));
};

So, what is the advantage over C++14? Or put another way: what does it take to implement perfect forwarding in C++14?

That's all for this section.

docs.title: C++20 Modules
docs.text:
When we use headers we wrote ourselves or third-party libraries, we usually pull them in with the #include directive to import a library — a technique everyone uses all the time. In effect, this approach copies all the code of one source file (the header) into another file.

This approach, however, runs into the following problems:

  • A source file may be included multiple times in the same target, so we usually use #pragma once or #ifndef to keep a source file from being included multiple times in the same translation unit.
  • Copying code makes compile times longer: once a header is modified, every file that indirectly includes that header has to be recompiled.
  • #include ordering problems, which sometimes cause baffling compile errors.

C++20 introduced a new way to replace the #include directive, called modules.

Let's take a deep dive into modules.

docs.title: 1. Module Units
docs.text:
A C++ module consists of one or more translation units (tu) containing specific keywords for module declarations. Such translation units are called module units.

A translation unit that is not a module unit is considered part of the global module. The global module is anonymous, has no interface, and contains regular non-module code.

docs.title: 1.1 Global Module Fragment
docs.text:
A module unit may be prefixed with a global module fragment. When headers cannot be imported (particularly when headers use preprocessor macros as configuration), this global module fragment can keep using the original code directly.

For example: in the code below, the part between module; and export module Foo; is the global module fragment.

module;
#include <iostream>
#ifdef Say
void hello();
#endif
export module Foo;
// purivew
void world();

One thing you must note: if the module has a global module fragment, the first declaration must be module; — in other words, putting this declaration anywhere else is an error.

docs.title: 1.2 purview
docs.text:
The purview can be understood as the module's entire scope. It starts at the module declaration and extends to the end of the translation unit.

For example: hello is not in it, while world and GetData are both in the purview.

module;
void hello();
// <- ​这里​不​在​Foo​模块​的​purview​内​
export module Foo;
// <- ​在​Foo​模块​的​purview​内​
void world();
export void GetData();

docs.title: 1.3 Private module fragment
docs.text:
The primary module interface unit may be suffixed with a private module fragment. This part may appear only in the primary module interface unit, and if it exists, the module unit it appears in must be the module's only unit. Its purpose is to wrap the module's interface and implementation in a single translation unit without exposing implementation details.

For example: I want to create a Shape and compute its area.

Only an interface for creating a concrete Shape needs to be exposed externally, calling a shared area-computing interface, so we can write the following module.

export module Shape;

export class Shape {
  public:
   virtual double CalculateArea() = 0;
};

export { std::shared_ptr<Shape> CreateRectangle(double length, double width); }


module :private; // here

class Rectangle : public Shape {
 private:
  double length;
  double width;

 public:
  Rectangle(double l, double w) : length(l), width(w) {}

  double CalculateArea() override { return length * width; }
};

std::shared_ptr<Shape> CreateRectangle(double length, double width) {
  return std::make_shared<Rectangle>(length, width);
}

Can we put all the internal details inside the private fragment? My own g++ version is 13; it does not support this yet and reports the following error:

For gcc's current support status, see here

https://gcc.gnu.org/projects/cxx-status.html

shape.cppm:14:1: sorry, unimplemented: private module fragment
   14 | module :private;

My local clang is version 16; I tested it and it runs fine!

➜  clang++ -std=c++20 shape.cppm --precompile -o shape.pcm  
➜  clang++ -std=c++20 shape.cc -fprebuilt-module-path=. shape.pcm -o shape
➜  ./shape 
area is 2

Of the three parts above, the global and private module fragments are not required for a module to exist; the purview is the part a module cannot do without.

docs.title: 2.1 Creating a Module
docs.text:
Creating a module is similar to defining a header file: it is also a file, usually with the .cppm suffix. We just use the export and module keywords in this file, followed by the module name, and we have created an exportable module. For example:

// foo.cppm
export module foo;

// main.cc
import foo;

The export keyword can be used on classes, variables, and so on. There are usually two ways to write it:

export void func();

export {
  void func();
  constexpr double PI{3.14};
};

In one form, the export keyword goes in front of an ordinary declaration; the other is the export block, similar to the namespace syntax, which can export multiple things.

docs.title: 2.2 Exporting
docs.text:
This raises an important question: what can be exported?

  • variables, classes, structs, functions, namespaces, template functions/classes, concepts can be exported
  • Entities with internal linkage cannot be exported, such as static variables and functions, and anonymous namespaces.
export static constexpr double PI = 3.14; // ​不可​导出​
  • Export declarations must appear at namespace level
namespace {
  export void print_no_export() { // ​匿名​命名​空间​，​不可​导出​
    std::cout << "print no export" << std::endl;
  }
};
namespace light {
  export void print_export() { // ok
    std::cout << "print export" << std::endl;
  }
};

struct Foo {
  export int a; // ​不能​导出​成员​变量​
};
  • Exporting a namespace implicitly exports everything inside it
export class Rectangle {
 private:
  double length;
  double width;
 public:
  Rectangle(double l, double w) : length(l), width(w) {} 

  double CalculateArea() { return length * width; } // ​隐式​导出​
};

export namespace {
  void print_export() { // ​隐式​导出​
    std::cout << "print export" << std::endl;
  }
};

export {
  void func();  // ​隐式​导出​
  constexpr double PI{3.14}; // ​隐式​导出​
};
  • The first declaration of an exported entity must be an export declaration. Subsequent declarations and definitions do not need the export keyword.
export class Foo; // ok
export class Foo; // ok，​只是​会​冗余​

class Foo { // ok，​隐式​export
 public:
  void print() { std::cout << "this is foo" << std::endl; }
};

class Bar;  // not export
export class Bar; // ​无效​，​第一个​声明​已经​是​不可​导出​，​后续​的​不可​导出​


Foo f; // ok
f.print(); // ok
Bar b; // not ok
  • A non-interface module unit cannot export
module foo;

export void print { }  // error: 'export' may only occur after a module interface declaration

docs.title: 2.3 Importing
docs.text:
The counterpart is importing, which also has its rules, for example:

  • A module cannot import itself

  • In a module unit, all imports must appear before any other declaration in that module unit. You cannot import at an arbitrary point inside a module unit.

void func() {}
import shape; // error: post-module-declaration imports must be contiguous

---------------
import shape; // ok
void func() {}
  • Only global-scope imports are allowed
namespace light {
  import shape; // not ok
};
  • Circular imports are not allowed
// shape.cppm
export module shape;
import circle; // ​循环​导入​

// circle.cppm
import shape;

docs.title: 2.4 include in Modules
docs.text: How do you use #include <iostream> inside a module?

docs.title: 2.4.1 #include in the purview region
docs.text:
Replace #include with import

export module foo;
import <iostream>;

For example:

Compiling with g++-13 as follows; you can pass iostream after c++-system-header to build the gcm.

g++-13 -std=c++20 -fmodules-ts -x c++-system-header iostream 
g++-13 -fmodules-ts -std=c++20 -x c++ shape.cppm circle.cppm shape.cc

For your own headers, such as consts.h, it turns out you can simply #include them inside the module, for example:

export module foo;
#include "consts.h"

docs.title: 2.4.2 #include in the Global Module Fragment region
docs.text:
Both #include and macros can be placed directly in this region, for example:

module;
#ifdef
#include <iostream>
#endif
export module foo;

docs.title: 3. Decomposing Modules
docs.text:
When we want to break a large module into smaller modules, we can use the following two approaches:

  • Module partitions.
  • These allow us to split a module into multiple files. This is effectively invisible to users, who simply import the module as usual.
  • Submodules.
  • These allow us to break a larger module into a hierarchy of any number of submodules. Users can choose to import the whole module, or only specific submodules.

docs.title: 3.1 Module Partitions
docs.text:
Syntax:

export module <module-name>:<part-name>;
import :<part-name>; // ​可以​在​import​前面​添加​export​导出​该​分区​接口​

For example: I have a shape; when consuming it, all you need is import shape and then calling the corresponding interfaces — here the interfaces of the circle partition and the rectangle partition are used respectively.

import shape;

int main() {
    DrawCircle();
    DrawRectangle();
    return 0;
}

shape has two partitions, one is circle and the other is rectangle, so the module shape.cppm contains:

export module shape;

export import :circle;
export import :rectangle;

The two partitions contain:

// circle.cppm
module;
#include <iostream>
export module shape:circle;
export void DrawCircle() { std::cout << "draw circle" << std::endl; }

--------------
// rectangle.cppm

module;
#include <iostream>
export module shape:rectangle;
export void DrawRectangle() { std::cout << "draw rectangle" << std::endl; }

After compiling with both clang and g++, clang-16 reports an error — not supported.

 error: sorry, module partitions are not yet supported

g++-13 supports it; note that when compiling you must go in the order partition -> main partition, otherwise it fails.

➜ g++-13 -fmodules-ts -std=c++20 -x c++ shape.cppm circle.cppm rectangle.cppm shape.cc
shape:circle: error: failed to read compiled module: No such file or directory
shape:circle: note: compiled module file is 'gcm.cache/shape-circle.gcm'
shape:circle: note: imports must be built before being imported
shape:circle: fatal error: returning to the gate for a mechanical issue

It should be changed to:

g++ -fmodules-ts -std=c++20 -x c++ circle.cppm rectangle.cppm shape.cppm shape.cc

docs.title: 3.2 Submodules
docs.text:
Syntax:

export module <module-name>.<sub_module-name>;
import <module-name>.<sub_module-name>; // ​可以​在​import​前面​添加​export​导出​该​分区​接口​

The example above can also be implemented with submodules: shape stays the main module, with circle and rectangle as the two submodules.

// shape.cppm
export module shape;

export import shape.circle;
export import shape.rectangle;

---------------------
// rectangle.cppm
module;
#include <iostream>
export module shape.rectangle;
export void DrawRectangle() { std::cout << "draw rectangle" << std::endl; }

---------------------

// circle.cppm
module;
#include <iostream>
export module shape.circle;
export void DrawCircle() { std::cout << "draw circle" << std::endl; }

Note that in usage the module partition form uses :, while the submodule form uses ..

The caller-side code is the same as for module partitions.

There are some usage differences, though: for example, when a partition is imported directly, using its interface triggers internal compiler error: Segmentation fault: 11, whereas a submodule can be imported and used normally.

// ​引入​子​分区​
import shape:circle;

int main() {
    DrawCircle(); // error
    return 0;
}


// ​引入​子​模块​
import shape.circle;

int main() {
    DrawCircle(); // ok
    return 0;
}

For submodules, the main module name cannot be omitted in the import. Above, when importing a partition module from within the main partition, we could use :circle; here .circle cannot be used. The error is as follows:

shape.cppm:3:8: error: 'import' does not name a type
    3 | export import .circle;

docs.title: 4. Interface and Implementation
docs.text:
When writing code, we usually split it into a "header file" and an "implementation file". With modules, this step is no longer needed. You can still follow the old writing style, though.

For example: drawing a shape.

  • Define the module shape.cppm
export module shape;

export class Shape {
 public:
  Shape();
  void Draw();
};
  • Implement the module shape.cc
import shape;
import <iostream>;

Shape::Shape() {}
void Shape::Draw() { std::cout << "draw a shape" << std::endl; }

This is basically the same as the usual .h and .cpp separation.

https://clang.llvm.org/docs/StandardCPlusPlusModules.html

https://timsong-cpp.github.io/cppwp/n4861/module.import#7.sentence-2

https://gcc.gnu.org/projects/cxx-status.html

docs.title: C++20 Ranges Library
docs.text:
ranges is one of the major features of C++20, and "views" are an important part of it. Before C++20, the standard library's algorithms were implemented in terms of iterators, for example: std::sort.

std::sort(v.begin() + 2, v.end())

Iterators + algorithms can pull off some complex operations — for example, sorting in reverse:

std::sort(v.rbegin(), v.rend())

But this comes with some problems:

  • It is easy to mix two incompatible iterators.
  • Algorithms compose too weakly, and intermediate variables have to be stored

For example: say we have a student information system and we want to compute the total GPA of students aged 21 to 25 with GPA >= 3.5, i.e. the sum over the students satisfying the preceding conditions. Before C++17, we could write pseudo-code like this:

std::vector<Student> students
std::vector<Student> selected;
std::copy_if(students.begin(), students.end(), std::back_inserter(selected),
             [](const Student& student) {
               return student.age >= 21 && student.age <= 25 && student.gpa >= 3.5;
             });

double s = std::accumulate(
    selected.begin(), selected.end(), 0.0,
    [](double sum, const Student& student) { return sum + student.gpa; });

Notice that filtering the students who satisfy the conditions requires copying them into selected, and only then summing over it.

C++20 introduced a more concise and efficient style: by using ranges and the pipe operator | to chain multiple operations, the sum can be computed directly without intermediate variables, for example:

double s = 0.0;
for (const auto& student :
     students | std::views::filter([](const auto& s) {
       return s.age >= 21 && s.age <= 25 && s.gpa >= 3.5;
     }) | std::views::transform([](const auto& s) { return s.gpa; })) {
  s += student;
}

You can see that multiple algorithms now connect seamlessly, cutting the memory allocations for intermediate temporaries, and readability improves greatly, with the pipe | chaining the different operations together.

Now let's explore C++20 ranges together.

docs.title: 1. Basic Concepts
docs.text:
1. range

A range is an abstraction representing a sequence. It can be any container that has iterators, or any object that defines begin() and end() functions. std::vector, std::list, and so on are all examples of ranges. Arrays can also be treated as ranges.

2. view

A view is read-only access to a range. It is a form of lazy evaluation — computation happens only when needed, which means it does not actually store data. For example, std::views::filter and std::views::transform are typical examples of views. They let us filter and transform a range without actually creating a new container.

3. algorithm

Algorithms are functions that operate on ranges or views; for example, std::sort and std::find are both algorithms.

4. |

The pipe operator | can chain views and algorithms together, feeding the result on the left as the input on the right. It makes the code clearer and more concise. For example, students | std::views::filter(...) passes the students range to std::views::filter for filtering, and then passes the result on to subsequent operations.

Taking the student computation above as an example: in this example we feed the students range through | as the input of the filter view, then feed that result as the input of the transform view, and finally get back a range; we loop over that range and sum it up with an accumulation to get the result.

double s = 0.0;
for (const auto& student :
     students | std::views::filter([](const auto& s) {
       return s.age >= 21 && s.age <= 25 && s.gpa >= 3.5;
     }) | std::views::transform([](const auto& s) { return s.gpa; })) {
  s += student;
}

As you can see, using ranges has the following benefits:

  • Better code readability
  • Lazy evaluation: Ranges introduce the concept of views, allowing lazy evaluation — results are computed only when needed.

For example, computation happens only at *v.begin().

auto v = std::views::reverse(vec);
std::cout << *v.begin() << std::endl;
  • Fewer errors: The design of Ranges helps reduce errors that are easy to make with traditional iterator operations, such as using incompatible iterators.
  • And so on.

The ranges library introduces different concepts to describe different kinds of ranges. These concepts help you better understand and constrain the properties of ranges in generic programming. Here are some commonly used range concepts:

https://en.cppreference.com/w/cpp/ranges

Concept Description Container examples std::ranges::input_range Can be iterated at least once from begin to end std::forward_list, std::list, std::deque, std::array, std::vector std::ranges::forward_range Can be iterated multiple times from begin to end std::forward_list, std::list, std::deque, std::array, std::vector std::ranges::bidirectional_range Iterators can also move backwards with -- std::list, std::deque, std::array, std::vector std::ranges::random_access_range You can jump to an element in constant time [] std::deque, std::array, std::vector std::ranges::contiguous_range Elements are always stored contiguously in memory std::array, std::vector

docs.title: 2. Usage
docs.text:
Using this feature is fairly simple: include the header and use the interfaces.

For example: filtering the even numbers out of a bunch of numbers.

#include <ranges>
auto evenNumbers = numbers | std::views::filter([](int x) { return x % 2 == 0; });

Compiling: just specify -std.

g++ -std=c++20 main.cc -o main

For compiler support, see the list below:

https://en.cppreference.com/w/cpp/compiler_support/20

gcc >= 10, clang >= 13 (partial), >= 15 fully supported.

docs.title: C++20 std::span Design and Pitfalls | C++​那些​事
docs.text: Last updated：2026-10-13

docs.title: 0. Motivation
docs.text:
In traditional C/C++ code, we usually access an array with a pointer plus a size, for example:

void print(int* arr, int sz) {
    for (int i = 0; i < sz; i++) {
        // todo
    }
}

span simplifies this operation, turning it into:

void print(std::span<int> arr) {
    for (auto x : arr) {
        // todo
    }
}

So what exactly is a span, what are its use cases, and what pitfalls does it have? This section explores these questions in detail.

docs.title: 1. What Is a span?
docs.text:
In C++20, a span is a lightweight, range-like container that provides access to a stretch of contiguous memory. As a view, a span does not own its data; it is simply a reference to the data, and it is commonly used to replace traditional C-style arrays or pointers. It can wrap arrays of any type as well as standard containers such as std::vector, providing a safer, more modern way to handle such data.

Several key points:

  • Contiguous memory
  • Does not own the data
  • A reference

The source code of span in gcc lives at libstdc++-v3/include/std/span.

template <typename _Type, size_t _Extent = dynamic_extent>
class span {};

The span type takes two important parameters:

  • _Type: the element type.
  • Extent: the array size. If it is dynamic_extent (the default), the size of the view can change dynamically.

docs.title: 2. Dynamic and Static span
docs.text: span has two modes: static and dynamic.

docs.title: 2.1 Static span
docs.text:
A static span determines its size at compile time; its Extent is a constant value. When using a static span, we need to know the size of the data at compile time.

For example:

int arr[5] = {1, 2, 3, 4, 5};
std::span<int, 5> s(arr);  // ​静态​ span，​大小​为​ 5

The size of a static span is fixed at compile time, so the compiler can apply certain optimizations, such as omitting bounds checks. But because Extent is a constant, a static span cannot have its size changed at runtime.

docs.title: 2.2 Dynamic span
docs.text:
The size of a dynamic span is determined at runtime; Extent defaults to dynamic_extent. This kind of span does not require the size to be known at compile time and can adapt to arrays or containers of any size.

For example:

int arr[5] = {1, 2, 3, 4, 5};
std::span<int> s(arr);  // ​动态​ span，​大小​在​运行​时​确定​

A dynamic span suits the cases where the size cannot be determined at compile time; it offers greater flexibility.

The implementation in the gcc source is fairly simple: it defaults to a very large integer (the unsigned value of -1), and the real value is computed at construction time.

inline constexpr size_t dynamic_extent = static_cast<size_t>(-1);

For example, ranges::size is used here to set the internal size; see the code below.

std::vector<int> data{1, 2, 3};
std::span<int> s(data);

Setting the dynamic size.

span(ranges::data(__range), ranges::size(__range))

docs.title: 3. subspan
docs.text:
span provides a very useful member function, subspan, which lets us extract a sub-view from an existing span without copying data. This is very handy when processing large data sets and avoiding unnecessary memory overhead.

The subspan() method has two overloads:

  1. One takes __offset and __count as parameters, where __offset is the starting position and __count is the size of the sub-range (defaulting to dynamic_extent, i.e. up to the end of the original span).
  2. The other takes no parameters and is implemented on top of templates.
constexpr auto
subspan() const noexcept
-> span<element_type, _S_subspan_extent<_Offset, _Count>()> {}

template<size_t _Offset, size_t _Count = dynamic_extent>
[[nodiscard]]
constexpr auto
subspan() const noexcept
-> span<element_type, _S_subspan_extent<_Offset, _Count>()> {}

Example 1:

std::span<int> s(arr);  
std::span<int> sub = s.subspan(1, 3);

Example 2:

std::span<int> s(arr);  
auto sub = s.subspan<2, 2>();

docs.title: 4. Usage Pitfalls
docs.text: Although span is a very useful tool, there are some common pitfalls to keep in mind when using it:

docs.title: 4.1 Do Not Let a span Refer to Memory That Has Been Freed
docs.text:
A span does not own the data; it is only a reference to it. So if the memory a span refers to is released (for example, the original array is destroyed or goes out of scope), accessing that span leads to undefined behavior.

For example:

std::span<int> create_span() {
    int arr[5] = {1, 2, 3, 4, 5};
    return std::span<int>(arr, 5);
}

// ​错误​：​返回​的​ span ​引用​了​栈​上​临时​变量​，​函数​返回​后​ arr ​被​销毁​
auto s = create_span();

To avoid this problem, make sure the data a span refers to stays valid for its lifetime. Consider holding the data in dynamically allocated memory, or making sure the data's lifetime matches the span's.

docs.title: 4.2 Problems When the Underlying Array Changes Size
docs.text:
A span's reference to the underlying data is direct, not a copy. When the underlying data changes, the span itself does not notice these changes. Therefore, when the size of the underlying array or container changes (for example, through memory reallocation), the original span may become invalid.

std::vector<int> vec = {1, 2, 3, 4, 5};
std::span<int> s(vec);  // s ​引用​ vec ​的​数据​
// ​改变​底层​容器​的​大小​
vec.push_back(6);  // vec ​大小​变为​ 6

// ​这里​ s ​仍然​引用​ vec ​的​数据​，​但​ vec ​可能​已经​重新分配​了​内存​
// ​这​可能​导致​ s ​引用​失效​或​未定义​行为​

docs.title: A Guide to C++20 New Features
docs.text:
In previous articles I covered a few important C++20 features here and there, for example:

This post will briefly list some of the more important features for reference, and explain why you should learn C++20 and what benefits it can bring to your code.

C++20 is the name of the ISO/IEC standard revision of the C++ programming language that follows C++17. C++ is a general-purpose, high-performance programming language widely used across application domains, including operating systems, browsers, and many other kinds of software.

C++20 introduces many new features and improvements designed to make C++ more expressive, more efficient, and easier to use. Some of the most important C++20 features include:

  • Concepts: make template programming more intuitive, reliable, and easier to use. With concepts, we can write more expressive and readable code while getting better compile-time error checking and more precise automatic deduction.
  • Coroutines: a way to write asynchronous code in a synchronous style, making it easier to write code that can be suspended and resumed without blocking the entire program.
  • Modules: a new way to organize and reuse code that simplifies building and distributing large software projects.
  • Ranges: introduces the ranges library (an extension and generalization of the algorithms and iterator libraries), providing a more intuitive, concise, and feature-rich way to process and manipulate collection data.
  • Spaceship operator: a new operator for three-way ordering comparison of objects, making it easier to write code that compares and sorts complex data structures.
  • constexpr lambdas: the ability to use lambdas as constexpr functions, allowing lambda expressions in more contexts, including constant expressions and template arguments.
  • Designated initializers: a more expressive syntax for initializing structs and arrays, making it easier to specify the values of individual members of a struct or array.

C++20 also includes many other improvements and changes, such as additional library facilities, performance improvements, and better support for modern hardware and platforms. All in all, C++20 represents a major step forward for the C++ language and is expected to have a significant impact on how C++ is used and developed in the future.

docs.title: The Benefits of C++20
docs.text:
C++20 introduces many new features and improvements aimed at the productivity and expressiveness of C++ code. Some benefits of C++20 include:

  • Performance improvements: C++20 includes many changes and improvements aimed at the performance of C++ code. For example, C++20 introduced the std::format library, a high-performance alternative to printf and sprintf for string formatting. C++20 also includes improvements to std::variant and std::optional that can help reduce the overhead of using these types in some situations. In addition, C++20 introduced the std::bit_cast function, providing a safe and effective way to perform type conversions.
  • Better support for modern hardware and platforms: C++20 includes many changes and improvements that make it easier to write code optimized for modern hardware and platforms. For example, C++20 introduced the std::atomic_ref type, which provides a way to perform atomic operations on non-atomic objects. C++20 also includes support for the std::endian type, allowing you to write portable code across architectures with different byte orders. In addition, C++20 introduced the std::span type, a way to represent a contiguous sequence of objects in memory that can be used to write code optimized for cache-friendly access patterns.
  • Modular programming: C++20 introduces support for modular programming, a new way of organizing code that lets developers split code into logically independent modules..
  • And so on

docs.title: Wrap-up
docs.text:
In short, C++20 is a major new version of the C++ programming language, introducing many new features and improvements aimed at the productivity and expressiveness of C++ code. Some of the key C++20 features include concepts, coroutines, modules, ranges, the spaceship operator, constexpr lambdas, designated initializers, and default member initializers for classes. These features can help improve the performance, flexibility, and modularity of C++ code, and make it easier to write code optimized for modern hardware and platforms.

If you are a C++ programmer, we encourage you to learn more about C++20 and start using its new features in your own code. C++20 is a powerful and versatile language that can help you write efficient, expressive, and maintainable code. By taking advantage of the new features and improvements C++20 introduces, you can boost your productivity and write code that better fits your project's needs.

docs.text: Last updated：2026-10-13

docs.title: C++20 [[likely]] and [[unlikely]]
docs.text:
C++20 introduced the two likelihood attributes [[likely]] and [[unlikely]], which give the compiler optimization hints that the corresponding code path is likely/unlikely to be executed.

At first glance, these seem like a rather nice pair of attributes: let the compiler optimize and thereby gain performance. But that is not actually the case.

The C++ standard draft explicitly states: Excessive usage of either of these attributes is liable to result in performance degradation.

That is: overusing either attribute may well degrade performance.

https://eel.is/c++draft/dcl.attr.likelihood#note-2

So in which situations are they useful, and in which are they unnecessary?

This article offers my own take.

docs.title: 1. Principles
docs.text:
Follow these principles when using them:

  1. Use them with care: only apply these attributes when you are certain that a branch or path is extremely likely — or extremely unlikely — to be taken at runtime.

For example, the code below checks whether a value is greater than 0. If the input data cannot guarantee that value is very probably (or certainly) greater than 0, then the optimization below is meaningless.

if (value > 0) [[likely]] {
    std::cout << "Value is positive: " << value << std::endl;
} else [[unlikely]] {
    std::cout << "Value is non-positive: " << value << std::endl;
}

For example, here is unlikely as used in the standard library. A member function of the _Variant_storage struct uses this attribute: the probability of being invalid is extremely low, so it can be marked with unlikely.

constexpr void
_M_reset()
{
  if (!_M_valid()) [[unlikely]]
    return;

  // do something
}
  1. Mark the dominant path: apply the attribute only on the dominant execution path, not on every possible path.

For example, in the if statement below two equivalent branches are marked likely, which does not mean much.

if (value > 10) [[likely]] {
    // ​主导​路径​：​值​大于​ 10
    std::cout << "Value is greater than 10: " << value << std::endl;
} else if (value > 5) [[likely]] {
    // ​次​主导​路径​：​值​大于​ 5 ​且​小于​等于​ 10
    std::cout << "Value is greater than 5 but less than or equal to 10: " << value << std::endl;
} else [[unlikely]] {
    // ​较​少​出现​的​路径​：​值​小于​等于​ 5
    std::cout << "Value is 5 or less: " << value << std::endl;
}

docs.title: 2. Example
docs.text:
Finally, a very common example: vector's at. We know it checks whether the index exceeds the vector's size, and that probability is fairly low, so we can use unlikely, for example:

int& at(std::vector<int>& vec, std::size_t i) {
  if (i >= vec.size()) [[unlikely]] {
      throw std::out_of_range("Out of bounds access");
  }
  return vec[i];
}

docs.title: C++20 [[no_unique_address]] | C++​那些​事
docs.text: Last updated：2026-10-13

docs.title: C++​那些​事​: Memory Optimization
docs.text: Memory is often a major concern when a program runs, and reducing memory usage while improving access speed is critical. To address these problems, C++20 introduced the no_unique_address feature, combined with the Empty Base Optimization (EBO), giving developers an effective way to optimize memory layout.

docs.title: 1. Empty Base Optimization (EBO)
docs.text:
EBO means that an empty base class (a class with no data members) takes up no extra memory in a derived class. The C++ compiler merges the instances of these empty base classes, avoiding unnecessary memory overhead. This is especially useful when designing complex class hierarchies, as it can effectively reduce object sizes.

#include <iostream>
class Empty {};

class Derived : public Empty {
  int value;

 public:
  Derived(int v) : value(v) {}
};

class Test {
  int value;

 public:
  Test(int v) : value(v) {}
  Empty e;
};

int main() {
  std::cout << sizeof(Derived) << std::endl;
  std::cout << sizeof(Test) << std::endl;
  return 0;
}

In the code above, the Derived class occupies only the size of an int in memory, not the size of int plus Empty. This is because the compiler takes advantage of EBO.

So what do you guess the output above is?

docs.title: 2. The no_unique_address Feature
docs.text:
C++20 introduced the no_unique_address feature, which lets us explicitly mark certain class members so that they occupy no extra space in memory. It is especially well suited to <0-byte objects>, for example:

In a unique_ptr where the Deleter is an empty struct/class, the resulting sizeof is 16; with C++20 it can take up no bytes, and the whole sizeof becomes 8.

template<class T, class Deleter>
class unique_ptr {
    T* pointer = nullptr;
    [[no_unique_address]] Deleter deleter;

   public:
    // ​其他​成员​函数​...
};

That's all for this section.

docs.title: C++20 Three-Way Comparison Operator <=> | C++​那些​事
docs.text: Last updated：2026-10-13

docs.title: Three Orderings
docs.text:
The three-way comparison operator <=>, also known as the spaceship operator, has three possible ordering return values. Let's dig into it from the gcc source code's point of view.

Note: for the lazy version, the examples for this section have been updated in the Knowledge Planet.

Usage: <=>

#include <compare>
#include <iostream>

int main() {
   auto c1 = 1.1 <=> 2.2;
   auto c2 = -1 <=> 1;
   std::cout << typeid(c1).name() << std::endl;
   std::cout << typeid(c2).name() << std::endl;
}

Output:

St16partial_ordering
St15strong_ordering
  1. 1.1 <=> 2.2: this compares two floating-point numbers. For floating-point numbers, the standard library returns std::partial_ordering, because the existence of NaN values means the comparison between them is not a strict total order. std::partial_ordering allows the result to be <, >, ==, or unordered.

We can use the static variables in the gcc code to see whether a partial_ordering is less, greater, equivalent, or unordered:

static const partial_ordering less;
static const partial_ordering equivalent;
static const partial_ordering greater;
static const partial_ordering unordered;

If we force a conversion, we get an error:

comp.cc:6:36: error: conversion from 'std::partial_ordering' to non-scalar type 'std::strong_ordering' requested
    6 |   std::strong_ordering c1 = 1.1 <=> 2.2;

2. `-1 <=> 1`: this compares two integers. For integers, the standard library returns `std::strong_ordering`, because integer comparison is a strict total order with no indeterminate cases. `std::strong_ordering` only ever returns `<`, `>`, or `==`.

Likewise, the following 4 static members can be used.

static const strong_ordering less;
static const strong_ordering equal;
static const strong_ordering equivalent;
static const strong_ordering greater;

Therefore, the type of c1 is std::partial_ordering while the type of c2 is std::strong_ordering, which also explains why the printed types differ.

Besides partial_ordering and strong_ordering, <=> can also return weak_ordering, whose static members are:

static const weak_ordering less;
static const weak_ordering equivalent;
static const weak_ordering greater;

docs.title: equal vs equivalent
docs.text:
In the three orderings above, you can see that "equal" shows up in two forms: equal and equivalent. What is the difference between the two?

Going straight to cppreference: there is no difference between them. However, std::strong_ordering is the only category that defines equality; all the other categories define only equivalence. This matches the static members above — strong_ordering has two, while the others only have equivalent.

If a comparison induces a strong ordering between the items being compared, equivalence and equality are the same. The reason there are two words for it is that this is not the case for the other kinds of ordering. Weak and partial have no equality at all; they only provide equivalence.

Equivalence means two objects can compare equal. Equality means something stronger: if they compare equal, one can be substituted for the other in any const usage — as long as a == b is true, the property f(a) == f(b) holds, where f denotes a function that reads only comparison-relevant state accessible through the argument's public const members. If a type's comparison permits equality (which is what strong ordering requires), it also permits equivalence. So for strong-ordering comparisons, the two are the same.

https://en.cppreference.com/w/cpp/utility/compare/strong_ordering

docs.title: Why Use the Three-Way Comparison Operator?
docs.text:
The three-way comparison operator (<=>) lets you determine the ordering relationship between two values in a single operation, whereas the traditional comparison operators need multiple comparisons.

Limitations of the traditional comparison operators:

  • If a == b is false, you cannot tell whether a < b or a > b.
  • If a != b is true, you cannot tell whether a < b or a > b.
  • If a < b is false, you cannot tell whether a == b or a > b.
  • If a > b is false, you cannot tell whether a == b or a < b.
  • If a <= b is true, you cannot tell whether a == b or a < b.
  • If a >= b is true, you cannot tell whether a == b or a > b.

These limitations show that the traditional comparison operators cannot determine the complete relationship between two values in one go; multiple comparisons are needed to obtain the full result.

That's all for this section.

docs.title: 0.Introduction
docs.text:
The source code analysis is based on gcc4.9.1.

C++ tr1, fully named Technical Report 1, is the first extension to the C++ standard library. The C++ standard c++0x would include it, along with some extensions to the language itself. tr1 includes the long-awaited smart pointers, regular expressions, and other content supporting generic programming. During the draft stage, the namespace for the newly added classes and templates was std::tr1.

docs.title: 1.std::tr1::array
docs.text:
Usage: 

#include <tr1/array>
std::tr1::array<int ,10> a;

The array in tr1 is fairly simple: it mimics the language's built-in arrays and makes them support iterator operations, so that like other containers it can be used with algorithms. In tr1, array has no constructor or destructor. The iterator is simply a pointer defined using the passed-in type.

Let's take a quick look at the source code of this static array:

template<typename _Tp, std::size_t _Nm>
struct array
{
    typedef _Tp                           value_type;
    typedef value_type&                           reference;
    typedef const value_type&                     const_reference;
    typedef value_type*                       iterator;
    typedef const value_type*                 const_iterator;
    typedef std::size_t                           size_type;
    typedef std::ptrdiff_t                         difference_type;
    typedef std::reverse_iterator<iterator>       reverse_iterator;
    typedef std::reverse_iterator<const_iterator>   const_reverse_iterator;
}
It uses reverse_iterator as the iterator for the rbegin and rend operations. It looks like there is one iterator above, but there are actually two; there is also another iterator, which simply uses a pointer defined via the passed-in type as the iterator.

You can think of it as the counterpart of the forward and reverse iterators in vector.

It is worth noting that tr1::array supports passing an array size of 0, for example:

std::tr1::array<int,0> a;
For this kind of writing, it maps to the following: 
// Support for zero-sized arrays mandatory.
value_type _M_instance[_Nm ? _Nm : 1];
Based on the passed-in size: if it is not 0, it is the passed-in size; otherwise it is 1.

docs.title: 2.std::array
docs.text:
Usage 

std::array<int ,10> a;

The array in std contains

Comparing the arrays of tr1 and std

template<typename _Tp, std::size_t _Nm>
struct array
{
    typedef _Tp                           value_type;
    typedef value_type*               pointer;
    typedef const value_type*                       const_pointer;
    typedef value_type&                           reference;
    typedef const value_type&                     const_reference;
    typedef value_type*                       iterator;
    typedef const value_type*                 const_iterator;
    typedef std::size_t                           size_type;
    typedef std::ptrdiff_t                            difference_type;
    typedef std::reverse_iterator<iterator>       reverse_iterator;
    typedef std::reverse_iterator<const_iterator>   const_reverse_iterator;

    // Support for zero-sized arrays mandatory.
    typedef _GLIBCXX_STD_C::__array_traits<_Tp, _Nm> _AT_Type;    // # define _GLIBCXX_STD_C std
    typename _AT_Type::_Type                         _M_elems;
}

We find two notable places inside array: 

// Support for zero-sized arrays mandatory.
typedef _GLIBCXX_STD_C::__array_traits<_Tp, _Nm> _AT_Type;    // # define _GLIBCXX_STD_C std
typename _AT_Type::_Type                         _M_elems;

Searching for __array_traits in the source code, we see: 

template<typename _Tp, std::size_t _Nm>
struct __array_traits
{
    typedef _Tp _Type[_Nm];

    static constexpr _Tp&
    _S_ref(const _Type& __t, std::size_t __n) noexcept
    { return const_cast<_Tp&>(__t[__n]); }
};

The two lines of code above can be understood as the following:

typedef _Tp _Type[100];
typedef _Type _M_elems;  // ​一个​含有​100​个​元素​的​数组​。

In actual code, if we want to define an array, we can write: 

int a[100];
//​或者​
typedef int T[100];
typedef T a;
Compared with tr1, the handling of the passed-in size is more complex: template partial specialization is used to handle the case where the passed size is 0.

template<typename _Tp, std::size_t _Nm>
struct __array_traits
{
    typedef _Tp _Type[_Nm];

    static constexpr _Tp&
    _S_ref(const _Type& __t, std::size_t __n) noexcept
    { return const_cast<_Tp&>(__t[__n]); }
};

template<typename _Tp>
struct __array_traits<_Tp, 0>
{
    struct _Type { };

    static constexpr _Tp&
    _S_ref(const _Type&, std::size_t) noexcept
    { return *static_cast<_Tp*>(nullptr); }
};

docs.title: STL string deep dive
docs.text:
When we use C++, we are fairly familiar with the basics of the library, especially std::string, which is used to create strings in C++. This is undoubtedly an improvement over the old C-style “strings” (character arrays terminated with a null character). However, the C++ standard library introduced more useful components in C++17 and C++20 that can help you write more efficient code.

In the header, the std::basic_string class is a template class that provides specializations for various string types, including std::string for common strings (i.e. std::basic_string) and std::wstring for wide strings (i.e. std::basic_string).

There are also fixed-width specific strings, such as std::u32string (i.e. std::basic_string) and std::u16string (i.e. std::basic_string).

In C++20, char8_t was introduced, which also brought std::u8string (i.e. std::basic_string). I don't know why we had to wait until C++20 for char8_t, so let me ask a question: which standard introduced char16_t and char32_t? See you in the comments

docs.title: C++11
docs.text:
Under the C++11 standard, string handling relies mainly on the std::string class, a dynamically memory-allocated string class. In addition, new fixed-width string types such as std::u32string and std::u16string were introduced, providing better support for handling Unicode characters.

#include <iostream>
#include <string>

int main() {
    // ​使用​std::string
    std::string str = "Hello, C++11!";

    // ​使用​std::u32string​和​std::u16string
    std::u32string u32str = U"Hello, Unicode!";
    std::u16string u16str = u"Hello, Unicode!";

    std::cout << str << std::endl;
    std::wcout << u32str << std::endl;
    std::wcout << u16str << std::endl;

    return 0;
}

docs.title: C++17
docs.text:
In C++17, the header was introduced, providing a lightweight read-only alternative to using the string types from the header. These string views are similar to the strings described previously. For example, the equivalent of std::u32string is std::u32string_view (i.e. std::basic_string_view).

This is particularly useful in functions that need to read a string but not modify it. Instead of creating a copy of the string for the function, we can simply take a view of an existing string! Moreover, is very flexible: not only can C++-style strings be converted to string views, even C-style strings can be converted to string views. Here is an example demonstrating simple usage of std::string_view: 

#include <iostream>
#include <string>
#include <string_view>

void printString(std::string_view str) {
  std::cout << str << std::endl;
}

int main() {
  std::string_view strv{"strv"}; // C++ string_view
  printString(strv);

  std::string str{"str"}; // C++ string
  printString(str);

  char cstr[] = "cstr"; // C-style string
  printString(cstr);

  return 0;
}

Output:

strv
str
cstr

In this example, the printString function takes a std::string_view as its parameter, which makes this function very lightweight and flexible, because no copies of any string are made; the function can be used in all sorts of ways by passing both C- and C++-style strings.

docs.title: C++20
docs.text:
In C++20, several new and useful member functions were introduced, including starts_with(…) and ends_with(…). As the names suggest, these functions determine whether a string (or string view) starts/ends with a certain character or a certain std::string_view. Here is a simple example:

#include <cassert>
#include <string>
#include <string_view>

int main() {
  const std::string str{"Hello World!"};

  assert(str.starts_with('H'));
  assert(str.ends_with('!'));

  assert(str.starts_with("Hello")); // ​隐式​转换​为​std::string_view
  assert(str.ends_with("World!")); // ​隐式​转换​为​std::string_view

  return 0;
}

docs.title: C++23
docs.text:
C++23 introduced contains, used to check whether a string contains a specified substring.

// ​这是​一个​假设​的​C++23​示例​，​实际上​并​不可​用​
#include <iostream>
#include <string>

int main() {
    std::string str = "C++23 introduces contains function.";

    if (str.contains("introduces")) {
        std::cout << "The string contains 'introduces'." << std::endl;
    } else {
        std::cout << "The string does not contain 'introduces'." << std::endl;
    }

    return 0;
}

https://en.cppreference.com/w/cpp/string/basic_string/contains

docs.title: Conclusion
docs.text: When working with strings in new C++ code, you should aim to make the code as flexible and memory-efficient as possible. Using can greatly help with these efforts. In addition, consider using the latest string member functions such as starts_with and ends_with to get readable and easy-to-implement string parsing code. And C++23 makes the contains check even simpler — things keep getting more modern.

docs.title: STL string interview questions in depth
docs.text:
Today I am sharing a string-related interview question with a total of 4 cases. You can leave a comment in the discussion section saying what will happen in each of these four places.

Everyone should be quite familiar with std::string, and std::string_view is a view introduced after C++17 — look it up if you are not familiar with it. Below are two literals, a string literal and a string_view literal, represented by s and sv.

The first two questions both involve a function returning a std::string_view, but with a difference: one is based on a c-style string, the other on a string.

The last two questions involve construction from a string literal and a string_view literal.

Alright, the problem is now described clearly — see you in the comments~

std::string_view getBar() {
  std::string b{"it is bar."};
  return b;
}

std::string_view getFoo() {
  return "It is foo.";
}

using namespace std::string_literals;
using namespace std::string_view_literals;
std::cout << getFoo() << std::endl;   // 1
std::cout << getBar() << std::endl;   // 2
std::string_view svf{"Hello foo"s};  
std::cout << svf << std::endl;              // 3
std::string_view svff{"Hello foo"sv};

docs.title: STL deque source code analysis | C++​那些​事
docs.text: Last updated：2026-10-13

docs.title: 0.Introduction
docs.text:
A deque is a segmented, continuous linear space open at both ends (simply put: a double-ended queue); elements can be inserted and removed at both the front and the back.

The biggest differences between deque and vector are:

  • deque allows inserting or removing elements at the front in constant time;

  • deque is a segmented continuous linear space, and a new segment of space can be added at any time;

Unlike vector, which — when memory runs short — must reallocate, copy data, and free the original space, deque avoids that; however, deque's iterator design is more complex than vector's, because its iterators cannot be ordinary pointers, so prefer vector when possible.

docs.title: 1.The deque controller
docs.text:
To the user, deque appears to use continuous space, but it is in fact a segmented continuous linear space. To manage the segmented space, the deque container introduces a map, called the controller: the map is a contiguous space whose every element is a pointer to a buffer, and the buffers are what actually store the deque's data.

In the figure above, buffer denotes a buffer, and the contiguous stretch of space shown as map size is the controller.

The controller holds map size, pointers to buffers, and the deque's start and finish iterators.

_Tp     **_M_map;
size_t      _M_map_size;
iterator    _M_start;
iterator    _M_finish;

Since a buffer is itself referenced via a pointer, _Tp is a pointer to a pointer.

deque inherits from _Deque_base, and _Deque_base contains an _M_impl.

From the figure below and the description above, we can see that the controller is implemented by _Deque_impl.

And deque uses the base class _Deque_base to accomplish memory management and controller management.

docs.title: 2.A sophisticated iterator
docs.text:
For deque, its iterator design is excellent!

As shown in the figure below:

First, a look at the more important members:

typedef _Tp             **_Map_pointer;
_Tp     *_M_cur;
_Tp     *_M_first;
_Tp     *_M_last;
_Map_pointer    _M_node;

What exactly are these? Judging by their names, the meaning is easy to grasp. For deque, which is a segmented continuous space, when the iterator performs operations, _M_cur points to the concrete element, _M_first points to the first element of the current buffer, _M_last points to the last element (not a valid element), and _M_node points into the controller. Hence it is a pointer to a pointer.

For example, when the iterator performs a ++ operation and the current buffer is exhausted, a pointer is needed that can go back to the controller, fetch the next buffer, reset the positions of the _M_first and _M_last pointers, and point _M_cur to the designated position in the new buffer.

Let's return to the figure from the beginning:

The iterator at the very top is the block diagram of the pointers above.

So how is the buffer size computed?

In the source code, the computation is based on the passed-in type: if the passed type is smaller than 512 bytes, the buffersize is 512/sizeof(_Tp); if it exceeds 512, it is 1.

static size_t _S_buffer_size()
_GLIBCXX_NOEXCEPT
{
    return(__deque_buf_size( sizeof(_Tp) ) );
}
The __deque_buf_size implementation

#ifndef _GLIBCXX_DEQUE_BUF_SIZE
#define _GLIBCXX_DEQUE_BUF_SIZE 512
#endif
inline size_t
__deque_buf_size( size_t
            __size )
{
    return(__size < _GLIBCXX_DEQUE_BUF_SIZE
            ? size_t( _GLIBCXX_DEQUE_BUF_SIZE / __size ) : size_t( 1 ) );
}
The previous few sections mentioned the traits extractor technique; every iterator needs to embed the following five typedefs:

typedef std::random_access_iterator_tag iterator_category;
typedef _Tp             value_type;
typedef _Ptr                pointer;
typedef _Ref                reference;
typedef ptrdiff_t           difference_type;

From this we can also tell that deque's iterator is a random access iterator: random_access_iterator_tag.

vector's iterator is this same one; as teacher ​侯捷​ explains, a contiguous buffer is a vector, which coincides with the iterator's tag type.

Now let's look at some operator overloads of this powerful iterator:

The detailed explanations are given inside the code.

Dereference operators

reference
operator*() const
_GLIBCXX_NOEXCEPT
{
    return(*_M_cur);
}


pointer
operator->() const
_GLIBCXX_NOEXCEPT
{
    return(_M_cur);
}
Of course, the -> above could also be implemented by directly calling the * operator, for example:

pointer
operator->() const
_GLIBCXX_NOEXCEPT
{
    return &(operator*());
}

The ++ and -- operators

// ​前置​++​操作符​
_Self &
operator++()
_GLIBCXX_NOEXCEPT
{
    // ​先​++，​判断​是否​到​了​buffer​的​末尾​，​如果​到​了​末尾​，​就要​跳到​下​一个​buffer。
    ++_M_cur;
    if ( _M_cur == _M_last ) // _M_last​指向​的​不是​有效​元素​，​保留​节点​  
    {
        _M_set_node( _M_node + 1 );
        _M_cur = _M_first;
    }
    return(*this);
}

// ​后置​++​操作符​
_Self
operator++( int )
_GLIBCXX_NOEXCEPT
{
    _Self __tmp = *this;
    ++*this;
    return(__tmp);
}

// ​前置​--​操作符​
_Self &
operator--()
_GLIBCXX_NOEXCEPT
{
    // ​先​判断​是否​到​了​起始​位置​，​如果​到​了​，​由于​需要​进行​--​操作​，​那么​就​应该​进入​前​一个​buffer
    if ( _M_cur == _M_first )
    {
        _M_set_node( _M_node - 1 );
        _M_cur = _M_last;
    }
    --_M_cur;
    return(*this);
} //​先​在​容器​头部​插入​与​第一个​元素​相同​的​元素​

// ​后置​--​操作符​
_Self
operator--( int )
_GLIBCXX_NOEXCEPT
{
    _Self __tmp = *this;    /* ​定义​一个​副本​ */
    --*this;                /* ​迭代​器自减​操作​ */
    return(__tmp);
}

The jump-n-distance operators

/*
* ​实现​随机​取​,​迭代​器​可以​直接​跳跃​n​个​距离​
* ​将​迭代​器​前移​n​个​距离​,​当​n​负值​时​就​为​下面​的​operator-=​操作​
*/
_Self &
operator+=( difference_type __n )

_GLIBCXX_NOEXCEPT
{
    const difference_type __offset = __n + (_M_cur - _M_first);
    /*
        * ​若​前移​n​个​距离​后​，​目标​依然​在​同一个​缓冲区​
        * ​则​直接​前移​n​个​距离​
        */
    if ( __offset >= 0 && __offset < difference_type( _S_buffer_size() ) )
        _M_cur += __n;
    else {
        /*
            * ​若​前移​n​个​距离​后​,​目标​超出​了​缓冲区​范围​
            * __offset>0   __offset / difference_type(_S_buffer_size())​计算​向​后​移动​多少​个​缓冲区​
            * __offset<=0  -difference_type((-__offset - 1) / _S_buffer_size()) - 1​计算​向前​移动​多少​个​缓冲区​
            */
        const difference_type __node_offset =
            __offset > 0 ? __offset / difference_type( _S_buffer_size() )
            : -difference_type( (-__offset - 1)
                        / _S_buffer_size() ) - 1;
        /* ​调整​到​正确​的​缓冲区​,​此时​_M_first​已经​修改​了​ */
        _M_set_node( _M_node + __node_offset );
        /* ​修改​为​正确​的​指针​位置​ */
        _M_cur = _M_first + (__offset - __node_offset
                        * difference_type( _S_buffer_size() ) );
    }
    return(*this);
}
The operators below are all implemented by calling the += operator above:

/*
    * ​操作符​+​重载​
    * ​返回​操作​之后​的​副本​
    */
_Self
operator+( difference_type __n ) const
_GLIBCXX_NOEXCEPT
{
    _Self __tmp = *this;
    /* ​调用​operator+=​操作​ */
    return(__tmp += __n);
}


/* ​利用​operator+=​操作​实现​ */
_Self &
operator-=( difference_type __n )
_GLIBCXX_NOEXCEPT
{
    return(*this += -__n);
}


/*
    * ​操作符​-​重载​
    * ​返回​操作​之后​的​副本​
    */
_Self
operator-( difference_type __n ) const
_GLIBCXX_NOEXCEPT
{
    _Self __tmp = *this;    /*  ​保存​副本​ */
    return(__tmp -= __n);   /* ​调用​operator-=​操作符​ */
}


/* ​返回​指定​位置​的​元素​，​即​实现​随机存取​ */
reference
operator[]( difference_type __n ) const
_GLIBCXX_NOEXCEPT
{
    return(*(*this + __n) );    /* ​该​函数调用​operator+,operator* */
}

Buffer jumping

The ++ and -- operators above call the _M_set_node function, whose role is to jump between buffers, updating the pointers _M_node, _M_first, and _M_last.

/**
    *  Prepares to traverse new_node.  Sets everything except
    *  _M_cur, which should therefore be set by the caller
    *  immediately afterwards, based on _M_first and _M_last.
    */
void
_M_set_node( _Map_pointer __new_node )
_GLIBCXX_NOEXCEPT
{
    _M_node     = __new_node;                                           /* ​指向​新​的​节点​ */
    _M_first    = *__new_node;                                          /* ​指向​新​节点​的​头部​ */
    _M_last     = _M_first + difference_type( _S_buffer_size() );       /* ​指向​新​节点​的​尾部​ */
}
With that, we have finished explaining the implementation details of deque's iterator.

docs.title: 3.deque
docs.text:
The begin() function

Returns _M_start.

iterator
begin()
_GLIBCXX_NOEXCEPT
{
    return(this->_M_impl._M_start);
}

The end() function

Returns _M_finish.

iterator
end()
_GLIBCXX_NOEXCEPT
{
    return(this->_M_impl._M_finish);
}

The size() function

size_type
size() const

_GLIBCXX_NOEXCEPT
{
    return(this->_M_impl._M_finish - this->_M_impl._M_start);
}

The resize() function

Based on the passed-in size: if it exceeds the total size, reallocate and expand by __new_size-size() of space; otherwise delete size()-__new_size of data. For example, with 20 slots now, resize(12) removes the data in the last 8 slots and frees that space.

void
resize( size_type __new_size )
{
    const size_type __len = size();
    if ( __new_size > __len )
        _M_default_append( __new_size - __len );
    else if ( __new_size < __len )
        _M_erase_at_end( this->_M_impl._M_start
                    + difference_type( __new_size ) );
}

The empty() function

Just compare the two pointer positions.

bool
empty() const

_GLIBCXX_NOEXCEPT
{
    return(this->_M_impl._M_finish == this->_M_impl._M_start);
}

The back function

reference
back()
_GLIBCXX_NOEXCEPT       // ​指向​finish​的​前​一个​位置​
{
    iterator __tmp = end();
    --__tmp;
    return(*__tmp);
}

The push_front function

void
push_front( const value_type &__x )
{
    //​若​当前​缓冲区​存在​可用​空间​
    if ( this->_M_impl._M_start._M_cur != this->_M_impl._M_start._M_first )
    {
        this->_M_impl.construct( this->_M_impl._M_start._M_cur - 1, __x );// ​直接​构造​对象​
        --this->_M_impl._M_start._M_cur;    // ​调整​指针​所指​位置​
    } else
        _M_push_front_aux( __x );   // ​需​分配​一段​新​的​连续​空间​
}

The push_back function

void
push_back( const value_type &__x )
{
    //​若​当前​缓冲区​存在​可用​空间​
    if ( this->_M_impl._M_finish._M_cur
            != this->_M_impl._M_finish._M_last - 1 )
    {
        this->_M_impl.construct( this->_M_impl._M_finish._M_cur, __x ); // ​直接​构造​对象​
        ++this->_M_impl._M_finish._M_cur;       //​调整​指针​所指​位置​
    } else     // ​若​当前​缓冲区​不​存在​可用​空间​
    // ​需​分配​一段​新​的​连续​空间​
        _M_push_back_aux( __x );
}
The corresponding pop operations are the reverse of the above.

The insert() function

The insert function is rather interesting: based on the passed iterator position, it checks whether it is at the beginning or the end — at the beginning it directly calls push_front, at the end it directly calls push_back, otherwise it inserts the element directly into the container.

template <typename _Tp, typename _Alloc>
typename deque<_Tp, _Alloc>::iterator
deque<_Tp, _Alloc>::
insert(iterator __position, const value_type& __x)
{
        if (__position._M_cur == this->_M_impl._M_start._M_cur)   
    {
        push_front(__x);
        return this->_M_impl._M_start;
    }
        else if (__position._M_cur == this->_M_impl._M_finish._M_cur)
    {
        push_back(__x);
        iterator __tmp = this->_M_impl._M_finish;
        --__tmp;
        return __tmp;
    }
        else  //​否则​在​容器​直接插入​数据​
        return _M_insert_aux(__position._M_const_cast(), __x);
}
And the function above that inserts the element directly into the container computes the insertion point: if it is relatively close to the front, insertion happens at the front; if close to the back, at the back:

template<typename _Tp, typename _Alloc>
typename deque<_Tp, _Alloc>::iterator
deque<_Tp, _Alloc>::
_M_insert_aux(iterator __pos, const value_type& __x)
{
    value_type __x_copy = __x; // XXX copy
    difference_type __index = __pos - this->_M_impl._M_start;  //​计算​插入​点​之前​元素​个数​
    if (static_cast<size_type>(__index) < size() / 2)   //​若​插入​点​之前​的​元素​较​少​
        {
        push_front(_GLIBCXX_MOVE(front())); //​先​在​容器​头部​插入​与​第一个​元素​相同​的​元素​
        iterator __front1 = this->_M_impl._M_start;
        ++__front1;
        iterator __front2 = __front1;
        ++__front2;
        __pos = this->_M_impl._M_start + __index;
        iterator __pos1 = __pos;
        ++__pos1;
        _GLIBCXX_MOVE3(__front2, __pos1, __front1); // ​元素​搬移​
        }
    else
    {
        push_back(_GLIBCXX_MOVE(back()));
        iterator __back1 = this->_M_impl._M_finish;
        --__back1;
        iterator __back2 = __back1;
        --__back2;
        __pos = this->_M_impl._M_start + __index;
        _GLIBCXX_MOVE_BACKWARD3(__pos, __back2, __back1);
    }
    *__pos = _GLIBCXX_MOVE(__x_copy);       // ​在​安插​点上​设定​新值​
    return __pos;
}
